Un élément de $S$ est dit irréductible s'il ne peut pas s'écrire comme un produit d'au moins deux éléments de $\mathbb{N}$. Montrer qu'il existe $N>0$ tel que tout élément de $S$ s'écrit comme produit d'au plus $N$ éléments irréductibles de $S$ (pas forcément distincts).

positive_text: Soit $p(k)$ le plus petit nombre premier ne divisant pas l'entier $k$. On définit une suite $\left(a_{n}\right)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ en choisissant $a_0$ comme un entier positif, puis en définissant $a_{n+1}$ comme le plus petit entier positif différent de $a_0, \ldots, a_n$ tel que $a_{n}^{a_{n+1}} - 1$ est divisible par $p\left(a_{n}\right)$. Démontrer que tout entier positif apparaît une et une seule fois dans cette suite.

negatives.text: Soit $p(k)$ le plus petit nombre premier ne divisant pas l'entier $k$. On définit une suite $\left(a_{n}\right)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ en choisissant $a_0$ comme un entier positif, puis en définissant $a_{n+1}$ comme le plus petit entier positif différent de $a_0, \ldots, a_n$ tel que $a_{n}^{a_{n+1}} + 1$ est divisible par $p\left(a_{n}\right)$. Démontrer que tout entier positif apparaît une et une seule fois dans cette suite.

Soit $p(k)$ le plus petit nombre premier ne divisant pas l'entier $k$. On définit une suite $\left(a_{n}\right)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ en choisissant $a_0$ comme un entier positif, puis en définissant $a_{n+1}$ comme le plus petit entier positif différent de $a_0, \ldots, a_n$ tel que $a_{n}^{a_{n+1}} - 1$ est divisible par $p\left(a_{n+1}\right)$. Démontrer que tout entier positif apparaît une et une seule fois dans cette suite.

positive_text: Soient $n$ cercles de rayon identique placés dans un plan de telle sorte qu'aucune paire de cercles ne soit tangente, et que l'ensemble des cercles forme un réseau connecté (on peut toujours passer d'un cercle à un autre sans quitter les cercles). Appelons $S$ l'ensemble des points où deux cercles se croisent. Démontrer que le nombre de points dans $S$ est au moins égal à $n$.

negatives.text: Soient $\mathrm{C}_{1}, \mathrm{C}_{2}, \ldots \mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{n}}$ des cercles de m\^eme rayon disposés dans le plan de sorte qu'ils ne soient jamais tangents 2 à 2 et qu'ils soient tous disjoints (autrement dit, les cercles ne se chevauchent pas). En notant $S$ l'ensemble des points d'intersection des cercles, montrer que $|S| \geqslant n$.

Soient $\mathrm{C}_{1}, \mathrm{C}_{2}, \ldots \mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{n}}$ des cercles de rayons différents disposés dans le plan de sorte qu'ils ne soient jamais tangents 2 à 2 et qu'ils forment un chemin connecté. En notant $S$ l'ensemble des points d'intersection des cercles, montrer que $|S| \geqslant n$.

Soient $\mathrm{C}_{1}, \mathrm{C}_{2}, \ldots \mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{n}}$ des cercles de m\^eme rayon disposés dans le plan de sorte qu'ils ne soient jamais tangents 2 à 2 et qu'ils forment un chemin connecté. En notant $S$ l'ensemble des points d'intersection des cercles, montrer que $|S| \geqslant 2n$.

positive_text: Soit $ABC$ un triangle. On note $\omega_{A}$ le cercle $A$-exinscrit, qui est tangent à $BC$, à la demi-droite $[AC)$ et à la demi-droite $[AB)$. On appelle $A_{1}$, $B_{1}$, $C_{1}$ les points de contact de $\omega_{A}$ sur ces trois objets. On note $P$ le milieu du segment reliant $B_{1}$ à $C_{1}$. La droite reliant $A_{1}$ à $P$ recoupe $\omega_{A}$ en un point $X$. On trace la tangente au cercle circonscrit de $ABC$ au point $A$ et la tangente à $\omega_{A}$ au point $X$. Ces deux tangentes se coupent en un point $R$. Démontrer que $RX = RP$.

negatives.text: Soit $ABC$ un triangle et soient $A_{1}$, $B_{1}$ et $C_{1}$ les points de contact respectifs du cercle $A$-exinscrit, noté $\omega_{A}$, avec le côté $BC$ et les demi-droites $[AC)$ et $[AB)$. Soit $P$ le milieu du segment $[B_{1}C_{1}]$. La droite $(A_{1}P)$ recoupe le cercle $\omega_{A}$ au point $X$. La tangente au cercle circonscrit au triangle $ABC$ au point $B$ et la tangente au cercle $\omega_{A}$ au point $X$ se coupent en $R$. Montrer que $RX = RP$.

Soit $ABC$ un triangle et soient $A_{1}$, $B_{1}$ et $C_{1}$ les points de contact respectifs du cercle $A$-exinscrit, noté $\omega_{A}$, avec le côté $BC$ et les demi-droites $[AC)$ et $[AB)$. Soit $P$ le milieu du segment $[B_{1}C_{1}]$. La droite $(A_{1}P)$ recoupe le cercle $\omega_{A}$ au point $X$. La tangente au cercle circonscrit au triangle $ABC$ au point $A$ et la tangente au cercle $\omega_{A}$ au point $A_{1}$ se coupent en $R$. Montrer que $RX = RP$.

Soit $ABC$ un triangle et soient $A_{1}$, $B_{1}$ et $C_{1}$ les points de contact respectifs du cercle $A$-exinscrit, noté $\omega_{A}$, avec le côté $BC$ et les demi-droites $[AC)$ et $[AB)$. Soit $P$ le milieu du segment $[B_{1}C_{1}]$. La droite $(A_{1}P)$ recoupe le cercle $\omega_{A}$ au point $X$. La tangente au cercle circonscrit au triangle $ABC$ au point $A$ et la tangente au cercle $\omega_{A}$ au point $X$ se coupent en $R$. Montrer que $RX = RA$.

positive_text: Soit $n$ un entier naturel tel que $n \geq 2$. On note $d$ le plus grand diviseur de $n$ différent de $n$ lui-même. On suppose que $d > 1$. Montrer que la somme $n + d$ n'est pas une puissance de 2.

negatives.text: Soit $n$ un entier naturel tel que $n \geq 2$. On note $d$ le plus petit diviseur de $n$ différent de $n$ lui-même. On suppose que $d > 1$. Montrer que la somme $n + d$ n'est pas une puissance de 2.
Soit $n$ un entier naturel tel que $n \geq 2$. On note $d$ le plus grand diviseur de $n$ différent de $n$ lui-même. On suppose que $d > 1$. Montrer que la somme $n - d$ n'est pas une puissance de 2.

positive_text: Soient $x$ et $y$ deux nombres réels. On sait que $2x + x^{2} = 2y + y^{2}$. Démontrez que si $x$ est un entier (positif, négatif, ou nul), alors $y$ est aussi un entier.

negatives.text: Soient $a$ et $b$ deux réels. Supposons que $2a + a^{2} = 2b + b^{2}$. Montrer que si $a$ est un entier pair, alors $b$ est aussi un entier pair.
Soient $a$ et $b$ deux réels. Supposons que $2a + a^{2} = 2b + b^{2}$. Montrer que si $a$ est un entier, alors $b$ est un nombre rationnel.
Soient $a$ et $b$ deux réels. Supposons que $a^{2} = b^{2}$. Montrer que si $a$ est un entier, alors $b$ est aussi un entier.

positive_text: Trouve tous les nombres entiers positifs ou nuls $n$ tels que $2023 + n!$ est un carré parfait.

negatives.text: Trouve tous les nombres entiers positifs ou nuls $n$ tels que $2023 \times n!$ est un carré parfait.
Trouve tous les nombres entiers positifs ou nuls $n$ tels que $2023 - n!$ est un carré parfait.
Trouve tous les nombres entiers positifs ou nuls $n$ tels que $2023 + (n+1)!$ est un carré parfait.

positive_text:

$$
\left(2 x^{2}+y z\right)\left(2 y^{2}+x z\right)\left(2 z^{2}+x y\right)=26 x^{2} y^{2} z^{2}
$$

negatives.text:

positive_text:
Soient $x$, $y$ et $z$ trois nombres réels tels que $0 \leq x, y, z \leq 2$. Démontrer que
$$
(x-y)(y-z)(x-z) \leq 2
$$

negatives.text:
Soient $a$, $b$ et $c$ des réels tels que $0 \leqslant a, b, c \leqslant 2$. Montrer que
$$
(a-b)(b-c)(a-c) \leqslant 4
$$

Soient $a$, $b$ et $c$ des réels tels que $0 \leqslant a, b, c \leqslant 2$. Montrer que

positive_text:
Soit $n$ un entier naturel tel que $n \geq 2$ et $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$ des nombres r\'eels compris entre 0 et 1. Trouver la valeur maximale possible pour le plus petit des nombres
$$
 a_1 - a_1 a_2,\ a_2 - a_2 a_3,\ \ldots,\ a_n - a_n a_1.
$$

negatives.text:

$$
 a_{1}-a_{1} a_{2},\ a_{2}-a_{2} a_{3},\ \ldots,\ a_{n}-a_{n} a_{1}.
$$

Soit $n \geqslant 2$ et $a_{1}, \ldots, a_{n} \in [0,1]$ des r\'eels. D\'eterminer la valeur maximale que peut prendre la somme des nombres
$$
 a_{1}-a_{1} a_{2},\ a_{2}-a_{2} a_{3},\ \ldots,\ a_{n}-a_{n} a_{1}.
$$

$$

$$

positive_text: Un nombre entier $n$ au moins égal à $2$ est écrit sur un tableau. Chaque jour, une personne choisit un nombre premier $p$ qui divise $n$, efface $n$ et écrit à la place $n + \frac{n}{p}$. Démontrer que le nombre $3$ sera choisi un nombre infini de fois.

negatives.text: Un entier $n \geqslant 2$ est écrit au tableau. Chaque jour, quelqu'un choisit $p$ un diviseur premier de l'entier écrit $n$ au tableau, efface celui-ci et écrit $n-\frac{n}{p}$ à la place. Montrer que $p=3$ est choisi une infinité de fois.

Un entier $n \geqslant 2$ est écrit au tableau. Chaque jour, quelqu'un choisit $p$ un diviseur premier de l'entier écrit $n$ au tableau, efface celui-ci et écrit $n+\frac{n}{p^2}$ à la place. Montrer que $p=3$ est choisi une infinité de fois.

Un entier $n \geqslant 2$ est écrit au tableau. Chaque jour, quelqu'un choisit $p$ un diviseur premier de l'entier écrit $n$ au tableau, efface celui-ci et écrit $n+\frac{n}{p}$ à la place. Montrer que $p=2$ est choisi une infinité de fois.

positive_text: Pour tous nombres réels strictement positifs $x$, $y$, $z$, démontrer l'inégalité suivante : $$\frac{x}{9 y z+1} + \frac{y}{9 z x+1} + \frac{z}{9 x y+1} \geq \frac{x+y+z}{1+(x+y+z)^2}.$$

negatives.text: Pour tous nombres réels strictement positifs $x$, $y$, $z$, démontrer l'inégalité suivante : $$\frac{x}{9 y z+1} + \frac{y}{9 z x+1} + \frac{z}{9 x y+1} \geq \frac{1}{1+(x+y+z)^2}.$$

positive_text: Soient $x, y, z$ trois nombres réels positifs. Démontrer que $$\frac{x^{4}+1}{y^{3}+y^{2}+y}+\frac{y^{4}+1}{z^{3}+z^{2}+z}+\frac{z^{4}+1}{x^{3}+x^{2}+x} \geq 2.$$

positive_text: Dans un triangle $ABC$, soit $\omega$ le cercle inscrit, et $D$, $E$, $F$ les points où $\omega$ touche les côtés $BC$, $CA$, et $AB$ respectivement. Tracer la perpendiculaire à $BC$ passant par $C$; elle coupe la droite $EF$ au point $M$. De même, tracer la perpendiculaire à $BC$ passant par $B$; elle coupe $EF$ au point $N$. Ensuite, tracer les droites $DM$ et $DN$; elles coupent à nouveau le cercle $\omega$ en $P$ et $Q$ respectivement. Démontrer que les distances $DP$ et $DQ$ sont égales.

negatives.text: Dans un triangle $ABC$, soit $\omega$ le cercle inscrit, et $D$, $E$, $F$ les points où $\omega$ touche les côtés $BC$, $CA$, et $AB$ respectivement. La perpendiculaire à $(BC)$ en $C$ coupe la droite $(EF)$ en $M$ et la perpendiculaire à $(BC)$ en $A$ coupe la droite $(EF)$ en $N$. La droite $(DM)$ recoupe $\omega$ en $P$ et la droite $(DN)$ recoupe $\omega$ en $Q$. Montrer que $DP = DQ$.

positive_text: Zwei Sehnen, $AC$ und $BD$, in einem Kreis mit Mittelpunkt $M$, schneiden sich im Punkt $P$. Der Umkreis des Dreiecks $PBC$ hat seinen Mittelpunkt in $E$, und der Umkreis des Dreiecks $PDA$ seinen Mittelpunkt in $F$. Die beiden Umkreise schneiden sich ein zweites Mal im Punkt $Q$. Zeige, dass die Strecken $MF$ und $QE$ gleich lang sind.

positive_text:

a) Zeige, dass $S$ niemals eine ganze Zahl sein kann.
b) Bestimme (mit Erklärung!) für $b = 2 \cdot (a - 1)$ eine Zahl $k$ aus den natürlichen Zahlen so, dass $S$ zwischen $k$ und $k+1$ liegt.

positive_text: Die Zahlen von $1$ bis $n^2$ werden auf die Felder eines $n \times n$-Schachbretts zufällig verteilt ($n \geq 2$). In jeder Zeile und in jeder Spalte vergleichen wir alle Paare von Zahlen. Für jedes Paar berechnen wir den Quotienten, indem wir die größere Zahl durch die kleinere teilen. Die kleinste dieser Quotienten nennen wir die Charakteristik $C$ der Anordnung. Was ist die größtmögliche Charakteristik $C$, die in so einer Anordnung vorkommen kann? (Deine Antwort soll begründet werden.)

negatives.text: Die natürlichen Zahlen von $1$ bis $n^2$ werden zufällig auf die Felder eines $n \times n$-Quadrats verteilt ($n \geq 2$). Für jedes Paar von Zahlen innerhalb einer Reihe oder einer Diagonalen dividieren wir die größere durch die kleinere Zahl. Der kleinste dieser $n^2(n-1)$ Quotienten werde als Charakteristik $C$ der zufälligen Anordnung bezeichnet. Welches ist der größtmögliche Wert für $C$? (Die Antwort ist zu begründen.)

Der kleinste dieser $n^2(n-1)$ Unterschiede werde als Charakteristik $C$ der zufälligen Anordnung bezeichnet. Welches ist der größtmögliche Wert für $C$? (Die Antwort ist zu begründen.)

positive_text: Es seien $n$ reelle Zahlen $x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{n}$ und $n$ reelle Zahlen $y_{1}, y_{2}, \ldots, y_{n}$ gegeben. Spalte von $A$ ist. Zeige, dass dann $A = B$ gilt.

Zeige, dass dann $A = B$ gilt.

positive_text:
Sei $E = \{-1, 0, 1\}$ und $M$ eine Menge von Punkten im Koordinatensystem mit ganzzahligen Koordinaten. Alle Punkte in $M$ sollen durch Strecken verbunden werden, sodass es einen Weg zwischen jedem Paar von Punkten in $M$ gibt, wobei man nur die Strecken benutzen darf. Die Strecken dürfen dabei zusätzliche Punkte enthalten, die nicht in $M$ liegen.

Bestimme die kürzeste mögliche Gesamtlänge des Netzwerks von Strecken, wenn:

a) $M = \{(i, j) \mid i, j \in E$ und $i \cdot j = 0\}$

b) $M = \{(i, j) \mid i, j \in E\}$

negatives.text:
Sei $E = \{-1, 0, 1\}$ und $M$ eine Menge von Gitterpunkten der Ebene. Die Punkte aus $M$ sind so durch ein Streckennetz $(S)$ miteinander verbunden, dass man von jedem Punkt aus $M$ zu jedem anderen Punkt aus $M$ gelangen kann ohne $(S)$ zu verlassen. Dabei können die Strecken des Streckennetzes außer den Gitterpunkten auch andere Endpunkte enthalten. Man ermittle die kürzeste Gesamtlänge des Streckennetzes, falls:

a) $M = \{(i, j) \mid i, j \in E$ und $i \cdot j = 0\}$

b) $M = \{(i, j) \mid i, j \in E$ und $i^2 + j^2 = 1\}$

Bestimme alle Paare $(n, k)$, für die eine solche Färbung möglich ist.

positive_text: Ein reguläres $n$-Eck hat $n$ Ecken und $n$ Kanten. Die Ecken und Kanten sind im Uhrzeigersinn durchnummeriert von 1 bis $n$, wobei Kante $i$ direkt vor Ecke $i$ liegt. Jede Ecke $e_i$ und jede Kante $k_i$ wird mit einer nichtnegativen ganzen Zahl belegt. Die Bedingungen lauten: (1) Die Zahlen an den Ecken $(e_{1}, e_{2}, \ldots, e_{n})$ bilden eine Umordnung der Zahlen an den Kanten $(k_{1}, k_{2}, \ldots, k_{n})$. positive_text: Let $A$ be a set of positive numbers with only finitely many elements. Define a new set $B$ by taking all possible fractions $\frac{x}{y}$ where $x$ and $y$ are elements of $A$, and define another set $C$ by taking all possible products $xy$ where $x$ and $y$ are elements of $A$. If $|X|$ represents the number of elements in set $X$, prove that: $|A| \cdot |B| \le |C|^2$.

negatives.text: Let $A$ be a finite set of positive reals, let $B = \left\{\frac{x}{y}: x, y \in A\right\}$ and let $C = \left\{x + y: x, y \in A\right\}$. If we denote $\text{card}X = |X|$, show that: $|A| \cdot |B| \le |C|^2$.

positive_text: Consider an acute triangle $\triangle ABC$, with $AB < AC$, and let it be inscribed in a circle $c$ with center $O$ and radius $R$. positive_text: Imagine a group of students at a math competition, where friendship is mutual (if Alice is friends with Bob, then Bob is friends with Alice). A weakly-friendly circle is a group of $n \ge 3$ students $S_1, S_2, \dots, S_n$ where each student is not friends with the next one in the circle (i.e., $S_i$ is not friends with $S_{i+1}$, for $1 \le i \le n$, and $S_{n+1} = S_1$), and there are no other non-friend relationships among the students in the group. Now suppose this condition holds: For any student $P$, and any weakly-friendly circle $\mathcal{S}$ that does not include $P$, there is at most one student in $\mathcal{S}$ who is not friends with $P$. Prove that all students can be divided into three rooms such that any two students in the same room are friends.

negatives.text: In a mathematical competition some competitors are friends; friendship is always mutual. We say that $n \ge 3$ different competitors $A_1, A_2, \dots, A_n$ form a weakly-friendly circle if $A_i$ is not a friend of $A_{i+1}$, for $1 \le i \le n$ ($A_{n+1} = A_1$), and there are no other pairs of non-friends among the components of this cycle. The following property is satisfied: For every competitor $C$, and every weakly-friendly cycle $\mathcal{A}$ of competitors not including $C$, the set of competitors $D$ in $\mathcal{A}$ which are not friends of $C$ has at least one element. Prove that all competitors of this mathematical competition can be arranged into three rooms, such that every two competitors that are in the same rooms are friends.

positive_text: In triangle $\triangle ABC$, let $M$ be the midpoint of side $BC$. Outside the triangle, a parallelogram $BCDE$ is constructed such that $BE$ is parallel to $AM$ and half the length of $AM$. Prove that the line $EM$ goes through the midpoint of segment $AD$.

positive_text:

- For each position $i$, the number $a_i$ is between $0$ and $i$, inclusive.
- For each number $\kappa$, the sum $\binom{\kappa}{a_0} + \binom{\kappa}{a_1} + \dots + \binom{\kappa}{a_\kappa}$ equals $2^\kappa$.

Show that for any whole number $n$, there is some position $i$ where $a_i = n$.

negatives.text:

(\alpha) $0 \le \alpha_i \le i$, for every integer $i \ge 0$,

(\beta) $\binom{\kappa}{\alpha_0} + \binom{\kappa}{\alpha_1} + \dots + \binom{\kappa}{\alpha_{\kappa - 1}} = 2^\kappa$, for every integer $\kappa \ge 0$.

Prove that for every integer $n \ge 0$, there exists $i \ge 0$ such that $\alpha_i = n$.

Consider a function $f$ defined on the positive real numbers with these properties: (1) $f(1) = 1$, (2) $f(x + 1) = x f(x)$, and (3) $f(x) = 10^{g(x)}$, where $g(x)$ is a real-valued function satisfying $$ g(ty + (1-t)z) \leq t g(y) + (1-t) g(z) $$ for all real numbers $y$ and $z$ and for all $t$ such that $0 \leq t \leq 1$.
a. Show that $t [g(n) - g(n-1)] \leq g(n+t) - g(n) \leq t [g(n+1) - g(n)]$ for all integers $n$ and for all $t$ with $0 \leq t \leq 1$.
b. Show that $\frac{4}{3} \leq f\left(\frac{1}{2}\right) \leq \frac{4}{3} \sqrt{2}$.

positive_text:
Imagine $n$ points on a flat surface. All pairs of points are connected with a line segment (an edge), and each segment is painted one of $k$ available colors.

a. When there are 6 points and 3 colors, can you find a way to color the edges so that no triangle or loop is formed using edges of just one color?

b. Show that for any positive integer $k$, if the number of points $n$ is at least $2k + 1$, then no matter how the edges are colored, there must be at least one triangle or loop made up entirely of edges of a single color.

negatives.text:
There are $n$ vertices on a plane. A graph $G$ is formed by connecting every two vertices by exactly one edge, and painting all edges, each in one colour, chosen from $k$ given colours.

a. For $n = 6$ and $k = 3$, show that it is possible to paint the edges so that the graph contains no open path painted in one colour only.

b. Prove that for every positive integral value of $k$, if the number of vertices $n \ge 2k+1$, then it is always possible to find a mono-coloured closed circuit in $G$.

b. Prove that for every positive integral value of $k$, if the number of vertices $n \ge 2k$, then it is always possible to find a mono-coloured closed circuit in $G$.

ii. the diagonal $AC$ is longer than the diagonal $BD$.

positive_text: Let $I$ be the incenter and $O$ be the circumcenter of triangle $ABC$. Suppose triangle $ABC$ is not equilateral (so $I$ and $O$ are different points). Show that the angle $\angle AIO$ is less than or equal to $90^\circ$ exactly when $2BC$ is less than or equal to $AB + AC$.

negatives.text: Let $I$ and $O$ be the incentre and circumcentre of $\triangle ABC$, respectively. Assume $\triangle ABC$ is not equilateral (so $I \neq O$). Prove that $\angle BAO \leq 90^\circ$ if and only if $2BC \leq AB + CA$.

positive_text: Suppose $n$ subjects have been tested by a group of students ($n \ge 3$). In each subject, exactly three students scored the highest. Also, for any pair of subjects, there is exactly one student who scored the highest in both of those subjects. What is the smallest value of $n$ for which these conditions imply that one student scored the highest in all $n$ subjects?

negatives.text: Suppose $n$ subjects have been tested by a group of students ($n \ge 3$). In each subject, exactly three students scored the highest. What is the smallest value of $n$ for which these conditions imply that one student scored the highest in all $n$ subjects?

positive_text:
A positive integer $ n $ is called *good* if we can find two positive integers $ a $ and $ b $ such that $ a + b = n $ and $ ab $ is a multiple of $ n $. For example, $ 9 $ is good because $ 3 + 6 = 9 $ and $ 3 \times 6 $ is divisible by $ 9 $. Moreover, $ n $ is called *very good* if we can choose $ a $ and $ b $ to be different. So, $ 9 $ is very good.

a. Given that $ 2003 $ is a prime number, show that $ 2003 $ is not good.

b. Is $ 2002 $ good?

c. Find all positive integers that are good but not very good. Justify your answers.

negatives.text:

For instance, $ 9 $ is good since $ 3 + 6 = 9 $ and $ 3 \times 6 $ is divisible by $ 9 $. Furthermore, $ n $ is said to be *very good* if we can choose $ a $ and $ b $ to be distinct. Hence $ 9 $ is very good.

Let $K_1$ and $K_2$ be the circles which pass through $C$ and are tangent to $AB$ at $A$ and $B$ respectively. Let $K$ be the circle of radius $r$ which is externally tangent to $K_1$, $K_2$ and tangent to the line $AB$.

a. Express $r$ in terms of $a, b, c$ and $R$.

b. Suppose $r = \frac{R}{2}$. Find $\angle C$.

positive_text:
Let $D$ be a point on side $BC$ of triangle $ABC$ such that the sum of the lengths $AB$ and $BD$ is equal to the sum of the lengths $AC$ and $CD$. The segment $AD$ intersects the incircle of triangle $ABC$ at two points, $X$ and $Y$, with $X$ being closer to $A$. Let $E$ be the point where the incircle touches the side $BC$. Show that
(i) the segment $EY$ is perpendicular to $AD$,
(ii) the length of $XD$ is twice the length of $IA'$, where $I$ is the incenter of triangle $ABC$ and $A'$ is the midpoint of $BC$.

negatives.text:
Let $D$ be a point on side $BC$ of triangle $ABC$ such that $AB + BD = AC + CD$. The line segment $AD$ cuts the incircle of triangle $ABC$ at $X$ and $Y$ with $X$ closer to $A$. Let $E$ be the point of contact of the incircle of triangle $ABC$ on the side $AC$. Show that
(i) $EY$ is perpendicular to $AD$,
(ii) $XD = 2IA'$, where $I$ is the incentre of the triangle $ABC$ and $A'$ is the midpoint of $BC$.

Let $D$ be a point on side $BC$ of triangle $ABC$ such that $AB + BD = AC + CD$. The line segment $AD$ cuts the incircle of triangle $ABC$ at $X$ and $Y$ with $X$ closer to $A$. Let $E$ be the point of contact of the incircle of triangle $ABC$ on the side $BC$. Show that
(i) $EX$ is perpendicular to $AD$,
(ii) $XD = 2IA'$, where $I$ is the incentre of the triangle $ABC$ and $A'$ is the midpoint of $BC$.

Let $D$ be a point on side $BC$ of triangle $ABC$ such that $AB + BD = AC + CD$. The line segment $AD$ cuts the incircle of triangle $ABC$ at $X$ and $Y$ with $X$ closer to $A$. Let $E$ be the point of contact of the incircle of triangle $ABC$ on the side $BC$. Show that
(i) $EY$ is perpendicular to $AD$,
(ii) $XD = 2IB'$, where $I$ is the incentre of the triangle $ABC$ and $B'$ is the midpoint of $AC$.

positive_text: Suppose you have a four-sided figure $ABCD$ that can be drawn on a circle (a cyclic quadrilateral), and it is given that the sum of the lengths of sides $AD$ and $BC$ equals the length of side $AB$. Prove that the point where the angle bisectors of $\angle ADC$ and $\angle BCD$ meet lies somewhere along the line segment $AB$.

negatives.text: Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral such that $AD + BC = CD$. Show that the intersection of the bisectors of $\angle ADC$ and $\angle BCD$ is on line $AB$.
Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral such that $AD + BC = AB$. Show that the intersection of the bisectors of $\angle ADC$ and $\angle BCD$ is on line $CD$.
Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral such that $AD + BC = AB$. Show that the intersection of the bisectors of $\angle ABC$ and $\angle BCD$ is on line $AB$.

positive_text:
\text{Let } A, B, \text{ and } C \text{ be real numbers with the following properties:}
(i) \sin A \cos B + |\cos A \sin B| = \sin A |\cos A| + |\sin B \cos B|,
(ii) \tan C \text{ and } \cot C \text{ exist and are defined}.
\text{Find the smallest possible value of } (\tan C - \sin A)^2 + (\cot C - \cos B)^2.

negatives.text:
\text{Let } A, B, \text{ and } C \text{ be real numbers such that}
(i) \sin A \cos B + |\cos A \sin B| = \sin A |\cos A| + |\sin B \cos B|,
(ii) \tan C \text{ and } \cot C \text{ are defined}.
\text{Find the maximum value of } (\tan C - \sin A)^2 + (\cot C - \cos B)^2.

\text{Let } A, B, \text{ and } C \text{ be real numbers such that}
(i) \sin A \cos B + |\cos A \sin B| = \sin A |\cos A| + |\sin B \cos B|,
(ii) \tan C \text{ is defined, but } \cot C \text{ is not}.
\text{Find the minimum value of } (\tan C - \sin A)^2 + (\cot C - \cos B)^2.

\text{Let } A, B, \text{ and } C \text{ be real numbers such that}
(i) \sin A \cos B + |\cos A \sin B| = \sin A |\cos A| + |\sin B \cos B|,
(ii) \tan C \text{ and } \cot C \text{ are defined}.
\text{Find the minimum value of } (\tan C + \sin A)^2 + (\cot C + \cos B)^2.

positive_text: \text{Consider a triangle } ABC \text{ where side } AB \text{ is labeled } c, BC \text{ is labeled } a, \text{ and } CA \text{ is labeled } b. \text{ Prove that} $$\frac{\cos A}{a^3} + \frac{\cos B}{b^3} + \frac{\cos C}{c^3} \ge \frac{3}{2abc}.$

negatives.text: \text{Let } ABC \text{ be a triangle with } AB = c, BC = a \text{ and } CA = b. \text{ Show that} $$\frac{\cos A}{a^2} + \frac{\cos B}{b^2} + \frac{\cos C}{c^2} \ge \frac{3}{2abc}.$
\text{Let } ABC \text{ be a triangle with } AB = c, BC = a \text{ and } CA = b. \text{ Show that} $$\frac{\cos A}{a^3} + \frac{\cos B}{b^3} + \frac{\cos C}{c^3} \le \frac{3}{2abc}.$
\text{Let } ABC \text{ be a triangle with } AB = c, BC = a \text{ and } CA = b. \text{ Show that} $$\frac{\cos A}{a^3} + \frac{\cos B}{b^3} + \frac{\cos C}{c^3} \ge \frac{1}{2abc}.$

positive_text: In triangle $ABC$, where $AB = AC$, the incircle with center $O$ touches sides $BC$, $CA$, and $AB$ at points $K$, $L$, and $M$, respectively. Let $N$ be the point where lines $OL$ and $KM$ intersect, and let $Q$ be the point where lines $BN$ and $CA$ intersect. Let $P$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $A$ to the line $BQ$. Suppose the length of segment $BP$ is equal to the sum of the lengths of segments $AP$ and $2PQ$. Find the possible value(s) of the ratio $\frac{AB}{BC}$.

negatives.text: The incircle (with centre $O$) of an isosceles triangle $ABC$ with $AB = AC$ meets $BC$, $CA$, $AB$ at $K$, $L$, $M$ respectively. Let $N$ be the intersection of the lines $OL$ and $KM$, and let $Q$ be the intersection of the lines $BN$ and $CA$. Let $P$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $A$ to $BQ$. Suppose $BP = AP + PQ$. Determine the possible value(s) of $\frac{AB}{BC}$.

The incircle (with centre $O$) of an isosceles triangle $ABC$ with $AB = AC$ meets $BC$, $CA$, $AB$ at $K$, $L$, $M$ respectively. Let $N$ be the intersection of the lines $OL$ and $KM$, and let $Q$ be the intersection of the lines $BN$ and $CA$. Let $P$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $A$ to $BQ$. Suppose $BP = 2AP + PQ$. Determine the possible value(s) of $\frac{AB}{BC}$.

The incircle (with centre $O$) of an isosceles triangle $ABC$ with $AB = AC$ meets $BC$, $CA$, $AB$ at $K$, $L$, $M$ respectively. Let $N$ be the intersection of the lines $OL$ and $KM$, and let $Q$ be the intersection of the lines $BN$ and $CA$. Let $P$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $A$ to $BQ$. Suppose $BP = 3PQ$. Determine the possible value(s) of $\frac{AB}{BC}$.

positive_text:
Consider a right triangle $\triangle ABC$ where $\angle C = 90^\circ$. An altitude $CD$ is drawn from point $C$ to side $AB$, with $D$ lying on $AB$. Let $\omega$ be the circle that passes through points $B$, $C$, and $D$. Another circle $\omega_1$ lies inside triangle $ACD$, and touches the sides $AD$ and $AC$ at points $M$ and $N$, respectively. Additionally, $\omega_1$ is tangent to $\omega$.
(1) Prove that $BD \cdot CN + BC \cdot DM = CD \cdot BM$.
(2) Prove that $BM = BC$.

negatives.text:
Let $\triangle ABC$ be a right-angled triangle with $\angle C = 90^\circ$. $CD$ is the altitude from $C$ to $AB$, with $D$ on $AB$. $\omega$ is the circumcircle of $\triangle BCD$. $\omega_1$ is a circle situated in $\triangle ACD$, which is tangent to the segments $AD$ and $AC$ at $M$ and $N$ respectively, and is also tangent to circle $\omega$.
(i) Show that $BD \cdot CN + BC \cdot DM = CD \cdot BM$.
(ii) Show that $BM = CD$.

positive_text: \text{Suppose } x, y, z \text{ are positive numbers with } xyz = 1. \text{ Prove that} $$ \frac{1}{x^2(y+z)} + \frac{1}{y^2(z+x)} + \frac{1}{z^2(x+y)} \ge \frac{3}{2}. $$

negatives.text: \text{Let } a, b, c \text{ be positive real numbers such that } abc = 1. \text{ Show that} $$ \frac{1}{a(b+c)} + \frac{1}{b(c+a)} + \frac{1}{c(a+b)} \ge \frac{3}{2}. $$
\text{Let } a, b, c \text{ be positive real numbers such that } ab + bc + ca = 1. \text{ Show that} $$ \frac{1}{a^2(b+c)} + \frac{1}{b^2(c+a)} + \frac{1}{c^2(a+b)} \ge \frac{3}{2}. $$
\text{Let } a, b, c \text{ be positive real numbers such that } abc = 1. \text{ Show that} $$ \frac{1}{a^2(b+c)} + \frac{1}{b^2(c+a)} + \frac{1}{c^2(a+b)} \le \frac{3}{2}. $$

positive_text: In triangle $ABC$, let $O$ be the center of the excircle that touches side $BC$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of side $AC$, and let $P$ be the point where the line through $M$ and $O$ intersects $BC$. Prove that if the measure of angle $BAC$ is twice the measure of angle $ACB$, then the lengths $AB$ and $BP$ are equal.

negatives.text: Let $O$ be the centre of the incircle, touching the side $BC$ of $\triangle ABC$. $M$ is the midpoint of $AC$ and $P$ is the intersection of lines $MO$ and $BC$. Show that if $\angle BAC = 2\angle ACB$, then $AB = BP$.

Let $O$ be the centre of the excircle, touching the side $BC$ of $\triangle ABC$. $M$ is the midpoint of $AB$ and $P$ is the intersection of lines $MO$ and $BC$. Show that if $\angle BAC = 2\angle ACB$, then $AB = BP$.

positive_text: In triangle $ ABC $, where $ AB $ is longer than $ AC $, let $ I $ be the point where the angle bisectors meet (the incenter). Draw a line through $ I $ that is perpendicular to $ AI $. This line meets the extension of side $ BC $ at a point $ P $. Prove that $ IP^2 = BP \cdot CP $.

negatives.text: Let $ I $ be the incenter of a triangle $ ABC $ with $ AB > AC $. A line through $ I $ perpendicular to $ BI $ cuts $ BC $ produced at $ P $. Show that $ IP^2 = BP \cdot CP $.
Let $ I $ be the incenter of a triangle $ ABC $ with $ AB > AC $. A line through $ I $ perpendicular to $ AI $ cuts $ AB $ produced at $ P $. Show that $ IP^2 = BP \cdot CP $.

positive_text: Let triangle $ABC$ have $M$ as the midpoint of side $BC$. A circle goes through point $A$ and touches the line $BC$ at point $M$. This circle also intersects sides $AB$ and $AC$ at points $D$ and $E$, respectively. If the points $B$, $C$, $E$, and $D$ lie on the same circle, prove that triangle $ABC$ is isosceles with $AB = AC$.

negatives.text: Let triangle $ABC$ have $M$ as the midpoint of side $BC$. A circle goes through point $A$ and touches the line $BC$ at point $M$. This circle also intersects sides $AB$ and $AC$ at points $D$ and $E$, respectively. If the points $A$, $B$, $C$, and $E$ lie on the same circle, prove that triangle $ABC$ is isosceles with $AB = AC$.

Let triangle $ABC$ have $M$ as the midpoint of side $BC$. A circle goes through point $A$ and touches the line $BC$ at point $M$. This circle also intersects sides $AB$ and $AC$ at points $D$ and $E$, respectively. If the points $A, C, D, E$ are concyclic, prove that triangle $ABC$ is isosceles with $AB = AC$.

Let triangle $ABC$ have $M$ as the midpoint of side $BC$. A circle goes through point $A$ and touches the line $BC$ at point $M$. This circle also intersects sides $AB$ and $AC$ at points $D$ and $E$, respectively. If the points $A, B, D, E$ are concyclic, prove that triangle $ABC$ is isosceles with $AB = AC$.

positive_text: Let $a_1 = 4$, and suppose for each natural number $n$, the next term satisfies $a_{n+1} \ge a_n + n + 2$. Prove that the sum $\frac{1}{a_1} + \frac{1}{a_2} + \dots + \frac{1}{a_{2010}}$ is less than $\frac{3}{2}$.

negatives.text: Let $a_1 = 4$, and suppose for each natural number $n$, the next term satisfies $a_{n+1} \ge a_n + n + 1$. Prove that the sum $\frac{1}{a_1} + \frac{1}{a_2} + \dots + \frac{1}{a_{2010}}$ is less than $\frac{3}{2}$.

Let $a_1 = 4$, and suppose for each natural number $n$, the next term satisfies $a_{n+1} \ge a_n + n + 2$. Prove that the sum $\frac{1}{a_1} + \frac{1}{a_2} + \dots + \frac{1}{a_{2010}}$ is greater than $\frac{3}{2}$.

positive_text:
Let $x$, $y$, $z$ and $w$ be real numbers such that each is at least $1$. Prove that

a.  $xyzw(x+y+z+w-4)^4 \ge (x-1)(y-1)(z-1)(w-1)(x+y+z+w)^4$,

b.  $\dfrac{w}{x+y+z} + \dfrac{x}{y+z+w} + \dfrac{y}{z+w+x} + \dfrac{z}{w+x+y} \ge \dfrac{4}{3}$.

negatives.text:
Let $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$ be positive real numbers, all larger than or equal to $1$. Prove that

a.  $abcd(a+b+c+d-4)^4 \ge (a-1)(b-1)(c-1)(d-1)(a+b+c+d)^3$,

b.  $\dfrac{d}{a+b+c} + \dfrac{a}{b+c+d} + \dfrac{b}{c+d+a} + \dfrac{c}{d+a+b} \ge \dfrac{4}{3}$.

Let $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$ be positive real numbers, all larger than or equal to $1$. Prove that

a.  $abcd(a+b+c+d-4)^4 \ge (a-1)(b-1)(c-1)(d-1)(a+b+c+d)^4$,

b.  $\dfrac{d}{a+b+c} + \dfrac{a}{b+c+d} + \dfrac{b}{c+d+a} + \dfrac{c}{d+a+b} \ge \dfrac{5}{4}$.

Let $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$ be positive real numbers, all larger than or equal to $1$. Prove that

a.  $abcd(a+b+c+d-4)^4 \ge (a-1)(b-1)(c-1)(d-1)(a+b+c+d)^4$,

b.  $\dfrac{d}{a+b+c} + \dfrac{a}{b+c+d} + \dfrac{b}{c+d+a} + \dfrac{c}{d+a+b} \le \dfrac{4}{3}$.

positive_text: Find a function $f : [0, \infty) \to [0, \infty)$ such that $f(2x + 1) = 4f(x) + 9$ holds for all $x \ge 0$.

negatives.text: Find a function $f : \mathbb{R}^{\ge 0} \to \mathbb{R}^{\ge 0}$ satisfying $f(2x + 1) = 4f(x) + 3$ for all $x \ge 0$.
Find a function $f : \mathbb{R}^{\ge 0} \to \mathbb{R}^{\ge 0}$ satisfying $f(2x + 1) = 2f(x) + 9$ for all $x \ge 0$.
Find a function $f : \mathbb{R}^{\ge 0} \to \mathbb{R}^{\ge 0}$ satisfying $f(2x) = 4f(x) + 9$ for all $x \ge 0$.

positive_text: Suppose a function $f$ is defined for all nonzero real numbers $x$ and satisfies the equation $$ \frac{2}{x}f(-x) + f\left(\frac{1}{x}\right) = x $$ for any nonzero $x$. Determine the value of $f(8)$.

negatives.text: Suppose a function $f$ is defined for all nonzero real numbers $x$ and satisfies the equation $$ \frac{1}{x}f(-x) + f\left(\frac{1}{x}\right) = x $$ for any nonzero $x$. Determine the value of $f(8)$.

Suppose a function $f$ is defined for all nonzero real numbers $x$ and satisfies the equation $$ \frac{2}{x}f(-x) + f\left(\frac{1}{x}\right) = 2x $$ for any nonzero $x$. Determine the value of $f(8)$.
Suppose a function $f$ is defined for all nonzero real numbers $x$ and satisfies the equation $$ \frac{2}{x}f(x) + f\left(\frac{1}{x}\right) = x $$ for any nonzero $x$. Determine the value of $f(8)$.

positive_text: Suppose $a$, $b$, and $c$ are three different nonzero real numbers. Consider the three cubic equations: $ax^3 + bx + c = 0$, $bx^3 + cx + a = 0$, and $cx^3 + ax + b = 0$. If all three equations share a common solution, show that at least one of the equations has three real solutions (they don't have to be different from each other).

negatives.text: Let $a$, $b$, $c$ be distinct nonzero real numbers. If the equations $ax^3 + bx + c = 0$, $bx^3 + cx + a = 0$ and $cx^3 + ax + b = 0$ have a common root, prove that all of these equations have three real roots (not necessarily distinct).

Let $a$, $b$, $c$ be distinct nonzero real numbers. If the equations $ax^3 + bx + c = 0$, $bx^3 + cx + a = 0$ and $cx^3 + ax + b = 0$ have a common root, prove that at least one of these equations has three distinct real roots.

Let $a$, $b$, $c$ be distinct nonzero real numbers. If the equations $ax^3 + bx + c = 0$, $bx^3 + cx + a = 0$ and $cx^3 + ax + b = 0$ have a common root, prove that none of these equations has three real roots.

positive_text: Find all integer pairs $(a, b)$ such that $$(b^2 + 11(a - b))^2 = a^3 b.$$

negatives.text: Find all integer pairs $(a, b)$ such that $$(b^2 + 11(a + b))^2 = a^3 b.$$
Find all integer pairs $(a, b)$ such that $$(b^2 + 11(a - b))^2 = a^2 b.$$
Find all integer pairs $(a, b)$ such that $$(b^2 + 11(a - b)) = a^3 b.$$

positive_text: In triangle ABC, AB equals AC, so it is an isosceles triangle. A point P lies inside the triangle such that the angle between BC and CP is 30 degrees, the angle between AP and BP is 150 degrees, and the angle between CA and AP is 39 degrees. Find the measure of the angle between BA and AP.

negatives.text: In triangle ABC, AB = AC. P is a point inside triangle ABC such that \angle BCP = 30^\circ, \angle APB = 120^\circ, and \angle CAP = 39^\circ. Find \angle BAP.
In triangle ABC, AB = AC. P is a point inside triangle ABC such that \angle BCP = 30^\circ, \angle APB = 150^\circ, and \angle CAP = 45^\circ. Find \angle BAP.
In triangle ABC, AB = AC. P is a point inside triangle ABC such that \angle CBP = 30^\circ, \angle APB = 150^\circ, and \angle CAP = 39^\circ. Find \angle BAP.

positive_text: Consider triangle ABC with area 1, where side AB is longer than side AC. The angle at A is divided in half by a line that meets side BC at point D. If we reflect point C across this angle bisector to get a new point C', then triangle DBC' is similar to triangle ABC. What is the length of AB when the total perimeter of triangle ABC is as small as possible?

negatives.text: Triangle ABC has area 1 and satisfies AB > AC. The internal bisector of \angle A meets BC at D, and \triangle DBC' is similar to \triangle ABC where C' is the image of C upon reflection across AD. When the area of \triangle ABC is maximised, find the length of AB.

Triangle ABC has area 1 and satisfies AB > AC. The internal bisector of \angle A meets BC at D, and \triangle DBC' is similar to \triangle ABC where C' is the image of C upon reflection across AB. When the perimeter of \triangle ABC is minimised, find the length of AB.

Triangle ABC has area 1 and satisfies AB < AC. The internal bisector of \angle A meets BC at D, and \triangle DBC' is similar to \triangle ABC where C' is the image of C upon reflection across AD. When the perimeter of \triangle ABC is minimised, find the length of AB.

positive_text: Let $k$ be a number such that $-1 < k < 1$. The line $y = x + k$ intersects the parabola $y = 1 - x^2$ at two points $A$ and $B$. A third point $C$ is fixed at $(1, 0)$. What is the largest possible area of triangle $ABC$?

negatives.text: Let $k$ be a real number such that $-1 < k < 1$. The straight line $y = x + k$ meets the curve $y = 1 - x^2$ at $A$ and $B$. If $C$ denotes the point $(0, 1)$, find the greatest possible area of $\triangle ABC$.

Let $k$ be a real number such that $-1 < k < 1$. The straight line $y = x + k$ meets the curve $y = 1 - x^2$ at $A$ and $B$. If $C$ denotes the point $(1, 0)$, find the least possible area of $\triangle ABC$.

Let $k$ be a real number such that $-1 < k < 1$. The straight line $y = x + k$ meets the curve $y = 1 - x^2$ at $A$ and $B$. If $C$ denotes the point $(1, 0)$, find the greatest possible area of $\triangle ABC$ when $k < 0$.

positive_text: In triangle $ABC$, suppose $\angle ABC$ is greater than $\angle BCA$, and $\angle BCA$ is at least $30^\circ$. The angle bisector of $\angle ABC$ meets side $AC$ at point $D$, and the angle bisector of $\angle BCA$ meets side $AB$ at point $E$. The lines $BD$ and $CE$ intersect at point $P$. Given that $PD = PE$ and the triangle's incircle has a radius of 1, find the largest possible length of side $BC$.

negatives.text: In triangle $ABC$, suppose $\angle ABC$ is greater than $\angle BCA$, and $\angle BCA$ is at least $30^\circ$. The angle bisector of $\angle ABC$ meets side $AC$ at point $D$, and the angle bisector of $\angle BCA$ meets side $AB$ at point $E$. The lines $BD$ and $CE$ intersect at point $P$. Given that $PD = PE$ and the triangle's incircle has a radius of 2, find the largest possible length of side $BC$.

In triangle $ABC$, suppose $\angle ABC$ is greater than $\angle BCA$, and $\angle BCA$ is at least $30^\circ$. The angle bisector of $\angle ABC$ meets side $AC$ at point $D$, and the angle bisector of $\angle BCA$ meets side $AB$ at point $E$. The lines $BD$ and $CE$ intersect at point $P$. Given that $PC = PE$ and the triangle's incircle has a radius of 1, find the largest possible length of side $BC$.

In triangle $ABC$, suppose $\angle ABC$ is greater than $\angle BCA$, and $\angle BCA$ is at least $30^\circ$. The angle bisector of $\angle ABC$ meets side $AC$ at point $D$, and the angle bisector of $\angle BCA$ meets side $AB$ at point $E$. The lines $BD$ and $CE$ intersect at point $P$. Given that $PD = PE$ and the triangle's circumcircle has a radius of 1, find the largest possible length of side $BC$.

positive_text: In triangle $ABC$, let $D$ lie on side $AB$ and $E$ on side $AC$, such that line segment $DE$ is parallel to $BC$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$. Suppose there is a point $P$ such that $DB = DP$, $EC = EP$, and the line segment $AP$ intersects the segment $BC$ (excluding the endpoints). If $\angle BPD = \angle CME$, prove that $\angle CPE = \angle BMD$.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle. Let $D$ and $E$ be respectively points on the segments $AB$ and $AC$, and such that $DE \parallel BC$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$. Let $P$ be a point such that $DB = DP$, $EC = EP$ and such that the open segments (segments excluding the endpoints) $AP$ and $BC$ intersect. Suppose $\angle BPD = \angle CME$. Show that $\angle CPE = \angle CME$.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle. Let $D$ and $E$ be respectively points on the segments $AB$ and $AC$, and such that $DE \parallel BC$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$. Let $P$ be a point such that $DB = DP$, $EC = EP$ and such that the open segments (segments excluding the endpoints) $AP$ and $BC$ intersect. Suppose $\angle DPC = \angle CME$. Show that $\angle CPE = \angle BMD$.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle. Let $D$ and $E$ be respectively points on the segments $AB$ and $AC$, and such that $DE \parallel BC$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$. Let $P$ be a point such that $DB = DP$, $EC = EP$ and such that the open segments (segments excluding the endpoints) $AP$ and $BC$ intersect. Suppose $\angle BPD = \angle CME$. Show that $\angle CPE = \angle CMD$.

positive_text: In triangle $ABC$, angle $A$ is $54^\circ$ and angle $C$ is $24^\circ$. A point $P$ lies on side $AC$ so that the length of $AP$ equals the length of $BC$. What is the measure of angle $CBP$?

negatives.text: In $\triangle ABC$, $\angle A = 54^\circ$ and $\angle C = 24^\circ$. $P$ is a point on $AB$ such that $AP = BC$. Find $\angle CBP$.
In $\triangle ABC$, $\angle A = 54^\circ$ and $\angle C = 24^\circ$. $P$ is a point on $AC$ such that $AP = AB$. Find $\angle CBP$.

positive_text: Let $n$ be an integer with $n \ge 2$. Suppose there are $n$ different circles on a flat surface. Any pair of these circles intersect at exactly two points, and no three circles meet at a single point. At the start, there is a coin placed at each intersection point of the circles. Two players, $X$ and $Y$, take turns removing one coin at a time, starting with $X$. However, a player cannot remove a coin that lies on the same circle as the last coin removed by the other player in the previous turn. The game ends when no coins are left, and the player who cannot move loses. For which values of $n$ does $Y$ have a winning strategy?

negatives.text: Let $n \ge 2$ be an integer. There are $n$ distinct circles on the plane such that any two circles have two distinct intersections and no three circles have a common intersection. Initially there is a coin on each of the intersection points of the circles. Starting from $X$, players $X$ and $Y$ alternately take away a coin, with the restriction that one cannot take away a coin lying on the same circle as the last coin just taken away by the opponent in the previous step. The one who cannot do so will lose. In particular, one loses when there is no coin left. For what values of $n$ does $X$ has a winning strategy?

Let $n \ge 2$ be an integer. There are $n$ distinct circles on the plane such that any two circles have two distinct intersections and no three circles have a common intersection. Initially there is a coin on each of the intersection points of the circles. Starting from $X$, players $X$ and $Y$ alternately take away a coin, with the restriction that one cannot take away a coin lying on the same circle as the last coin just taken away by the opponent in the previous step. The one who cannot do so will lose. In particular, one loses when there is no coin left. For what values of $n$ does $Y$ has a winning strategy if players can take away coins from the same circle as the previous move?

positive_text: \text{Consider a triangle } ABC \text{ with integer side lengths. Let } M \text{ be the midpoint of side } BC. The incircle, with center } I, \text{ touches sides } AB \text{ and } AC \text{ at points } E \text{ and } F \text{ respectively. Let } D \text{ be the point where a perpendicular from } M \text{ meets } EF. It is given that the quadrilateral } ADMI \text{ forms a parallelogram, and that the perimeter of the triangle is } 65. \text{ What is the product of the lengths of the three sides?}

negatives.text: \text{Let } ABC \text{ be a triangle with integral sides. } M \text{ is the midpoint of } BC. \text{ The in-circle with centre } I \text{ touches } AB \text{ and } AC \text{ at } E \text{ and } F \text{ respectively and } D \text{ is the projection of } M \text{ on } EF. Suppose that } AMDI \text{ is a trapezoid and } AB + BC + CA = 65. \text{ Find } AB \times BC \times CA.

positive_text: Quadrilateral $ABCD$ has $AB$ parallel to $CD$. Points $M$ and $N$ are the midpoints of sides $AB$ and $CD$, respectively. If the length of diagonal $AC$ is 6, the length of diagonal $BD$ is 8, and the length of segment $MN$ is 4, find the area of trapezium $ABCD$.

negatives.text: Let $ABCD$ be a trapezium with $AB \parallel CD$. Let $M$ and $N$ be the midpoints of $AB$ and $CD$, respectively. If $AC = 6$, $BD = 8$, and $MN = 6$, find the area of $ABCD$.
Let $ABCD$ be a trapezium with $AB \parallel CD$. Let $M$ and $N$ be the midpoints of $AB$ and $CD$, respectively. If $AC = 6$, $BD = 6$, and $MN = 4$, find the area of $ABCD$.

positive_text: Suppose $k$ is an integer. Consider the quadratic equation $kx^2 + (4k - 2)x + (4k - 7) = 0$. If this equation has at least one integer solution, find the sum of all possible values of $k$.

negatives.text: Let $k$ be an integer. If the equation $kx^2 + (4k-2)x + (4k-7) = 0$ has a rational root, find the sum of all possible values of $k$.
Let $k$ be an integer. If the equation $kx^2 + (4k-2)x + (4k-7) = 0$ has two distinct integral roots, find the sum of all possible values of $k$.
Let $k$ be an integer. If the equation $kx^2 + (4k-2)x + (4k-7) = 0$ has a root that is a perfect square, find the sum of all possible values of $k$.

positive_text: Suppose $ p $ is a prime number greater than $ 5 $, and there is some whole number $ k $ such that $ p $ divides $ k^2 + 5 $. Show that there exist positive whole numbers $ m $ and $ n $ for which $ p^2 = m^2 + 5n^2 $.

negatives.text: Let $ p $ be a prime number greater than $ 5 $. Suppose there is an integer $ k $ such that $ k^2 + 5 $ is divisible by $ p $. Prove that there are positive integers $ m $ and $ n $ such that $ p = m^2 + 5n^2 $.

Let $ p $ be a prime number greater than $ 5 $. Suppose there is an integer $ k $ such that $ k^2 - 5 $ is divisible by $ p $. Prove that there are positive integers $ m $ and $ n $ such that $ p^2 = m^2 + 5n^2 $.

Let $ p $ be a prime number greater than $ 5 $. Suppose there is an integer $ k $ such that $ k^2 + 5 $ is divisible by $ p $. Prove that there are positive integers $ m $ and $ n $ such that $ p^2 = m^2 - 5n^2 $.

positive_text: A quadrilateral $ABCD$ is drawn inside a circle centered at $O$. The diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ meet at point $E$. The points $M$ and $N$ are the midpoints of the arcs $AB$ and $CD$ on the circle that do not contain the other two vertices. The line $EO$ intersects the line $MN$ at point $P$. If $BC = 5$, $AC = 11$, $BD = 12$, and $AD = 10$, find the value of $\frac{MN}{NP}$.

negatives.text: Let $ABCD$ be inscribed in a circle with centre $O$. Let $E$ be the intersection point of $AC$ and $BD$. $M$ and $N$ are the midpoints of the arcs $AB$ and $CD$ respectively (the arcs not containing any other vertices). Let $P$ be the intersection point of $EO$ and $MN$. Suppose $BC = 5$, $AC = 11$, $BD = 12$ and $AB = 10$. Find $\frac{MN}{NP}$.

Let $ABCD$ be inscribed in a circle with centre $O$. Let $E$ be the intersection point of $AC$ and $BD$. $M$ and $N$ are the midpoints of the arcs $AB$ and $CD$ respectively (the arcs not containing any other vertices). Let $P$ be the intersection point of $EO$ and $MN$. Suppose $BC = 5$, $AC = 11$, $BD = 12$ and $AD = 10$. Find $\frac{MP}{NP}$.

Let $ABCD$ be inscribed in a circle with centre $O$. Let $E$ be the intersection point of $AC$ and $BD$. $M$ and $N$ are the midpoints of the arcs $AB$ and $CD$ respectively (the arcs not containing any other vertices). Let $P$ be the intersection point of $EO$ and $MN$. Suppose $BC = 5$, $AC = 11$, $BD = 12$ and $AD = 10$. Find $\frac{MN}{EP}$.

positive_text: In triangle $ABC$, the angle bisector of $\angle A$ intersects side $BC$ at point $D$. A circle $\Gamma$ passes through point $A$ and is tangent to side $BC$ at $D$. This circle also intersects sides $AB$ and $AC$ again at points $E$ and $F$, respectively. The lines $BF$ and $CE$ intersect $\Gamma$ again at points $P$ and $Q$. The lines $AP$ and $AQ$ meet side $BC$ at points $X$ and $Y$. Show that the length of segment $XY$ is half the length of segment $BC$.

negatives.text: Let the internal angle bisector of $\angle BAC$ of $\triangle ABC$ meet side $BC$ at $D$. Let $\Gamma$ be the circle through $A$ tangent to $BC$ at $D$. Suppose $\Gamma$ meets sides $AB$ and $AC$ at $E$ and $F$ again, respectively. Lines $BE$ and $CF$ meet $\Gamma$ again at $P$ and $Q$, respectively. Let $AP$ and $AQ$ intersect side $BC$ at $X$ and $Y$, respectively. Prove that $XY = \frac{1}{2}BC$.

Let the internal angle bisector of $\angle BAC$ of $\triangle ABC$ meet side $BC$ at $D$. Let $\Gamma$ be the circle through $A$ tangent to $BC$ at $D$. Suppose $\Gamma$ meets sides $AB$ and $AC$ at $E$ and $F$ again, respectively. Lines $BF$ and $CE$ meet $\Gamma$ again at $P$ and $Q$, respectively. Let $BP$ and $CQ$ intersect side $BC$ at $X$ and $Y$, respectively. Prove that $XY = \frac{1}{2}BC$.

Let the internal angle bisector of $\angle BAC$ of $\triangle ABC$ meet side $BC$ at $D$. Let $\Gamma$ be the circle through $A$ tangent to $BC$ at $D$. Suppose $\Gamma$ meets sides $AB$ and $AC$ at $E$ and $F$ again, respectively. Lines $BF$ and $CE$ meet $\Gamma$ again at $P$ and $Q$, respectively. Let $AP$ and $AQ$ intersect side $BC$ at $X$ and $Y$, respectively. Prove that $XY = \frac{1}{3}BC$.

positive_text: Consider the sequence $\{a_n\}$ where $a_1 = 5$ and each term is defined by the rule $a_{n+1} = a_n^2 - 3a_n + 3$ for $n = 1, 2, 3, \dots$. Show that $a_n > 3^{2^{n-1}}$ for all positive integers $n$.

negatives.text: The sequence $\{x_n\}$ is defined by $x_1 = 5$ and $x_{k+1} = x_k^2 - 3x_k + 3$ for $k = 1, 2, 3, \dots$. Prove that $x_k < 3^{2^{k-1}}$ for any positive integer $k$.
The sequence $\{x_n\}$ is defined by $x_1 = 5$ and $x_{k+1} = x_k^2 - 2x_k + 3$ for $k = 1, 2, 3, \dots$. Prove that $x_k > 3^{2^{k-1}}$ for any positive integer $k$.
The sequence $\{x_n\}$ is defined by $x_1 = 5$ and $x_{k+1} = x_k^2 - 3x_k + 3$ for $k = 1, 2, 3, \dots$. Prove that $x_k > 2^{2^{k-1}}$ for any positive integer $k$.

positive_text: Consider a sequence $\{b_n\}$ of integers such that for every positive integer $n$, the equation $b_n + b_{n+1} = 2b_{n+2}b_{n+3} + 2016$ holds. Determine all possible values for $b_1$ and $b_2$.

negatives.text: Let $\{a_n\}$ be a sequence of integers satisfying the following condition for all positive integral values of $n$: $a_n + a_{n+1} = 2a_{n+2}a_{n+3} + 2017$. Find all possible values of $a_1$ and $a_2$.

Let $\{a_n\}$ be a sequence of integers satisfying the following condition for all positive integral values of $n$: $a_n + a_{n+1} = 2a_{n+3}a_{n+4} + 2016$. Find all possible values of $a_1$ and $a_2$.

Let $\{a_n\}$ be a sequence of integers satisfying the following condition for all positive integral values of $n$: $a_n + a_{n+1} = a_{n+2}a_{n+3} + 2016$. Find all possible values of $a_1$ and $a_2$.

positive_text: Let $ABCD$ be a quadrilateral that fits perfectly on a circle. Extend side $DA$ beyond $A$ to a point $P$ so that the length $AP$ is the same as $BC$. Also, extend side $DC$ beyond $C$ to a point $Q$ so that the length $CQ$ is the same as $AB$. Let $M$ be the middle point of the segment $PQ$. Prove that the line from $A$ to $M$ is at a right angle with the line from $C$ to $M$.

negatives.text: Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral. Extend $DA$ and $DC$ to $P$ and $Q$ respectively such that $AP = CD$ and $CQ = DA$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $PQ$. Show that $MA \perp MC$.

positive_text: Consider an isosceles triangle $ABC$ with $AB = AC$. A circle $\Gamma$ is drawn outside triangle $ABC$ and touches the side $AC$ exactly at point $C$. A point $D$ is on $\Gamma$ such that the circle passing through points $A$, $B$, and $D$ is tangent from the inside to $\Gamma$. When segment $AD$ is extended, it intersects $\Gamma$ again at a point $E$. Prove that the line segment $BE$ is tangent to $\Gamma$.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $AB = AC$. A circle $\Gamma$ lies outside triangle $ABC$ and is tangent to line $AB$ at $C$. Point $D$ lies on $\Gamma$ such that the circumcircle of triangle $ABD$ is internally tangent to $\Gamma$. Segment $AD$ meets $\Gamma$ again at $E$. Prove that $BE$ is tangent to $\Gamma$.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $AB = AC$. A circle $\Gamma$ lies outside triangle $ABC$ and is tangent to line $AC$ at $C$. Point $D$ lies on $\Gamma$ such that the circumcircle of triangle $ABD$ is externally tangent to $\Gamma$. Segment $AD$ meets $\Gamma$ again at $E$. Prove that $BE$ is tangent to $\Gamma$.

Point $D$ lies on $\Gamma$ such that the circumcircle of triangle $ABD$ is internally tangent to $\Gamma$. Segment $BD$ meets $\Gamma$ again at $E$. Prove that $BE$ is tangent to $\Gamma$.

positive_text: Find all whole numbers $n$ that are at least 3 such that there are $n$ different points on a flat surface where each point is the center of a circle that goes through three of the points.

negatives.text: Find all integers $n \ge 3$ with the following property: there exist $n$ distinct points on the plane such that each point is the centroid of a triangle formed by 3 of the points.

Find all integers $n \ge 3$ with the following property: there exist $n$ distinct points on the plane such that each point is the circumcentre of a triangle formed by 3 of the points, but the points are collinear.
Find all integers $n \ge 3$ with the following property: there exist $n$ distinct points on the plane such that each point is the circumcentre of a triangle formed by 2 of the points.

positive_text: Let $a$ be a real number. Consider the function $f(x) = \frac{a}{x-1} + \frac{1}{x-2} + \frac{1}{x-6}$, defined for $x$ in the interval $(3, 5)$. It is given that $f(x)$ has its maximum at $x = 4$. Determine the value of $a$.

negatives.text: Let $a$ be a real number. Suppose the function $f(x) = \frac{a}{x-1} + \frac{1}{x-2} + \frac{1}{x-6}$ defined in the interval $3 < x < 5$ attains its minimum at $x = 4$. Find the value of $a$.
Let $a$ be a real number. Suppose the function $f(x) = \frac{a}{x-1} + \frac{1}{x-2} + \frac{1}{x-6}$ defined in the interval $1 < x < 2$ attains its maximum at $x = 1.5$. Find the value of $a$.

positive_text: In triangle $ABC$, where $AB = AC$, the incircle $\Gamma$ touches sides $AB$ and $AC$ at points $F$ and $E$, respectively. The center of the incircle is point $I$. Let $\Omega$ be the circle that passes through points $A$, $F$, and $E$. The two external common tangents to $\Gamma$ and $\Omega$ intersect at a point $P$. Suppose one of these tangents is parallel to $AC$. Show that the angle between $PB$ and $IB$ is a right angle.

negatives.text: Let $\triangle ABC$ be an isosceles triangle with $AB = AC$. The incircle $\Gamma$ of $\triangle ABC$ has centre $I$, and it is tangent to the sides $AB$ and $AC$ at $F$ and $E$ respectively. Let $\Omega$ be the circumcircle of $\triangle AFE$. The two external common tangents of $\Gamma$ and $\Omega$ intersect at a point $P$. If one of these external common tangents is parallel to $BC$, prove that $\angle PBI = 90^\circ$.

If one of these external common tangents is parallel to $AC$, prove that $\angle PCI = 90^\circ$.

positive_text: Let $ABCD$ be a quadrilateral inscribed in a circle $\Gamma$ with $AB = AD$. Let $E$ be a point on $CD$ so that the length of $DE$ equals that of $BC$. The line $AE$ intersects the circle again at $F$. The lines $AC$ and $BF$ meet at $M$. If $P$ is the reflection of $C$ over $M$, prove that the lines $PE$ and $BF$ are parallel.

negatives.text: Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral inscribed in a circle $\Gamma$ such that $AB = AD$. Let $E$ be a point on the segment $CD$ such that $BC = DE$. The line $BE$ intersects $\Gamma$ again at $F$. The chords $AC$ and $BF$ meet at $M$. Let $P$ be the symmetric point of $C$ about $M$. Prove that $PE$ and $BF$ are parallel.

Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral inscribed in a circle $\Gamma$ such that $AB = AD$. Let $E$ be a point on the segment $CD$ such that $BC = DE$. The line $AE$ intersects $\Gamma$ again at $F$. The chords $AC$ and $DF$ meet at $M$. Let $P$ be the symmetric point of $C$ about $M$. Prove that $PE$ and $BF$ are parallel.

Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral inscribed in a circle $\Gamma$ such that $AB = AD$. Let $E$ be a point on the segment $CD$ such that $BC = DE$. The line $AE$ intersects $\Gamma$ again at $F$. The chords $AC$ and $BF$ meet at $M$. Let $P$ be the symmetric point of $B$ about $M$. Prove that $PE$ and $BF$ are parallel.

positive_text: Find all real numbers $a$, $b$, and $c$ such that $$(2^{2a} + 1)(2^{2b} + 2)(2^{2c} + 8) = 2^{a + b + c + 5}.$$

negatives.text: Find all real triples $(a, b, c)$ satisfying $$(2^{2a} + 1)(2^{2b} + 2)(2^{2c} + 8) = 2^{a+b+c+6}.$$
Find all real triples $(a, b, c)$ satisfying $$(2^{2a} + 1)(2^{2b} + 2)(2^{2c} + 8) = 2^{a+b+c+5} + 1.$$
Find all real triples $(a, b, c)$ satisfying $$(2^{2a} + 1)(2^{2b} + 2)(2^{2c} + 8) = 2^{2a + 2b + 2c + 5}.$$

positive_text: In triangle $ABC$, the length of side $AC$ is $k$ times the length of side $AB$, where $k > 1$. The angle bisector of $\angle BAC$ intersects $BC$ at point $D$. A circle is drawn with $AC$ as its diameter, and this circle intersects the extension of $AD$ at a point $E$. Find the ratio $\frac{AD}{AE}$ in terms of $k$.

negatives.text: In $\triangle ABC$, $AC = kAB$, with $k > 1$. The internal angle bisector of $\angle BAC$ meets $BC$ at $D$. The circle with $AB$ as diameter cuts the extension of $AD$ at $E$. Express $\frac{AD}{AE}$ in terms of $k$.

In $\triangle ABC$, $AC = kAB$, with $k > 1$. The internal angle bisector of $\angle BAC$ meets $BC$ at $D$. The circle with $AC$ as diameter cuts the segment $AD$ at $E$. Express $\frac{AD}{AE}$ in terms of $k$.

In $\triangle ABC$, $AC = kAB$, with $k > 1$. The internal angle bisector of $\angle BAC$ meets $BC$ at $D$. The circle with $AC$ as diameter cuts the extension of $AD$ at $E$. Express $\frac{AE}{AD}$ in terms of $k$.

positive_text: In an acute triangle $ABC$, with $BC > AB$, place a point $D$ on segment $AC$ such that $BD = BA$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of side $BC$. Draw the circumcircle of triangle $CDM$, and draw the tangents at points $D$ and $M$ to this circle. These tangents meet at a point $E$. The line from $B$ to $E$ intersects $AC$ at a point $F$. Prove that the points $A$, $B$, $M$, and $F$ lie on a circle.

negatives.text: In acute $\triangle ABC$, $BC > AB$. Let $D$ be the point on the side $AC$ such that $BD = BC$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$. The tangents at $D$ and $M$ to the circumcircle of $\triangle CDM$ intersect at point $E$. The line $BE$ intersects the side $AC$ at $F$. Prove that $A, B, M, F$ are concyclic.

In acute $\triangle ABC$, $BC > AB$. Let $D$ be the point on the side $AC$ such that $BD = BA$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $AB$. The tangents at $D$ and $M$ to the circumcircle of $\triangle CDM$ intersect at point $E$. The line $BE$ intersects the side $AC$ at $F$. Prove that $A, B, M, F$ are concyclic.

In acute $\triangle ABC$, $BC > AB$. Let $D$ be the point on the side $AC$ such that $BD = BA$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$. The tangents at $D$ and $C$ to the circumcircle of $\triangle CDM$ intersect at point $E$. The line $BE$ intersects the side $AC$ at $F$. Prove that $A, B, M, F$ are concyclic.

positive_text: Consider an acute triangle $\triangle ABC$ with its circumcircle $\Gamma$. Let $P$ be the point on $\Gamma$ that is halfway along the shorter arc from $B$ to $C$. Let $AP$ intersect $BC$ at a point $D$, and let $M$ be the midpoint of side $AB$. Suppose there is a point $E$ such that $AE$ is perpendicular to $AB$, and $BE$ is perpendicular to $MP$. Prove that the lengths $AE$ and $DE$ are equal.

negatives.text: Let $\triangle ABC$ be an acute triangle with circumcircle $\Gamma$, and let $P$ be the midpoint of the minor arc $BC$ of $\Gamma$. Let $AP$ meet $BC$ at $D$, and let $M$ be the midpoint of $AB$. Also, let $E$ be the point such that $AE \perp AB$ and $CE \perp MP$. Prove that $AE = DE$.

positive_text: Imagine a square grid with $n$ rows and $n$ columns, where $n$ is an even number at least 4. Each square is colored black or white so that no two neighboring squares (sharing a side) have the same color. Suppose we have two squares, $A$ and $B$, that are not on the edge of the grid and are of different colors. Show that a piece can move from $A$ to $B$ by stepping only to neighboring squares, visiting each square on the grid exactly once.

negatives.text: Imagine a square grid with $n$ rows and $n$ columns, where $n$ is an even number at least 4. Each square is colored black or white so that no two neighboring squares (sharing a side) have the same color. Suppose we have two squares, $A$ and $B$, that are not on the edge of the grid and are of the same color. Show that a piece can move from $A$ to $B$ by stepping only to neighboring squares, visiting each square on the grid exactly once.

Each square is colored black or white so that no two neighboring squares (sharing a side) have the same color. Suppose we have two squares, $A$ and $B$, that are on the edge of the grid and are of different colors. Show that a piece can move from $A$ to $B$ by stepping only to neighboring squares, visiting each square on the grid exactly once.

Suppose we have two squares, $A$ and $B$, that are not on the edge of the grid and are of different colors. Show that a piece can move from $A$ to $B$ by stepping only to neighboring squares, visiting each square on the grid exactly once.

positive_text: In triangle $ABC$, let $M$ be the midpoint of side $BC$, and let $G$ be the centroid of the triangle. Pick a point $D$ on the segment from $G$ to $M$. Draw a line through $D$ that intersects side $AB$ at point $E$ and side $AC$ at point $F$, with neither $E$ nor $F$ being the point $A$. Prove that the total area of the quadrilaterals $BEGF$ and $CFGE$ is at least $\frac{4}{9}$ of the area of triangle $ABC$. When is this total area exactly $\frac{4}{9}$ of the area of triangle $ABC$?

negatives.text:
Let $ABC$ be a triangle. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$, and let $G$ be the centroid of $\triangle ABC$. Let $D$ be a point on the segment $GM$. A straight line passing through $D$ meets the sides $AB$ and $AC$ at $E$ and $F$ respectively (with $E, F \ne A$). Show that
$$
[BEGF] + [CFGE] \ge \frac{1}{3}[ABC].
$$
When does the equality hold?

Let $ABC$ be a triangle. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$, and let $G$ be the centroid of $\triangle ABC$. Let $D$ be a point on the segment $GM$. A straight line passing through $D$ meets the side $AB$ at $E$ and the side $BC$ at $F$ (with $E, F \ne A$). Show that
$$
[BEGF] + [CFGE] \ge \frac{4}{9}[ABC].
$$
When does the equality hold?

positive_text: Suppose $n$ is a whole number, and you choose $4n+2$ numbers from the set $\{0, 1, 2, 3, \dots, 5^n\}$. Show that you can find three numbers $a$, $b$, and $c$ among your choices so that $a < b < c$ and $c + 2a > 3b$.

negatives.text: Let $n$ be an integer, and let $A$ be a subset of $\{0, 1, 2, 3, \dots, 5^n\}$ consisting of $4n+2$ numbers. Prove that there exist $a, b, c \in A$ such that $a < b < c$ and $c + 2a < 3b$.
Let $n$ be an integer, and let $A$ be a subset of $\{0, 1, 2, 3, \dots, 5^n\}$ consisting of $4n$ numbers. Prove that there exist $a, b, c \in A$ such that $a < b < c$ and $c + 2a > 3b$.
Let $n$ be an integer, and let $A$ be a subset of $\{0, 1, 2, 3, \dots, 5^n\}$ consisting of $4n+2$ numbers. Prove that there exist $a, b, c \in A$ such that $a < b < c$ and $c + a > 2b$.

positive_text: Consider a parallelogram $ABCD$, where angle $B$ is less than 90 degrees. A circle touches the sides $BC$, $CD$, and $DA$. This circle crosses the diagonal $AC$ at two points, $M$ and $N$, with $M$ being closer to $A$. Given that $AM = 9$, $MN = 16$, and $NC = 2$, calculate the area of the parallelogram $ABCD$.

negatives.text: Consider a parallelogram $ABCD$, where angle $B$ is less than 90 degrees. A circle touches the sides $AB$, $CD$, and $DA$. This circle crosses the diagonal $AC$ at two points, $M$ and $N$, with $M$ being closer to $A$. Given that $AM = 9$, $MN = 16$, and $NC = 2$, calculate the area of the parallelogram $ABCD$.

Consider a parallelogram $ABCD$, where angle $B$ is less than 90 degrees. A circle is tangent to $BC$, $CD$, and $DA$. This circle intersects the side $AB$ at two points, $M$ and $N$, with $M$ being closer to $A$. Given that $AM = 9$, $MN = 16$, and $NC = 2$, calculate the area of the parallelogram $ABCD$.

positive_text: In triangle $ABC$, side $AB$ is shorter than side $AC$. The angle bisector of $\angle A$ intersects side $BC$ at a point $D$. Another line that splits the angle $\angle A$ into two equal parts from the outside meets the extension of side $BC$ at a point $E$. It is given that $EB = 2022$, and both $BD$ and $DC$ are whole numbers. How many different values can $BD$ take?

negatives.text: In $\triangle ABC$, $AB < AC$. The internal bisector of $\angle BAC$ meets $BC$ at $D$, while the external bisector of $\angle BAC$ meets $CB$ produced at $E$. If $EC = 2022$ and the lengths of $BD$ and $DC$ are integers, how many possible lengths of $BD$ are there?
