positive_text:
An $(n + 1)$-tuple $(h_1, h_2, \dots, h_{n+1})$ where each $h_i$ is an $n$-variable polynomial with real coefficients is called **good** if the following holds:
For any $n$ functions $f_1, f_2, \dots, f_n : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, if the compositions $h_i(f_1(x), f_2(x), \dots, f_n(x))$ are polynomials in $x$ for all $i$, then $f_1(x), f_2(x), \dots, f_n(x)$ must themselves be polynomials.

a) Show that for all positive integers $n$, there exists a **good** $(n+1)$-tuple $(h_1, h_2, \dots, h_{n+1})$ such that each $h_i$ has degree greater than one.

b) Show that for all $n > 1$, there is no **good** $(n+1)$-tuple $(h_1, h_2, \dots, h_{n+1})$ where all $h_i$ are symmetric polynomials.

negatives.text:
An $(n + 1)$-tuple $(h_1, h_2, \dots, h_{n+1})$ where each $h_i$ is an $n$-variable polynomial with real coefficients is called **good** if the following holds:
For any $n$ functions $f_1, f_2, \dots, f_n : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, if the compositions $h_i(f_1(x), f_2(x), \dots, f_n(x))$ are polynomials in $x$ for all $i$, then $f_1(x), f_2(x), \dots, f_n(x)$ must themselves be polynomials.

a) Show that for all positive integers $n$, there exists a **good** $(n+1)$-tuple $(h_1, h_2, \dots, h_{n+1})$ such that each $h_i$ has degree greater than one.

b) Show that for all $n > 1$, there is no **good** $(n+1)$-tuple $(h_1, h_2, \dots, h_{n+1})$ where all $h_i$ are linear polynomials.

An $(n + 1)$-tuple $(h_1, h_2, \dots, h_{n+1})$ where each $h_i$ is an $n$-variable polynomial with real coefficients is called **good** if the following holds:
For any $n$ functions $f_1, f_2, \dots, f_n : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, if the compositions $h_i(f_1(x), f_2(x), \dots, f_n(x))$ are polynomials in $x$ for all $i$, then $f_1(x), f_2(x), \dots, f_n(x)$ must themselves be polynomials.

a) Show that for all positive integers $n$, there exists a **good** $(n+1)$-tuple $(h_1, h_2, \dots, h_{n+1})$ such that each $h_i$ has degree greater than one.

b) Show that for all $n > 1$, there is no **good** $(n+1)$-tuple $(h_1, h_2, \dots, h_{n+1})$ where all $h_i$ are monomials.

An $(n + 1)$-tuple $(h_1, h_2, \dots, h_{n+1})$ where each $h_i$ is an $n$-variable polynomial with real coefficients is called **good** if the following holds:
For any $n$ functions $f_1, f_2, \dots, f_n : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, if the compositions $h_i(f_1(x), f_2(x), \dots, f_n(x))$ are polynomials in $x$ for all $i$, then $f_1(x), f_2(x), \dots, f_n(x)$ must themselves be polynomials.

a) Show that for all positive integers $n$, there exists a **good** $(n+1)$-tuple $(h_1, h_2, \dots, h_{n+1})$ such that each $h_i$ has degree greater than one.

b) Show that for all $n > 1$, there is no **good** $(n+1)$-tuple $(h_1, h_2, \dots, h_{n+1})$ where all $h_i$ are homogeneous polynomials.

positive_text: There are 6 points on a flat surface with the property that no three of them lie on the same straight line. It is given that for any 4 of these points, there is one point whose power with respect to the circle defined by the other three is always a fixed number $ k $ (note: the power is negative if the point is inside the circle). Show that $ k = 0 $ and that all 6 points lie on a single circle.

negatives.text: There are 6 points on the plane such that no three of them are collinear. We know that among every 4 points of them, there exists a point that its power with respect to the circle passing through the other three points is a constant value $ k $. Prove that all 6 points lie on a circle.

There are 6 points on the plane such that no three of them are collinear. We know that among every 4 points of them, there exists a point that its power with respect to the circle passing through the other three points is a constant value $ k $. Prove that $ k = 1 $ and all 6 points lie on a circle.

There are 6 points on the plane such that no three of them are collinear. We know that among every 3 points of them, there exists a point that its power with respect to the circle passing through the other two points is a constant value $ k $. Prove that $ k = 0 $ and all 6 points lie on a circle.

positive_text: \text{Consider triangle } ABC \text{ with a circumcircle } \omega_1 \text{ and } \angle C = 2\angle B. \text{ A line that just touches } \omega_1 \text{ at } A \text{ meets } BC \text{ at } E. \text{ A circle } \omega_2 \text{ goes through } B \text{ and touches } AC \text{ at } C. \text{ This circle cuts } AB \text{ again at } F. \text{ A line from } E \text{ that just touches } \omega_2 \text{ at } K \text{ (with } BC \text{ between } A \text{ and } K). \text{ Let } M \text{ be the center point of the arc } BC \text{ of } \omega_1 \text{ that does not include } A. \text{ Show that the points } M, F, A, K \text{ lie on a circle.}

negatives.text: \text{Let } ABC \text{ be a triangle with circumcircle } \omega_1 \text{ and } \angle C = 2\angle B. \text{ A tangent line to } \omega_1 \text{ at } B \text{ intersects } AC \text{ at } E. \text{ Let } \omega_2 \text{ be a circle passing through } B \text{ and tangent to } AC \text{ at } C. \text{ This circle intersects } AB \text{ for the second time at } F. \text{ A line through } E \text{ is tangent to } \omega_2 \text{ at } K \text{ (where } AC \text{ lies between } B \text{ and } K). \text{ Let } M \text{ be the midpoint of arc } BC \text{ of } \omega_1 \text{ (not containing } A). \text{ Prove that } MFAK \text{ is a cyclic quadrilateral.}

\text{Let } ABC \text{ be a triangle with circumcircle } \omega_1 \text{ and } \angle C = 2\angle B. \text{ A tangent line to } \omega_1 \text{ at } A \text{ intersects } BC \text{ at } E. \text{ Let } \omega_2 \text{ be a circle passing through } A \text{ and tangent to } AC \text{ at } C. \text{ This circle intersects } AB \text{ for the second time at } F. \text{ A line through } E \text{ is tangent to } \omega_2 \text{ at } K \text{ (where } BC \text{ lies between } A \text{ and } K). \text{ Let } M \text{ be the midpoint of arc } BC \text{ of } \omega_1 \text{ (not containing } A). \text{ Prove that } MFAK \text{ is a cyclic quadrilateral.}

\text{Let } ABC \text{ be a triangle with circumcircle } \omega_1 \text{ and } \angle C = 2\angle B. \text{ A tangent line to } \omega_1 \text{ at } A \text{ intersects } BC \text{ at } E. \text{ Let } \omega_2 \text{ be a circle passing through } B \text{ and tangent to } AB \text{ at } C. \text{ This circle intersects } AB \text{ for the second time at } F. \text{ A line through } E \text{ is tangent to } \omega_2 \text{ at } K \text{ (where } BC \text{ lies between } A \text{ and } K). \text{ Let } M \text{ be the midpoint of arc } BC \text{ of } \omega_1 \text{ (not containing } A). \text{ Prove that } MFAK \text{ is a cyclic quadrilateral.}

positive_text: Let triangle $ABC$ have points $P$ and $Q$ on side $BC$, where $BP = CQ$ and $P$ is closer to $B$ than $Q$. The circle passing through $A, P, Q$ intersects $AB$ and $AC$ at points $E$ and $F$, respectively. Let $T$ be the intersection of lines $EP$ and $FQ$. Draw two lines through the midpoint of $BC$, one parallel to $AB$ and the other to $AC$. These lines intersect $EP$ and $FQ$ at points $X$ and $Y$, respectively. Show that the circles passing through $T, X, Y$ and $A, P, Q$ touch each other at a single point.

negatives.text: In triangle $ABC$, points $P, Q$ lie on side $BC$ such that $BP = CQ$ and $P$ lies between $B, Q$. The circumcircle of triangle $APQ$ intersects sides $AB$ and $AC$ at $E$ and $F$, respectively. The point $T$ is the intersection point of $EP$ and $FQ$. Two lines passing through the midpoint of $AB$ and parallel to $AC$ and $BC$, intersect $EP$ and $FQ$ at points $X$ and $Y$, respectively. Prove that the circumcircles of triangles $TXY$ and $APQ$ are tangent to each other.

In triangle $ABC$, points $P, Q$ lie on side $BC$ such that $BP = CQ$ and $P$ lies between $B, Q$. The circumcircle of triangle $APQ$ intersects sides $AB$ and $AC$ at $E$ and $F$, respectively. The point $T$ is the intersection point of $EP$ and $FQ$. Two lines passing through the midpoint of $BC$ and parallel to $AB$ and $BC$, intersect $EP$ and $FQ$ at points $X$ and $Y$, respectively. Prove that the circumcircles of triangles $TXY$ and $APQ$ are tangent to each other.

In triangle $ABC$, points $P, Q$ lie on side $BC$ such that $BP = 2CQ$ and $P$ lies between $B, Q$. The circumcircle of triangle $APQ$ intersects sides $AB$ and $AC$ at $E$ and $F$, respectively. The point $T$ is the intersection point of $EP$ and $FQ$. Two lines passing through the midpoint of $BC$ and parallel to $AB$ and $AC$, intersect $EP$ and $FQ$ at points $X$ and $Y$, respectively. Prove that the circumcircles of triangles $TXY$ and $APQ$ are tangent to each other.

positive_text:
Determine all functions $f: \mathbb{Z}^+ \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}^+$ such that:
* For any two positive integers $x$ and $y$, the sum $f(x) + f(y)$ is a multiple of $x + y$.
* For any positive integer $x$ with $x \ge 1395$, it is true that $2f(x) \le x^3$.

negatives.text:
Determine all functions $f: \mathbb{Z}^+ \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}^+$ such that:
* For any two positive integers $x$ and $y$, the sum $f(x) + f(y)$ is a multiple of $x + y$.
* For any positive integer $x$ with $x \ge 1395$, it is true that $2f(x) \ge x^3$.

Determine all functions $f: \mathbb{Z}^+ \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}^+$ such that:
* For any two positive integers $x$ and $y$, the sum $f(x) + f(y)$ is a multiple of $x + y$.
* For any positive integer $x$ with $x \ge 1395$, it is true that $2f(x) \le x^2$.

Determine all functions $f: \mathbb{Z}^+ \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}^+$ such that:
* For any two positive integers $x$ and $y$, the sum $f(x) + f(y)$ is a multiple of $x + y$.
* For any positive integer $x$ with $x \ge 1395$, it is true that $2f(x) \le x^3 + 1$.

positive_text: Let $\omega$ be the circle that passes through all the vertices of an isosceles triangle $ABC$ with $AB = AC$. Let $P$ be a point on $\omega$ and $Q$ a point on side $BC$ such that $AP = AQ$. The line $AP$ intersects the line $BC$ at point $R$. Show that the two tangents drawn from $B$ and $C$ to the incircle of triangle $AQR$ (excluding the side $BC$) meet at a point that lies on $\omega$.

negatives.text: Let $\omega$ be the circumcircle of isosceles triangle $ABC$ where $AB = AC$. Points $P$ and $Q$ lie on $\omega$ and $BC$ respectively such that $AP = AQ$. Lines $AP$ and $BC$ intersect at $R$. Prove that the tangents from $B$ and $C$ to the circumcircle of triangle $AQR$ (different from $BC$) are concurrent on $\omega$.

Let $\omega$ be the circumcircle of isosceles triangle $ABC$ where $AB = AC$. Points $P$ and $Q$ lie on $\omega$ and $BC$ respectively such that $AP = AQ$. Lines $BP$ and $BC$ intersect at $R$. Prove that the tangents from $B$ and $C$ to the incircle of triangle $AQR$ (different from $BC$) are concurrent on $\omega$.

Let $\omega$ be the circumcircle of isosceles triangle $ABC$ where $AB = AC$. Points $P$ and $Q$ lie on $\omega$ and $BC$ respectively such that $AP = AQ$. Lines $AP$ and $BC$ intersect at $R$. Prove that the tangents from $A$ and $C$ to the incircle of triangle $AQR$ (different from $BC$) are concurrent on $\omega$.

positive_text: Two circles, one centered at $O$ and the other called $\omega_2$, intersect at points $A$ and $B$. The center $O$ is also on the circle $\omega_2$. Drop a perpendicular from $O$ to the line segment $AB$ and call the foot of this perpendicular $S$. The line $OS$ meets $\omega_2$ again at a point $P$. Draw the angle bisector of $\angle ASP$ and let it intersect the first circle again at a point $L$, such that $A$ and $L$ are on the same side of the line $OP$. Now choose a point $K$ on $\omega_2$ so that the length $PK$ is the same as $PS$, with $A$ and $K$ on the same side of $OP$. Prove that the segments $SL$ and $KL$ are equal in length.

negatives.text: Two circles $\omega_1(O)$ and $\omega_2$ intersect each other at $A, B$. And $O$ lies on $\omega_2$. Let $S$ be the foot of perpendicular line to $AB$ from $O$. Line $OS$ intersects $\omega_2$ for the second time at $P$. The bisector of $\angle ASP$ intersects $\omega_1$ at $L$ ($A$ and $L$ are on the same side of the line $OP$). Let $K$ be a point on $\omega_2$ such that $PS = PK$ ($A$ and $K$ are on the opposite side of the line $OP$). Prove that $SL = KL$.

positive_text: Suppose $ABCD$ is an isosceles trapezoid with bases $AB$ and $CD$, where $AB \parallel CD$. A point $P$ lies inside the trapezoid such that $\angle APB > \angle ADC$ and $\angle DPC > \angle ABC$. Prove that the sum of the lengths of the two bases is greater than the sum of the lengths of the two non-parallel sides.

negatives.text: Suppose $ABCD$ is an isosceles trapezoid with bases $AB$ and $CD$, where $AB \parallel CD$. A point $P$ lies inside the trapezoid such that $\angle APB = \angle ADC$ and $\angle DPC > \angle ABC$. Prove that $AB + CD > AD + BC$.

Suppose $ABCD$ is an isosceles trapezoid with bases $AB$ and $CD$, where $AB \parallel CD$. A point $P$ lies inside the trapezoid such that $\angle APB > \angle ADC$ and $\angle DPC = \angle ABC$. Prove that $AB + CD > AD + BC$.

Suppose $ABCD$ is an isosceles trapezoid with bases $AB$ and $CD$, where $AB \parallel CD$. A point $P$ lies inside the trapezoid such that $\angle APB > \angle ADC$ and $\angle DPC > \angle ABC$. Prove that $AB + CD < AD + BC$.

positive_text: Let triangle $ABC$ have its circumcircle. On the tangent to the circle at $B$ and at $C$, place points $X$ and $Y$ so that $BX = AB$ and $CY = AC$, with $X$, $Y$, and $A$ all on the same side of the line $BC$. If $I$ is the incenter of triangle $ABC$, prove that $$\angle BAC + \angle XIY = 180^\circ$$

negatives.text: Let triangle $ABC$ have its circumcircle. On the tangent to the circle at $B$ and at $C$, place points $X$ and $Y$ so that $BX = AB$ and $CY = AC$, with $X$, $Y$, and $A$ all on the same side of the line $BC$. If $I$ is the excenter of triangle $ABC$, prove that $$\angle BAC + \angle XIY = 180^\circ$$

Let triangle $ABC$ have its circumcircle. On the tangent to the circle at $B$ and at $C$, place points $X$ and $Y$ so that $BX = AB$ and $CY = AC$, with $X$, $Y$, and $A$ all on the same side of the line $BC$. If $I$ is the incenter of triangle $ABC$, prove that $$\angle BAC + \angle XCI = 180^\circ$$

positive_text: In triangle $ABC$, let $M$ be the midpoint of side $BC$. There is a circle $\omega$ inside triangle $ABC$ that touches sides $AB$ and $AC$ at points $E$ and $F$, respectively. From point $M$, two tangent lines are drawn to the circle $\omega$, touching it at points $P$ and $Q$. The point $P$ is chosen such that it lies on the same side of the line $AM$ as point $B$. If lines $PM$ and $BF$ meet at point $X$, and lines $QM$ and $CE$ meet at point $Y$, and if the length of $PM$ is half the length of $BC$, show that the line $XY$ is tangent to the circle $\omega$.

negatives.text: In triangle $ABC$, let $M$ be the midpoint of side $BC$. There is a circle $\omega$ inside triangle $ABC$ that touches sides $AB$ and $AC$ at points $E$ and $F$, respectively. From point $M$, two tangent lines are drawn to the circle $\omega$, touching it at points $P$ and $Q$. The point $P$ is chosen such that it lies on the same side of the line $AM$ as point $B$. If lines $PM$ and $BF$ meet at point $X$, and lines $QM$ and $CE$ meet at point $Y$, and if the length of $PM$ is half the length of $AC$, show that the line $XY$ is tangent to the circle $\omega$.

positive_text:
Suppose $x$ and $y$ are different real numbers with the property that $x^4 - y^4 = x - y$. Show that the inequality
$$
\frac{x - y}{x^6 - y^6} \le \frac{4}{3}(x + y)
$$
holds true.

negatives.text:
Let $x$, $y$ be distinct real numbers such that $x^4 + y^4 = x - y$. Prove that
$$
\frac{x - y}{x^6 - y^6} \le \frac{4}{3}(x + y)
$$

Let $x$, $y$ be distinct real numbers such that $x^4 - y^4 = x + y$. Prove that
$$
\frac{x - y}{x^6 - y^6} \le \frac{4}{3}(x + y)
$$

Let $x$, $y$ be distinct real numbers such that $x^4 - y^4 = x - y$. Prove that
$$
\frac{x + y}{x^6 - y^6} \le \frac{4}{3}(x + y)
$$

positive_text:
Find all functions $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ such that:
(1) For any real numbers $a$ and $b$, $a + f(b + f(a)) = b + f(a + f(b))$,
(2) The set of all possible values $\frac{f(a) - f(b)}{a - b}$, where $a$ and $b$ are different real numbers, forms an interval (i.e., if two such values exist, all numbers between them also exist in the set).

negatives.text:
Find all functions $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ that satisfy the following conditions:
(a) $x + f(y + f(x)) = y + f(x + f(y))$, $\forall x, y \in \mathbb{R}$
(b) The set $I = \left\{\frac{f(x) - f(0)}{x - 0} \mid x \in \mathbb{R}, x \neq 0\right\}$ is an interval.

Find all functions $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ that satisfy the following conditions:
(a) $x + f(y + f(x)) = y + f(x + f(y))$, $\forall x, y \in \mathbb{R}$
(b) The set $I = \left\{\frac{f(x) - f(y)}{x - y} \mid x, y \in \mathbb{R}, x \neq y\right\}$ is a finite set.

Find all functions $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ that satisfy the following conditions:
(a) $x + f(y + f(x)) = y + f(x + f(y))$, $\forall x, y \in \mathbb{R}$
(b) The set $I = \left\{\frac{f(x) - f(y)}{x - y} \mid x, y \in \mathbb{R}, x \neq y\right\}$ is the set $\{1\}$.

positive_text: In trapezoid $ABCD$ with $BC = AD$ and $AB$ parallel to $CD$, diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ intersect at point $P$. The circle passing through points $A$, $P$, and $B$ intersects segment $BC$ again at point $X$. A point $Y$ is chosen on segment $AX$ so that $DY$ is parallel to $BC$, with $C$ and $Y$ on opposite sides of line $AD$. Show that the angle $\angle YDA$ is twice the angle $\angle YCA$.

negatives.text: In isosceles trapezoid $ABCD$ where $BC = AD$ and $AB \parallel CD$, point $P$ is the intersection of diagonals $AC$ and $BD$. Let $X$ be the second intersection point of $AD$ and circumcircle of triangle $APB$ and let $Y$ be a point on $AX$ such that $DY \parallel BC$ ($C$ and $Y$ are on different sides of line $AD$). Prove that $\angle YDA = 2 \times \angle YCA$.

In isosceles trapezoid $ABCD$ where $BC = AD$ and $AB \parallel CD$, point $P$ is the intersection of diagonals $AC$ and $BD$. Let $X$ be the second intersection point of $BC$ and circumcircle of triangle $APB$ and let $Y$ be a point on $AX$ such that $DY \parallel BC$ ($C$ and $Y$ are on the same side of line $AD$). Prove that $\angle YDA = 2 \times \angle YCA$.

positive_text: Two circles, $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$, intersect each other. Points $A$ and $C$ are on $\omega_1$, and points $B$ and $D$ are on $\omega_2$, such that $AB$ and $CD$ are both common tangents to the two circles. Let $M$ be the midpoint of segment $AB$. From point $M$, draw tangent lines (other than $AB$) to $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$; these tangents intersect line $CD$ at points $Y$ and $X$, respectively. Let $I$ be the incenter of triangle $MXY$. Prove that $IC = ID$.

negatives.text: Two circles, $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$, intersect each other. Points $A$ and $C$ are on $\omega_1$, and points $B$ and $D$ are on $\omega_2$, such that $AB$ and $CD$ are both common tangents to the two circles. Let $M$ be the midpoint of segment $AB$. From point $M$, draw tangent lines (other than $AB$) to $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$; these tangents intersect line $AB$ at points $Y$ and $X$, respectively. Let $I$ be the incenter of triangle $MXY$. Prove that $IC = ID$.

Two circles, $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$, intersect each other. Points $A$ and $C$ are on $\omega_1$, and points $B$ and $D$ are on $\omega_2$, such that $AB$ and $CD$ are both common tangents to the two circles. Let $M$ be the midpoint of segment $AB$. From point $M$, draw tangent lines (other than $AB$) to $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$; these tangents intersect line $CD$ at points $Y$ and $X$, respectively. Let $I$ be the circumcenter of triangle $MXY$. Prove that $IC = ID$.

Two circles, $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$, intersect each other. Points $A$ and $C$ are on $\omega_1$, and points $B$ and $D$ are on $\omega_2$, such that $AB$ and $CD$ are both common tangents to the two circles. Let $M$ be the midpoint of segment $AB$. From point $M$, draw tangent lines (other than $AB$) to $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$; these tangents intersect line $CD$ at points $Y$ and $X$, respectively. Let $I$ be the incenter of triangle $MXY$. Prove that $IA = IB$.

positive_text: Let triangle $ABC$ be acute, and let $H$ be the point where the altitudes of the triangle meet. Let $\omega$ be the circle that passes through points $B$, $H$, and $C$, and let $O'$ be the center of this circle. Let $\Gamma$ be the circle that goes through the midpoints of the sides of triangle $ABC$. Choose a point $X$ on the arc of $\omega$ that contains $H$ but not $A$. Draw a line from $A$ through $X$, and let it intersect $\Gamma$ again at point $Y$, with $X$ between $A$ and $Y$. Let $P$ be a point on $\Gamma$ such that the distances from $P$ to $X$ and $Y$ are equal. Prove that the angle between the lines $O'P$ and $PX$ is a right angle.

negatives.text: In acute triangle $ABC$, $H$ is the orthocenter. Let $\omega$ be the circumcircle of triangle $BHC$, and $O'$ be its center. $\Gamma$ is the circle that passes through the midpoints of the edges of triangle $ABC$. Point $X$ is an arbitrary point lying on arc $BHC$ of $\omega$. Line $AX$ intersects $\Gamma$ for the second time at point $Y$, where $X$ lies between $A$ and $Y$. $P$ is a point on $\Gamma$ such that $PX = 2PY$. Prove that $\angle O'PX = 90^\circ$.

In acute triangle $ABC$, $H$ is the orthocenter. Let $\omega$ be the circumcircle of triangle $BHC$, and $O'$ be its center. $\Gamma$ is the circle that passes through the midpoints of the edges of triangle $ABC$. Point $X$ is an arbitrary point lying on arc $BHC$ of $\omega$. Line $AX$ intersects $\Gamma$ for the second time at point $Y$, where $X$ lies between $A$ and $Y$. $P$ is a point on $\Gamma$ such that $PX = PY$. Prove that $\angle O'PY = 90^\circ$.

positive_text:
Let $P(x)$ be a non-constant polynomial with real coefficients where $P(0) = 0$. Show that for any positive number $M$, there is some whole number $d$ such that for any monic polynomial $Q(x)$ of degree $\geq d$, the number of integer values of $k$ satisfying
$$
|P(Q(k))| \leq M
$$
is less than or equal to the degree of $Q(x)$.

negatives.text:
Let $P(x)$ be a non-constant polynomial with real coefficients such that $P(0) = 0$. For all positive real numbers $M$, prove that there is a positive integer $d$ such that for any monic polynomial $Q(x)$ of degree greater than or equal to $d$, total number of integers $k$ where
$$
|P(k)| \leq M
$$
is at most $\deg Q(x)$.

Let $P(x)$ be a non-constant polynomial with real coefficients such that $P(0) = 0$. For all positive real numbers $M$, prove that there is a positive integer $d$ such that for any monic polynomial $Q(x)$ of degree greater than or equal to $d$, total number of integers $k$ where
$$
|P(Q(k))| \geq M
$$
is at most $\deg Q(x)$.

positive_text: In triangle $ABC$, where all angles are less than 90 degrees, altitudes $BE$ and $CF$ intersect at $H$. Let $O$ be the center of the circle that passes through points $A$, $B$, and $C$. Let $M$ be the center point of segment $BC$. On segment $EF$, place a point $P$ such that line $HP$ is perpendicular to line $HO$. On segment $HA$, place a point $Q$ such that line $PQ$ is perpendicular to line $HM$. Show that the length of segment $QA$ is three times the length of segment $QH$.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be an acute-angled triangle. The altitudes $BE$, $CF$ meet at $H$. $O$ is the circumcenter of triangle $ABC$. $M$ is the midpoint of $BC$. $P$ is the point on $EF$ such that $HP \perp HO$. $Q$ is the point on $HB$ such that $PQ \perp HM$. Prove that $QA = 3QH$.

Let $ABC$ be an acute-angled triangle. The altitudes $BE$, $CF$ meet at $H$. $O$ is the circumcenter of triangle $ABC$. $M$ is the midpoint of $BC$. $P$ is the point on $EF$ such that $HP \perp HO$. $Q$ is the point on $HA$ such that $PQ \perp HO$. Prove that $QA = 3QH$.

positive_text: Consider an isosceles triangle $\triangle ABC$ where $AB = AC$. Let $I$ be the incenter of the triangle. A circle $\omega$ goes through points $C$ and $I$ and is tangent to the segment $AI$. This circle $\omega$ intersects side $AC$ at a point $Q$ and the circumcircle of $\triangle ABC$ at a point $D$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of side $AB$, and let $N$ be the midpoint of segment $CQ$. Show that the lines $AD$, $MN$, and $BC$ all meet at a single point.

negatives.text: Let $\triangle ABC$ be an isosceles triangle ($AB = AC$) with incenter $I$. Circle $\omega$ passes through $C$ and $I$ and is tangent to $BI$. The circle $\omega$ intersects $AC$ and circumcircle of $\triangle ABC$ at $Q$ and $D$, respectively. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $AB$ and $N$ be the midpoint of $CQ$. Prove that $AD$, $MN$ and $BC$ are concurrent.

Let $\triangle ABC$ be an isosceles triangle ($AB = AC$) with incenter $I$. Circle $\omega$ passes through $C$ and $I$ and is tangent to $AI$. The circle $\omega$ intersects $AB$ and circumcircle of $\triangle ABC$ at $Q$ and $D$, respectively. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $AB$ and $N$ be the midpoint of $CQ$. Prove that $AD$, $MN$ and $BC$ are concurrent.

Let $\triangle ABC$ be an isosceles triangle ($AB = AC$) with incenter $I$. Circle $\omega$ passes through $C$ and $I$ and is tangent to $AI$. The circle $\omega$ intersects $AC$ and circumcircle of $\triangle ABC$ at $Q$ and $D$, respectively. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $AB$ and $N$ be the midpoint of $AQ$. Prove that $AD$, $MN$ and $BC$ are concurrent.

positive_text: Show that for any integer $ k > 1 $, there exists a real number $ x $ such that for all integers $ n $ with $ 1 < n < 1398 $: $$ \{x^n\} < \{x^{n-1}\} $$ if and only if $ n $ is divisible by $ k $.

negatives.text: For every positive integer $ k > 1 $, prove that there exists a real number $ x $ such that for every positive integer $ n < 1398 $: $$ \{x^n\} > \{x^{n-1}\} \iff k \mid n. $$
For every positive integer $ k > 1 $, prove that there exists a real number $ x $ such that for every positive integer $ n < 1398 $: $$ \{x^n\} < \{x^{n+1}\} \iff k \mid n. $$
For every positive integer $ k > 1 $, prove that there exists a real number $ x $ such that for every positive integer $ n < 1398 $: $$ \{x^n\} < \{x^{n-1}\} \iff k \nmid n. $$

positive_text: Let $\triangle ABC$ be an acute isosceles triangle with $AB = AC$ and $\angle BAC > 60^\circ$. Let $O$ be the center of the circle that passes through all three vertices of $\triangle ABC$. Place a point $P$ on the circle that passes through points $B$, $O$, and $C$ such that $BP$ is parallel to $AC$. Then place a point $K$ on segment $AP$ so that the length of $BK$ is the same as the length of $BC$. Show that the line $CK$ divides the arc $\widearc{BC}$ of the circle through $B$, $O$, and $C$ into two equal parts.

negatives.text: Consider an acute-angled triangle $\triangle ABC$ with $AB = AC$ and $\angle A > 60^\circ$. Let $O$ be the circumcenter of $\triangle ABC$. Point $P$ lies on the circumcircle of $\triangle BOC$ such that $BP \parallel AC$, and point $K$ lies on segment $AP$ such that $BK = AC$. Prove that line $CK$ bisects the arc $\widearc{BC}$ of circumcircle of $\triangle BOC$.

Consider an acute-angled triangle $\triangle ABC$ with $AB = AC$ and $\angle A > 60^\circ$. Let $O$ be the circumcenter of $\triangle ABC$. Point $P$ lies on the circumcircle of $\triangle BOC$ such that $BP \parallel AC$, and point $K$ lies on segment $AP$ such that $BK = BC$. Prove that line $CK$ bisects the arc $\widearc{AB}$ of circumcircle of $\triangle BOC$.

positive_text: \text{Let } n > 2 \text{ be a natural number. Show that there are no positive integers } x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n \text{ all greater than 1 such that:} \quad (x_1x_2\dots x_n)^2 = x_1^3 + x_2^3 + \dots + x_n^3

negatives.text: \text{Let } n > 2 \text{ be a natural number. Prove that the following equation has no solution } x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n \text{ in positive integers numbers greater than 1:} \quad (x_1x_2\dots x_n)^2 = x_1^2 + x_2^2 + \dots + x_n^2

\text{Let } n > 2 \text{ be a natural number. Prove that the following equation has no solution } x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n \text{ in positive integers numbers greater than 1:} \quad (x_1x_2\dots x_n)^2 = x_1^3 + x_2^3 + \dots + x_n^3 + 1

\text{Let } n > 2 \text{ be a natural number. Prove that the following equation has no solution } x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n \text{ in positive integers numbers greater than 1:} \quad (x_1x_2\dots x_n)^2 = x_1^3 + x_2^3 + \dots + x_n^3, \text{ where all } x_i \leq 1

positive_text:
We say that a positive integer $n$ is special if the following condition holds: For any rearrangement $\sigma$ of the numbers $1, 2, \dots, n$, we can find $n$ polynomial functions $P_1, P_2, \dots, P_n$ and a small positive number $\epsilon$ such that:

1. All the polynomials have the same value at $x = 0$.
2. When $x$ is just a little bit less than $0$ (but still greater than $-\epsilon$), the values of the polynomials follow the order $P_1(x) > P_2(x) > \dots > P_n(x)$.
3. When $x$ is just a little bit more than $0$ (but still less than $\epsilon$), the values of the polynomials follow the order $P_{\sigma(1)}(x) > P_{\sigma(2)}(x) > \dots > P_{\sigma(n)}(x)$.

Find all such special numbers $n$.

negatives.text:
We call an integer number $n > 0$ interesting if for each permutation $\sigma$ of $1, 2, \dots, n$ there exist polynomials $P_1, P_2, \dots, P_n$ and $\epsilon > 0$ such that:
$$
i)\ P_1(0) = P_2(0) = \dots = P_n(0).
$$
$$
ii)\ P_1(x) > P_2(x) > \dots > P_n(x) \text{ for } -\epsilon < x < 0.
$$
$$
iii)\ P_{\sigma(1)}(x) > P_{\sigma(2)}(x) > \dots > P_{\sigma(n)}(x) \text{ for } 0 < x < \epsilon.
$$
$$
iv)\ P_i(x) > 0 \text{ for all } x \in (-\epsilon, \epsilon) \text{ and all } i.
$$
Find all interesting numbers.

We call an integer number $n > 0$ interesting if for each permutation $\sigma$ of $1, 2, \dots, n$ there exist polynomials $P_1, P_2, \dots, P_n$ and $\epsilon > 0$ such that:
$$
i)\ P_1(0) = P_2(0) = \dots = P_n(0).
$$
$$
ii)\ P_1(x) > P_2(x) > \dots > P_n(x) \text{ for } -\epsilon < x < 0.
$$
$$
iii)\ P_{\sigma(1)}(x) > P_{\sigma(2)}(x) > \dots > P_{\sigma(n)}(x) \text{ for } 0 < x < \epsilon.
$$
$$
iv)\ P_i(x) = 0 \text{ for some } x \in (-\epsilon, \epsilon) \text{ and all } i.
$$
Find all interesting numbers.

positive_text: Let $ g $ be a function from the interval $[0, 1]$ to the real numbers with the following properties: For any way to split $[0, 1]$ into two non-empty parts $ A $ and $ B $, there is always a number in one part whose image under $ g $ lies in the other part. Also, $ g(x) > x $ for all $ x $ in $[0, 1] $. Show that there are infinitely many values of $ x $ for which $ g(x) = 1 $.

negatives.text: Let $ g $ be a function from the interval $[0, 1]$ to the real numbers with the following properties: For any way to split $[0, 1]$ into two non-empty parts $ A $ and $ B $, there is always a number in one part whose image under $ g $ lies in the other part. Also, $ g(x) < x $ for all $ x $ in $[0, 1] $. Show that there are infinitely many values of $ x $ for which $ g(x) = 0 $.

Let $ g $ be a function from the interval $[0, 1]$ to the real numbers with the following properties: For any way to split $[0, 1]$ into two non-empty parts $ A $ and $ B $, there is always a number in one part whose image under $ g $ lies in the other part. Also, $ g(x) > x $ for all $ x $ in $[0, 1] $. Show that there are infinitely many values of $ x $ for which $ g(x) = 0 $.

Let $ g $ be a function from the interval $[0, 1]$ to the real numbers with the following properties: For any way to split $[0, 1]$ into two non-empty parts $ A $ and $ B $, there is always a number in one part whose image under $ g $ lies in the other part. Also, $ g(x) > x $ for all $ x $ in $[0, 1] $. Show that there are infinitely many values of $ x $ for which $ g(x) = x $.

positive_text:
Let $a$, $b$, $c$ be non-zero and different real numbers. Suppose there are functions $f$ and $g$ that take positive real numbers and give real numbers, and satisfy the rule
$$
a f(xy) + b f\left(\frac{x}{y}\right) = c f(x) + g(y)
$$
for all positive real numbers $x$ and for all $y$ that are sufficiently large.
Show that there exists another function $h$ that also takes positive real numbers and gives real numbers such that
$$
f(xy) + f\left(\frac{x}{y}\right) = 2f(x) + h(y)
$$
holds for all positive real numbers $x$ and for all $y$ that are sufficiently large.

negatives.text:
Let $a$, $b$, $c$ be non-zero distinct real numbers so that there exist functions $f$, $g : \mathbb{R}^+ \to \mathbb{R}$ so that
$$
a f(xy) + b f\left(\frac{x}{y}\right) = c f(x) + g(y)
$$
for all positive real $x$ and large enough $y$.
Prove that there exists a function $h : \mathbb{R}^+ \to \mathbb{R}$ so that
$$
f(xy) - f\left(\frac{x}{y}\right) = 2f(x) + h(y)
$$
for all positive real $x$ and large enough $y$.

Let $a$, $b$, $c$ be non-zero distinct real numbers so that there exist functions $f$, $g : \mathbb{R}^+ \to \mathbb{R}$ so that
$$
a f(xy) + b f\left(\frac{x}{y}\right) = c f(x) + g(y)
$$
for all positive real $x$ and large enough $y$.
Prove that there exists a function $h : \mathbb{R}^+ \to \mathbb{R}$ so that
$$
f(xy) + f\left(\frac{x}{y}\right) = f(x) + h(y)
$$
for all positive real $x$ and large enough $y$.

Let $a$, $b$, $c$ be non-zero distinct real numbers so that there exist functions $f$, $g : \mathbb{R}^+ \to \mathbb{R}$ so that
$$
a f(xy) + b f\left(\frac{x}{y}\right) = c f(x) + g(y)
$$
for all positive real $x$ and large enough $y$.
Prove that there exists a function $h : \mathbb{R}^+ \to \mathbb{R}$ so that
$$
f(xy) + f\left(\frac{x}{y}\right) = 2f(x) + h(x)
$$
for all positive real $x$ and large enough $y$.

positive_text: An infinite set $ S $ of positive integers is called *good* if, for any three distinct elements $ a $, $ b $, and $ c $ in $ S $, every positive divisor of $ \frac{a^c - b^c}{a - b} $ is also in $ S $. Show that, for any positive integer $ n > 1 $, we can find a good set $ S $ that does not contain $ n $.

negatives.text: We call an infinite set $ S \subseteq \mathbb{N} $ *good* if for all pairwise distinct integers $ a $, $ b $, $ c \in S $, all positive divisors of $ \frac{a^b - b^c}{a - b} $ are in $ S $. For all positive integers $ n > 1 $, prove that there exists a good set $ S $ such that $ n \notin S $.

We call an infinite set $ S \subseteq \mathbb{N} $ *good* if for all pairwise distinct integers $ a $, $ b $, $ c \in S $, all positive divisors of $ \frac{a^c - b^c}{a - b} $ are in $ S $. For all positive integers $ n > 1 $, prove that there exists a good set $ S $ such that $ S $ is finite.

positive_text: A cyclic quadrilateral $ABCD$ has a circumcenter $O$. The diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ meet at point $P$. Points $M$ and $N$ are the midpoints of $AD$ and $BC$, respectively. Let $\omega_1$, $\omega_2$, and $\omega_3$ be the circumcircles of triangles $ADP$, $BCP$, and $OMN$. Points $E$ and $F$ are the second intersection points of $\omega_1$ and $\omega_3$, and $\omega_2$ and $\omega_3$, respectively. Show that the distances from $O$ to $E$ and $F$ are equal.

negatives.text: Cyclic quadrilateral $ABCD$ with circumcenter $O$ is given. Point $P$ is the intersection of diagonals $AC$ and $BD$. Let $M$ and $N$ be midpoints of the sides $AD$ and $BC$, respectively. Suppose that $\omega_1$, $\omega_2$ and $\omega_3$ are circumcircles of triangles $ABP$, $CDP$ and $OMN$, respectively. Let $E$ and $F$ be intersection points of $\omega_1$ and $\omega_3$, which is not on the arc $APD$ of $\omega_1$, and the intersection point of $\omega_2$ and $\omega_3$, which is not on the arc $BPC$ of $\omega_2$, respectively. Prove that $OE = OF$.

Cyclic quadrilateral $ABCD$ with circumcenter $O$ is given. Point $P$ is the intersection of diagonals $AC$ and $BD$. Let $M$ and $N$ be midpoints of the sides $AD$ and $BC$, respectively. Suppose that $\omega_1$, $\omega_2$ and $\omega_3$ are circumcircles of triangles $ADP$, $BCP$ and $OMN$, respectively. Let $E$ and $F$ be intersection points of $\omega_1$ and $\omega_3$, which is not on the arc $APD$ of $\omega_1$, and the intersection point of $\omega_2$ and $\omega_3$, which is not on the arc $BPC$ of $\omega_2$, respectively. Prove that $PE = PF$.

positive_text: Given triangle $ABC$ with $AB < AC$, let $I$ be the incenter, and let $E$ be the point where the $A$-excircle touches side $BC$. Choose a point $F$ on the external angle bisector of $\angle BAC$ such that $F$ and $E$ are on the same side of $AI$ and $\angle AIF = \angle AEB$. Let $Q$ be a point on $BC$ where $\angle AIQ = 90^\circ$. Suppose $\omega_b$ is a circle tangent to $FQ$ and $AB$ at $B$, and $\omega_c$ is a circle tangent to $FQ$ and $AC$ at $C$, both lying inside triangle $ABC$. If $M$ is the midpoint of the arc $BC$ that does not include $A$, prove that $M$ lies on the radical axis of $\omega_b$ and $\omega_c$.

negatives.text: In triangle $ABC$, with $AB < AC$, $I$ is the incenter, $E$ is the intersection of $A$-excircle, and $BC$. Point $F$ lies on the external angle bisector of $\angle BAC$ such that $E$ and $F$ lie on the same side of the line $AI$ and $\angle AIF = \angle AEB$. Point $Q$ lies on $BC$ such that $\angle AIQ = 90^\circ$. Circle $\omega_b$ is tangent to $FQ$ and $AB$ at $B$, circle $\omega_c$ is tangent to $FQ$ and $AC$ at $C$ and both circles are passing through the inside of triangle $ABC$. If $M$ is the midpoint of the arc $BC$, which contains $A$, prove that $M$ lies on the radical axis of $\omega_b$ and $\omega_c$.

In triangle $ABC$, with $AB < AC$, $I$ is the incenter, $E$ is the intersection of $A$-excircle, and $BC$. Point $F$ lies on the external angle bisector of $\angle BAC$ such that $E$ and $F$ lie on the same side of the line $AI$ and $\angle AIF = \angle AEB$. Point $Q$ lies on $BC$ such that $\angle AIQ = 90^\circ$. Circle $\omega_b$ is tangent to $FQ$ and $AC$ at $C$, circle $\omega_c$ is tangent to $FQ$ and $AB$ at $B$ and both circles are passing through the inside of triangle $ABC$. If $M$ is the midpoint of the arc $BC$, which does not contain $A$, prove that $M$ lies on the radical axis of $\omega_b$ and $\omega_c$.

In triangle $ABC$, with $AB < AC$, $I$ is the incenter, $E$ is the intersection of $A$-excircle, and $BC$. Point $F$ lies on the external angle bisector of $\angle BAC$ such that $E$ and $F$ lie on the same side of the line $AI$ and $\angle AIF = \angle AEB$. Point $Q$ lies on $BC$ such that $\angle AIQ = 90^\circ$. Circle $\omega_b$ is tangent to $FQ$ and $AB$ at $B$, circle $\omega_c$ is tangent to $FQ$ and $AC$ at $C$ and both circles are passing through the inside of triangle $ABC$. If $M$ is the midpoint of the arc $BC$, which does not contain $A$, prove that $M$ lies on the line $BC$.

positive_text: Suppose we have $n \ge 6$ points on a flat surface with the condition that no three points lie on the same straight line. A "road map" is defined as a set of line segments connecting these points, such that it is possible to travel between any two points using the segments, and no two segments cross each other except at the points. Show that it is possible to create three such road maps $G_1, G_2, G_3$ where each road map uses different segments — meaning no segment is shared between $G_1$, $G_2$, and $G_3$.

negatives.text: Suppose we have $n \ge 6$ points on a flat surface with the condition that no three points lie on the same straight line. A "road map" is defined as a set of line segments connecting these points, such that it is possible to travel between any two points using the segments, and no two segments cross each other except at the points. Show that it is possible to create three such road maps $G_1, G_2, G_3$ where each road map uses the same set of segments — meaning all three road maps use the exact same line segments.

Suppose we have $n \ge 6$ points on a flat surface with the condition that no three points lie on the same straight line. A "road map" is defined as a set of line segments connecting these points, such that it is possible to travel between any two points using the segments, and no two segments cross each other except at the points. Show that it is possible to create three such road maps $G_1, G_2, G_3$ where each road map has at least one edge in common with the others.

Suppose we have $n \ge 6$ points on a flat surface with the condition that no three points lie on the same straight line. positive_text: Suppose that $n$ is a whole number greater than or equal to 3. What is the largest whole number $k$ for which we can choose numbers $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$ from the interval $[0, 1)$ (not necessarily different) such that for each whole number $j$ from 1 to $k$, we can find a sum of some of the $a_i$'s that equals $j$?

negatives.text: Suppose that $3 \le n$ is a natural number. Find the maximum value of the natural number $k$, for which, there are real numbers $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n \in [0, 1)$ (not necessarily distinct) such that for every natural number $j$ satisfying $j < k$, there exists a sum of a certain number of $a_i$'s equal to $j$.

Suppose that $3 \le n$ is a natural number. Find the maximum value of the natural number $k$, for which, there are real numbers $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n \in [0, 1)$ (not necessarily distinct) such that for every natural number $j$ satisfying $j \le k$, there exists a product of a certain number of $a_i$'s equal to $j$.

Suppose that $3 \le n$ is a natural number. Find the maximum value of the natural number $k$, for which, there are real numbers $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n \in [0, 1)$ (not necessarily distinct) such that for every natural number $j$ satisfying $j \le k$, there exists a sum of exactly one $a_i$ equal to $j$.

positive_text: In an isosceles triangle $ABC$ where $AB = BC$, pick a point $P$ anywhere on the line dropping straight down from $B$ to $AC$. The circle passing through points $B$, $A$, and $P$ meets side $AC$ again at point $M$. Now reflect $M$ over the center of segment $AC$ to find point $N$. Draw a line from $N$ through $P$; this line meets the circle through $B$, $A$, and $P$ again at point $X$. Then draw a line from $A$ to $B$; this line meets the circle through $N$, $A$, and $P$ again at point $Y$. Draw a line that just touches the circle through $N$, $A$, and $P$ at point $A$; this line meets the line from $B$ to $P$ at point $Z$. Show that the line from $C$ to $Z$ touches the circle through $X$, $Y$, and $P$ without crossing it.

negatives.text: In an isosceles triangle $ABC$ ($BC = BA$), point $P$ is arbitrarily chosen on the altitude from vertex $B$. Suppose that the circumcircle of $BAP$ intersects $AB$ for the second time at point $M$. Let $N$ be the reflection of $M$ with respect to the midpoint of $AC$. $NP$ intersects the circumcircle of $BAP$ at $X$ ($X \neq P$), and $AB$ intersects the circumcircle of $NAP$ at $Y$ ($Y \neq A$). The tangent to the circumcircle of $NAP$ at $A$ intersects $BP$ at $Z$. Prove that $CZ$ is tangent to the circumcircle of $XYP$.

In an isosceles triangle $ABC$ ($BC = BA$), point $P$ is arbitrarily chosen on the altitude from vertex $B$. Suppose that the circumcircle of $BAP$ intersects $AC$ for the second time at point $M$. Let $N$ be the reflection of $M$ with respect to the midpoint of $AB$. $NP$ intersects the circumcircle of $BAP$ at $X$ ($X \neq P$), and $AB$ intersects the circumcircle of $NAP$ at $Y$ ($Y \neq A$). The tangent to the circumcircle of $NAP$ at $A$ intersects $BP$ at $Z$. Prove that $CZ$ is tangent to the circumcircle of $XYP$.

In an isosceles triangle $ABC$ ($BC = BA$), point $P$ is arbitrarily chosen on the altitude from vertex $B$. Suppose that the circumcircle of $BAP$ intersects $AC$ for the second time at point $M$. Let $N$ be the reflection of $M$ with respect to the midpoint of $AC$. $NP$ intersects the circumcircle of $BAP$ at $X$ ($X \neq P$), and $BC$ intersects the circumcircle of $NAP$ at $Y$ ($Y \neq A$). The tangent to the circumcircle of $NAP$ at $A$ intersects $BP$ at $Z$. Prove that $CZ$ is tangent to the circumcircle of $XYP$.

positive_text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle with incenter $I$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of the arc $BC$ (not containing $A$) on the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$. Let $X$ be a point on the external bisector of angle $\angle BAC$. The line $BX$ intersects the circumcircle of triangle $BIC$ again at $T$. Let $Y$ be a point on the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ such that the distance from $M$ to $Y$ equals the distance from $M$ to $A$. Prove that the line $TC$ is parallel to the line $AY$.

negatives.text: In the triangle $ABC$, $I$ is the incenter and $M$ is the midpoint of the part of arc $BC$ on the circumcircle of $ABC$ that doesn't contain $A$. $X$ is a point on the internal angle bisector of $\angle BAC$. The line $BX$ meets the circumcircle of $BIC$ at $T$, for the second time. The point $Y$ is on the circumcircle of $ABC$ such that $MA = MY$. Prove that $TC \parallel AY$.

In the triangle $ABC$, $I$ is the incenter and $M$ is the midpoint of the part of arc $BC$ on the circumcircle of $ABC$ that doesn't contain $A$. $X$ is a point on the external angle bisector of $\angle BAC$. The line $CX$ meets the circumcircle of $BIC$ at $T$, for the second time. The point $Y$ is on the circumcircle of $ABC$ such that $MA = MY$. Prove that $TC \parallel AY$.

In the triangle $ABC$, $I$ is the incenter and $M$ is the midpoint of the part of arc $BC$ on the circumcircle of $ABC$ that doesn't contain $A$. $X$ is a point on the external angle bisector of $\angle BAC$. The line $BX$ meets the circumcircle of $BIC$ at $T$, for the second time. The point $Y$ is on the circumcircle of $ABC$ such that $MB = MY$. Prove that $TC \parallel AY$.

positive_text:
Let triangle $ABC$ have midpoints $M$ and $N$ on sides $AB$ and $AC$, respectively. The lines $BN$ and $CM$ meet the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ again at points $N'$ and $M'$, respectively. Points $X$ and $Y$ lie on the line $BC$ extended such that $B$ is between $X$ and $C$, and $C$ is between $Y$ and $B$.

$$
\angle BXM' = \angle ACM, \angle CYN' = \angle ABN
$$

Show that the distances $AX$ and $AY$ are equal.

$$

Show that the distances $AX$ and $AY$ are equal.

positive_text:
Let $x, y, z$ be positive integers with $y > x > 1$ and $\gcd(z, xy) = 1$. Show that there exists a positive integer $n$ such that
$$
z \mid \binom{y^n}{x^n}
$$

negatives.text:
Let $a, b, c$ be natural numbers such that $b > a > 1$ and $\gcd(c, ab) = 1$. Prove that there exists a natural number $n$ such that
$$
c \mid \binom{a^n}{b^n}
$$

Let $a, b, c$ be natural numbers such that $b > a > 1$ and $\gcd(c, ab) = 1$. Prove that there exists a natural number $n$ such that
$$
c \mid \binom{b^{n+1}}{a^n}
$$

Let $a, b, c$ be natural numbers such that $b > a > 1$ and $\gcd(c, ab) = 1$. Prove that there exists a natural number $n$ such that
$$
c \mid \binom{b^n}{a^{n+1}}
$$

positive_text: In triangle $ABC$, with $\angle A > 90^\circ$, let points $E$ and $F$ be the feet of the perpendiculars from $B$ and $C$ to the opposite sides, respectively. The tangents to the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ at $B$ and $C$ intersect the line $EF$ at points $K$ and $L$, respectively. Given that $\angle CLB = 135^\circ$, let point $R$ lie on segment $BK$ so that $KR = KL$. Let point $S$ lie on the line $BK$, with $K$ between $B$ and $S$, and $\angle BLS = 135^\circ$. Show that the circle with diameter $RS$ is tangent to the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$.

positive_text: Imagine you have a number $n$ that is at least 4. Now, consider all the ways to rearrange the numbers $1, 2, \dots, n$. For each rearrangement, you multiply each number by its position and add up the results. For example, in the rearrangement $ (2, 1, 3) $ for $ n = 3 $, you would calculate $ 1\cdot2 + 2\cdot1 + 3\cdot3 = 2 + 2 + 9 = 13 $. Now, for your value of $ n $, how many different total values can you get by doing this for every possible rearrangement?

negatives.text: Let $n$ be a positive integer such that $n \ge 4$. For every permutation $(s_1, s_2, \dots, s_n)$ of the numbers $1, 2, \dots, n$, we calculate the following expression and write the result on the board: $$1s_1 + 2s_2 + 3s_3 + \dots + ns_n$$ In the end, what is the maximum value that will be written on the board?

Let $n$ be a positive integer such that $n \ge 4$. For every permutation $(s_1, s_2, \dots, s_n)$ of the numbers $1, 2, \dots, n$, we calculate the following expression and write the result on the board: $$1s_1 + 2s_2 + 3s_3 + \dots + ns_n$$ In the end, what is the sum of all the distinct values written on the board?

positive_text:
Find all sequences $(x_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of positive integers such that for every $n \ge 3$ we have:
$$
\frac{1}{x_1 x_3} + \frac{1}{x_2 x_4} + \frac{1}{x_3 x_5} + \dots + \frac{1}{x_{n-2} x_n} = 1 - \frac{1}{x_1^2 + x_2^2 + \dots + x_{n-1}^2}
$$

negatives.text:
Find all sequences $(a_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of positive integers such that for every $n \ge 3$ we have:
$$
\frac{1}{a_1 a_2} + \frac{1}{a_2 a_3} + \frac{1}{a_3 a_4} + \dots + \frac{1}{a_{n-2} a_{n-1}} = 1 - \frac{1}{a_1^2 + a_2^2 + \dots + a_{n-1}^2}
$$

Find all sequences $(a_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of positive integers such that for every $n \ge 3$ we have:
$$
\frac{1}{a_1 a_3} + \frac{1}{a_2 a_4} + \frac{1}{a_3 a_5} + \dots + \frac{1}{a_{n-2} a_n} = 1 - \frac{1}{a_1 + a_2 + \dots + a_{n-1}}
$$

Find all sequences $(a_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of positive integers such that for every $n \ge 3$ we have:
$$
\frac{1}{a_1 a_3} + \frac{1}{a_2 a_4} + \frac{1}{a_3 a_5} + \dots + \frac{1}{a_{n-2} a_n} = 1 + \frac{1}{a_1^2 + a_2^2 + \dots + a_{n-1}^2}
$$

positive_text: Consider a plane with $ n > 10 $ lines, where no three lines meet at a single point and no two lines are parallel. These lines divide the plane into finite regions. At least $ \frac{n^2}{8} + 1 $ of these regions are colored black. A triangle is called *good* if it contains exactly one black region. Show that there are at least $ \frac{n}{2} $ good triangles.

negatives.text: Let $ n > 10 $ be a positive integer. $ n $ lines are drawn on the plane such that no three are concurrent and no two are parallel. Among the finite regions formed by these lines, at least $ \frac{n^2}{8} $ of them are blackened. A triangle is called *good* if there is only one black region inside of it. Prove that we have at least $ \frac{n}{2} $ good triangles.

Among the finite regions formed by these lines, at least $ \frac{n^2}{8} + 1 $ of them are blackened. A triangle is called *good* if there are at most two black regions inside of it. Prove that we have at least $ \frac{n}{2} $ good triangles.

Let $ n > 10 $ be a positive integer. $ n $ lines are drawn on the plane such that no three are concurrent and no two are parallel. Among the finite regions formed by these lines, at least $ \frac{n^2}{8} + 1 $ of them are blackened. A triangle is called *good* if there is only one black region inside of it. Prove that we have at least $ \frac{n}{3} $ good triangles.

positive_text:
Consider a triangle $\triangle ABC$ with side lengths $BC = a$, $CA = b$, and $AB = c$. The angle bisectors of $\angle A$, $\angle B$, and $\angle C$ intersect the opposite sides at points $D$, $E$, and $F$, respectively. Let the lengths of the angle bisectors $AD$, $BE$, and $CF$ be $d$, $e$, and $f$. Show that the product $def$ is equal to
$$
\frac{4abc(a+b+c)\Delta}{(a+b)(b+c)(c+a)},
$$
where $\Delta$ is the area of triangle $ABC$.

negatives.text:
Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle with side lengths $BC = a$, $CA = b$, and $AB = c$. Let the medians from $A$, $B$, and $C$ intersect the opposite sides at $D$, $E$, and $F$, respectively. Denote the lengths of the medians $AD$, $BE$, and $CF$ by $d$, $e$, and $f$, respectively. Prove that
$$
def = \frac{4abc(a+b+c)\Delta}{(a+b)(b+c)(c+a)},$$
where $\Delta$ is the area of triangle $ABC$.

Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle with side lengths $BC = a$, $CA = b$, and $AB = c$. Let the internal bisectors of the angles $\angle BAC$, $\angle ABC$, and $\angle BCA$ intersect the sides $BC$, $CA$, and $AB$ at $D$, $E$, and $F$, respectively. Denote the lengths of the line segments $AD$, $BE$, and $CF$ by $d$, $e$, and $f$. Prove that
$$
def = \frac{4abc(a+b+c)}{(a+b)(b+c)(c+a)}.$$

positive_text:
Let $r$ and $n$ be whole numbers such that $r \le n$.

a. Show that the expression
$$
\frac{n+1-2r}{n+1-r} \cdot \binom{n}{r}
$$
is always an integer.

b. Show that the sum
$$
\sum_{r=0}^{\lfloor n/2 \rfloor} \frac{n+1-2r}{n+1-r} \cdot \binom{n}{r}
$$
is less than $2^{n-2}$ for every $n \ge 9$.

(Recall that $\binom{n}{r} = \frac{n!}{r!(n-r)!}$. Also, for any real number $x$, the floor function $\lfloor x \rfloor$ is the largest integer less than or equal to $x$.)

b. Show that the sum
$$
\sum_{r=0}^{\lfloor n/2 \rfloor} \frac{n+1-2r}{n+2-r} \cdot \binom{n}{r}
$$

positive_text:
Let $n$ be a positive integer and consider sequences of length $n$, where each term is $-1$, $0$, or $1$. For each such sequence, define its sum modulo 4. Let $f_k(n)$ be the number of such sequences whose sum modulo 4 is equal to $k$, where $k$ is in the set $\{0, 1, 2, 3\}$.

a. Show that $f_1(n) = f_3(n)$ for all positive integers $n$.

b. Show that for all positive integers $n$, the number of sequences whose sum is divisible by 4 is given by
$$
f_0(n) = \frac{3^n + 2 + (-1)^n}{4}.
$$

$$

positive_text:
Let $p(x)$ be a polynomial where all its coefficients are fractions or whole numbers. Show that you can find a positive whole number $n$ such that the polynomial $q(x)$, defined as
$$
q(x) = p(x + n) - p(x),
$$
has only whole number coefficients.

negatives.text:
Let $p(x)$ be a polynomial with rational coefficients. Prove that there exists a positive integer $n$ such that the polynomial $q(x)$ defined by
$$
q(x) = p(x + n) + p(x)
$$
has integer coefficients.

Let $p(x)$ be a polynomial with rational coefficients. Prove that there exists a positive integer $n$ such that the polynomial $q(x)$ defined by
$$
q(x) = p(x + n) - p(x)
$$

positive_text:
Suppose triangle $ABC$ is isosceles with $AB = AC$. A point $D$ lies on the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ on the same side of line $BC$ as point $A$. Prove that
$$
AB + AC \ge DB + DC
$$
and that equality holds only when $D = A$. Use this to show that among all triangles inscribed in a circle, the equilateral triangle has the largest perimeter.

negatives.text:

$$
|AB| + |AC| \ge |DB| + |DC|
$$
with equality if and only if $D = A$. Hence prove, of all triangles described in a circle, the equilateral triangle has the greatest perimeter.

Let $ABC$ be an isosceles triangle with $|AB| = |AC|$. If $D$ is a point on the circumcircle of $\triangle ABC$ on the same side of $BC$ as $A$, prove

$$

positive_text: In triangle $ABC$, the side $AB$ is shorter than the side $AC$. $$
\text{the length of } AD(\lambda) \text{ is less than or equal to the length of } AD(2 - \lambda) \text{ if and only if } \lambda \ge 1.
$$

negatives.text:
Let $ABC$ be a planar triangle. Let $\lambda \ge 0$. Define the point $D(\lambda)$ on the side $BC$ so that $D(\lambda)$ divides $BC$ in the ratio $c^\lambda : b^\lambda$. Prove that
$$
|AD(\lambda)| \le |AD(\lambda + 1)| \quad \text{iff} \quad \lambda \ge 1.
$$

Let $ABC$ be a planar triangle. Let $\lambda \ge 0$. Define the point $D(\lambda)$ on the side $BC$ so that $D(\lambda)$ divides $BC$ in the ratio $c^\lambda : b^\lambda$. Prove that

positive_text:

$$

positive_text: In the country of Harpland, there are coins of three different colors: green, white, and orange. Each coin has a value of a positive whole number of shillings, but coins of the same color can have different values. These coins are arranged in the shape of an equilateral triangle with $n$ coins along each side. For example, here is how it looks when $n = 6$: ![](attached_image_1.png). The arrangement follows these rules: (1) no coin is next to another coin of the same color; (2) the total value of all coins in any straight line running parallel to one side of the triangle is divisible by 3. Show that the total value of the green coins in the triangle is divisible by 3.
