Three strictly increasing sequences
$$
a_{1}, a_{2}, a_{3}, \ldots, \quad b_{1}, b_{2}, b_{3}, \ldots, \quad c_{1}, c_{2}, c_{3}, \ldots
$$
of positive integers are given. Every positive integer belongs to exactly one of the three sequences. For every positive integer $n$, the following conditions hold:
(i) $c_{a_{n}}=b_{n}+1$;
(ii) $a_{n+1}>b_{n}$;
(iii) the number $c_{n+1} c_{n}-(n+1) c_{n+1}+n c_{n}$ is even.
Find $a_{2010}, b_{2010}$, and $c_{2010}$.

Three strictly increasing sequences
$$
a_{1}, a_{2}, a_{3}, \ldots, \quad b_{1}, b_{2}, b_{3}, \ldots, \quad c_{1}, c_{2}, c_{3}, \ldots
$$
of positive integers are given. Every positive integer belongs to exactly one of the three sequences. For every positive integer $n$, the following conditions hold:
(i) $c_{a_{n}}=b_{n}+1$;
(ii) $a_{n+1}=b_{n}$;
(iii) the number $c_{n+1} c_{n}-(n+1) c_{n+1}-n c_{n}$ is even.
Find $a_{2010}, b_{2010}$, and $c_{2010}$.

Three strictly increasing sequences
$$
a_{1}, a_{2}, a_{3}, \ldots, \quad b_{1}, b_{2}, b_{3}, \ldots, \quad c_{1}, c_{2}, c_{3}, \ldots
$$
of positive integers are given. Every positive integer belongs to exactly one of the three sequences. For every positive integer $n$, the following conditions hold:
(i) $c_{a_{n}}=b_{n}+2$;
(ii) $a_{n+1}>b_{n}$;
(iii) the number $c_{n+1} c_{n}-(n+1) c_{n+1}-n c_{n}$ is even.
Find $a_{2010}, b_{2010}$, and $c_{2010}$.

positive_text:
For each integer $n \geq 2$, find the maximum real number $C_n$ such that for all positive real numbers $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n$, the inequality
$$
\frac{x_1^2 + x_2^2 + \cdots + x_n^2}{n} \geq \left(\frac{x_1 + x_2 + \cdots + x_n}{n}\right)^2 + C_n \cdot (x_1 - x_n)^2
$$
holds true.

negatives.text:
For each integer $n \geq 2$, determine the largest real constant $C_n$ such that for all positive real numbers $a_1, \ldots, a_n$, we have
$$
\frac{a_1^2+\cdots+a_n^2}{n} \geq\left(\frac{a_1+\cdots+a_n}{n}\right)^2+C_n \cdot\left(a_1-a_2\right)^2
$$

For each integer $n \geq 2$, determine the largest real constant $C_n$ such that for all positive real numbers $a_1, \ldots, a_n$, we have
$$
\frac{a_1^2+\cdots+a_n^2}{n} \geq\left(\frac{a_1+\cdots+a_n}{n}\right)^2+C_n \cdot\left(a_1-a_n\right)
$$

For each integer $n \geq 2$, determine the largest real constant $C_n$ such that for all positive real numbers $a_1, \ldots, a_n$, we have
$$
\frac{a_1^2+\cdots+a_n^2}{n} \geq\left(\frac{a_1+\cdots+a_n}{n}\right)^2+C_n \cdot\left(a_1-a_n\right)^2 + 1
$$

positive_text: Imagine a regular polygon with $ n $ sides, and a fortress is placed at each corner. At the same time, each fortress fires at one of the two neighboring fortresses and hits it. A result of the shooting is the list of fortresses that are hit, without caring if a fortress is hit once or multiple times. Let $ P(n) $ represent the number of different such results. Show that for any integer $ k \geq 3 $, the numbers $ P(k) $ and $ P(k+1) $ have no common factors other than 1.

negatives.text: In each vertex of a regular $ n $-gon there is a fortress. At the same moment each fortress shoots at one of the two nearest fortresses and hits it. The result of the shooting is the set of the hit fortresses; we do not distinguish whether a fortress was hit once or twice. Let $ P(n) $ be the number of possible results of the shooting. Prove that for every positive integer $ k \geq 3 $, $ P(k) $ and $ P(k+2) $ are relatively prime.

In each vertex of a regular $ n $-gon there is a fortress. At the same moment each fortress shoots at one of the two nearest fortresses and hits it. The result of the shooting is the set of the hit fortresses; we do not distinguish whether a fortress was hit once or twice. Let $ P(n) $ be the number of possible results of the shooting. Prove that for every positive integer $ k \geq 3 $, $ P(k) $ and $ P(k) $ are relatively prime.

In each vertex of a regular $ n $-gon there is a fortress. At the same moment each fortress shoots at one of the two nearest fortresses and hits it. The result of the shooting is the set of the hit fortresses; we do not distinguish whether a fortress was hit once or twice. Let $ P(n) $ be the number of possible results of the shooting. Prove that for every positive integer $ k \geq 3 $, $ P(k) $ and $ P(k+1) $ are not relatively prime.

positive_text:
Start with the number $44$ written on a board. At each step, every number $a$ on the board is replaced with four different numbers $a_1, a_2, a_3, a_4$ such that their average $\frac{1}{4}(a_1 + a_2 + a_3 + a_4)$ is equal to $a$. This process is repeated $30$ times, and after these steps, the board has $n = 4^{30}$ numbers $b_1, b_2, \ldots, b_n$. Prove that the average of the squares of these numbers satisfies
$$
\frac{b_1^2 + b_2^2 + \cdots + b_n^2}{n} \geq 2011.
$$

negatives.text:
Initially, only the integer $44$ is written on a board. An integer $a$ on the board can be replaced with four pairwise different integers $a_{1}, a_{2}, a_{3}, a_{4}$ such that the arithmetic mean $\frac{1}{4}\left(a_{1}+a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}\right)$ of the four new integers is equal to the number $a$. In a step we simultaneously replace all the integers on the board in the above way. After $30$ steps we end up with $n=4^{30}$ integers $b_{1}, b_{2}, \ldots, b_{n}$ on the board. Prove that
$$
\frac{b_{1}+b_{2}+\cdots+b_{n}}{n} \geqslant 2011.
$$

Initially, only the integer $44$ is written on a board. An integer $a$ on the board can be replaced with four pairwise different integers $a_{1}, a_{2}, a_{3}, a_{4}$ such that the arithmetic mean $\frac{1}{4}\left(a_{1}+a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}\right)$ of the four new integers is equal to the number $a$. In a step we simultaneously replace all the integers on the board in the above way. After $30$ steps we end up with $n=4^{30}$ integers $b_{1}, b_{2}, \ldots, b_{n}$ on the board. Prove that
$$
\frac{b_{1}^{2}+b_{2}^{2}+\cdots+b_{n}^{2}}{n} \leqslant 2011.
$$

Initially, only the integer $44$ is written on a board. An integer $a$ on the board can be replaced with four pairwise different integers $a_{1}, a_{2}, a_{3}, a_{4}$ such that the arithmetic mean $\frac{1}{4}\left(a_{1}+a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}\right)$ of the four new integers is equal to the number $a$. In a step we simultaneously replace all the integers on the board in the above way. After $30$ steps we end up with $n=4^{30}$ integers $b_{1}, b_{2}, \ldots, b_{n}$ on the board. Prove that
$$
\frac{b_{1}^{2}+b_{2}^{2}+\cdots+b_{n}^{2}}{n} \geqslant 44^{2}.
$$

positive_text: Let $n$ be an integer with $n \geq 3$. John and Mary play a game using a regular $n$-sided polygon. John assigns the numbers $1$ through $n$ to the sides, each used exactly once. Then Mary splits the polygon into $n-2$ triangles using $n-3$ non-crossing diagonals. Each diagonal is labeled with the number $1$. In each triangle, Mary writes the product of the numbers on its three sides. She then adds up all these products to get a total sum $S$. John wants to make $S$ as large as possible, and Mary wants to make $S$ as small as possible. What is the final value of $S$ if both play as well as they can?

negatives.text: Let $n \geqslant 3$ be an integer. John and Mary play the following game: First John labels the sides of a regular $n$-gon with the numbers $1,2, \ldots, n$ in whatever order he wants, using each number exactly once. Then Mary divides this $n$-gon into triangles by drawing $n-3$ diagonals which do not intersect each other inside the $n$-gon. All these diagonals are labeled with the number $2$ instead of $1$. Into each of the triangles the product of the numbers on its sides is written. Let $S$ be the sum of those $n-2$ products. Determine the value of $S$ if Mary wants the number $S$ to be as small as possible and John wants $S$ to be as large as possible and if they both make the best possible choices.

Let $n \geqslant 3$ be an integer. John and Mary play the following game: First John labels the sides of a regular $n$-gon with the numbers $1,2, \ldots, n$ in whatever order he wants, using each number exactly once. Then Mary divides this $n$-gon into triangles by drawing $n-3$ diagonals which do not intersect each other inside the $n$-gon. All these diagonals are labeled with number $1$. Into each of the triangles the product of the numbers on its sides is written. Let $S$ be the sum of those $n-2$ products. Determine the value of $S$ if Mary wants the number $S$ to be as large as possible and John wants $S$ to be as small as possible and if they both make the best possible choices.

Let $n \geqslant 3$ be an integer. John and Mary play the following game: First John labels the sides of a regular $n$-gon with the numbers $1,2, \ldots, n$ in whatever order he wants, using each number exactly once. Then Mary divides this $n$-gon into triangles by drawing $n-3$ diagonals which do not intersect each other inside the $n$-gon. All these diagonals are labeled with number $1$. Into each of the triangles the sum of the numbers on its sides is written. Let $S$ be the sum of those $n-2$ sums. Determine the value of $S$ if Mary wants the number $S$ to be as small as possible and John wants $S$ to be as large as possible and if they both make the best possible choices.

positive_text: Suppose $ k $ and $ m $ are positive integers with $ k > m $, and suppose that the expression $ k m (k^{2} - m^{2}) $ is divisible by $ k^{3} - m^{3} $. Show that $ (k - m)^{3} > 3 k m $.

negatives.text: Let $ k $ and $ m $, with $ k > m $, be positive integers such that the number $ k m (k^{2} - m^{2}) $ is divisible by $ k^{3} - m^{3} $. Prove that $ (k - m)^{3} < 3 k m $.
Let $ k $ and $ m $, with $ k > m $, be positive integers such that the number $ k m (k^{2} - m^{2}) $ is divisible by $ k^{3} + m^{3} $. Prove that $ (k - m)^{3} > 3 k m $.
Let $ k $ and $ m $, with $ k > m $, be positive integers such that the number $ k m (k^{2} + m^{2}) $ is divisible by $ k^{3} - m^{3} $. Prove that $ (k - m)^{3} > 3 k m $.

positive_text:
Determine all functions $ f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R} $ satisfying the equation
$$
 y^2 f(x) + x^2 f(y) + xy = xy f(x+y) + x^2 + y^2
$$
for all real numbers $ x $ and $ y $.

negatives.text:
Find all functions $ f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R} $ such that the equality
$$
 y^2 f(x) + x^2 f(y) - xy = xy f(x+y) + x^2 + y^2
$$
holds for all $ x, y \in \mathbb{R} $.

Find all functions $ f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R} $ such that the equality
$$
 y^2 f(x) + x^2 f(y) + xy = xy f(x+y) - x^2 - y^2
$$
holds for all $ x, y \in \mathbb{R} $.

positive_text: Suppose $x, y, z$ are positive numbers satisfying $\frac{x}{1+x} + \frac{y}{1+y} + \frac{z}{1+z} = 2$. Show that $\frac{\sqrt{x} + \sqrt{y} + \sqrt{z}}{2} \geq \frac{1}{\sqrt{x}} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{y}} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{z}}$.

negatives.text: Let $a, b, c$ be positive real numbers such that $\frac{a}{1+a} + \frac{b}{1+b} + \frac{c}{1+c} = 2$. Prove that $\frac{\sqrt{a} + \sqrt{b} + \sqrt{c}}{2} \leqslant \frac{1}{\sqrt{a}} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{b}} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{c}}$.

Let $a, b, c$ be positive real numbers such that $\frac{a}{1+a} + \frac{b}{1+b} + \frac{c}{1+c} = 1$. Prove that $\frac{\sqrt{a} + \sqrt{b} + \sqrt{c}}{2} \geqslant \frac{1}{\sqrt{a}} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{b}} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{c}}$.

positive_text: Imagine a grid of size $n \times n$, where $n$ is an integer greater than or equal to 3. Each point on the grid has integer coordinates $(x, y)$ with $1 \leq x, y \leq n$. You are to choose as many points as possible from this grid, forming a subset $S$. The condition is that no three points in $S$ can form a right triangle. What is the maximum number of points you can include in $S$?

negatives.text: For an integer $n \geqslant 3$, let $\mathcal{M}$ be the set $\{(x, y) \mid x, y \in \mathbb{Z}, 1 \leqslant x \leqslant n, 1 \leqslant y \leqslant n\}$ of points in the plane. What is the maximum possible number of points in a subset $S \subseteq \mathcal{M}$ which does not contain three distinct points being the vertices of an equilateral triangle?

For an integer $n \geqslant 3$, let $\mathcal{M}$ be the set $\{(x, y) \mid x, y \in \mathbb{Z}, 1 \leqslant x \leqslant n, 1 \leqslant y \leqslant n\}$ of points in the plane. What is the maximum possible number of points in a subset $S \subseteq \mathcal{M}$ which does not contain three distinct points being collinear?

For an integer $n \geqslant 3$, let $\mathcal{M}$ be the set $\{(x, y) \mid x, y \in \mathbb{Z}, 1 \leqslant x \leqslant n, 1 \leqslant y \leqslant n\}$ of points in the plane. What is the maximum possible number of points in a subset $S \subseteq \mathcal{M}$ which does not contain three distinct points being the vertices of an isosceles triangle?

positive_text: Let $n$ be an integer with $n \geq 3$. A competition has $3n$ people, and there are $n$ different languages. Each person knows exactly three of these languages. Show that it is always possible to select at least $\left\lceil\frac{2n}{9}\right\rceil$ languages so that no person knows more than two of the selected ones. (Here, $\lceil x \rceil$ means the smallest whole number greater than or equal to $x$.)

negatives.text: Let $n \geq 3$ be an integer. At a competition, there are $3n$ participants, $n$ languages are spoken, and each participant speaks exactly three different languages. Prove that at least $\left\lfloor\frac{2n}{9}\right\rfloor$ of the spoken languages can be chosen such that no participant speaks more than two of the chosen languages.

Let $n \geq 3$ be an integer. At a competition, there are $3n$ participants, $n$ languages are spoken, and each participant speaks exactly three different languages. Prove that at least $\left\lceil\frac{n}{9}\right\rceil$ of the spoken languages can be chosen such that no participant speaks more than two of the chosen languages.

positive_text: Consider a convex pentagon $ABCDE$ where each side has the same length. Suppose the diagonals $AD$ and $EC$ intersect at a point $S$, and the angle $\angle ASE$ is $60^\circ$. Show that at least two sides of the pentagon are parallel.

negatives.text: Let $ABCDE$ be a convex pentagon with all five sides equal in length. The diagonals $AD$ and $EC$ meet in $S$ with $\angle ASE=90^\circ$. Prove that $ABCDE$ has a pair of parallel sides.
Let $ABCDE$ be a convex pentagon with all five sides equal in length. The diagonals $AD$ and $EC$ meet in $S$ with $\angle ASE=60^\circ$. Prove that $ABCDE$ has all sides equal.
Let $ABCDE$ be a convex pentagon with all five sides equal in length. The diagonals $AD$ and $EC$ meet in $S$ with $\angle ASE=60^\circ$. Prove that $ABCDE$ is regular.

positive_text:
Let $x, y, z$ be positive real numbers such that
$$
x+y+z=\frac{1}{x^{2}}+\frac{1}{y^{2}}+\frac{1}{z^{2}}
$$
Prove that
$$
2(x+y+z) \geq \sqrt[3]{7 x^{2} y+1}+\sqrt[3]{7 y^{2} z+1}+\sqrt[3]{7 z^{2} x+1}
$$
Find all triples $(x, y, z)$ for which equality occurs.

negatives.text:
Let $a, b, c$ be positive real numbers such that
$$
a+b+c=\frac{1}{a^{2}}+\frac{1}{b^{2}}+\frac{1}{c^{2}}
$$
Prove that
$$
2(a+b+c) \geq \sqrt[3]{7 a b^{2}+1}+\sqrt[3]{7 b c^{2}+1}+\sqrt[3]{7 c a^{2}+1}
$$
Find all triples $(a, b, c)$ for which equality holds.

Let $a, b, c$ be positive real numbers such that
$$
a+b+c=\frac{1}{a}+\frac{1}{b}+\frac{1}{c}
$$
Prove that
$$
2(a+b+c) \geq \sqrt[3]{7 a^{2} b+1}+\sqrt[3]{7 b^{2} c+1}+\sqrt[3]{7 c^{2} a+1}
$$
Find all triples $(a, b, c)$ for which equality holds.

Let $a, b, c$ be positive real numbers such that
$$
a+b+c=\frac{1}{a^{2}}+\frac{1}{b^{2}}+\frac{1}{c^{2}}
$$
Prove that
$$
2(a+b+c) \leq \sqrt[3]{7 a^{2} b+1}+\sqrt[3]{7 b^{2} c+1}+\sqrt[3]{7 c^{2} a+1}
$$
Find all triples $(a, b, c)$ for which equality holds.

positive_text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle where sides $AC$ and $BC$ are equal in length. Suppose there is a point $N$ inside the triangle such that $2 \angle ANB = 180^\circ + \angle ACB$. Draw a line parallel to $AN$ through point $C$, and let $D$ be the point where this line intersects line $BN$. Let $P$ be the point where the bisectors of angles $CAN$ and $ABN$ meet. Prove that the line $DP$ is perpendicular to $AN$.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be an isosceles triangle with $AC = BC$. Let $N$ be a point inside the triangle such that $2 \angle ANB = 180^\circ + \angle CAB$. Let $D$ be the intersection of the line $BN$ and the line parallel to $AN$ that passes through $C$. Let $P$ be the intersection of the angle bisectors of the angles $CAN$ and $ABN$. Show that the lines $DP$ and $AN$ are perpendicular.

Let $ABC$ be an isosceles triangle with $AC = BC$. Let $N$ be a point inside the triangle such that $2 \angle ANB = 180^\circ + \angle ACB$. Let $D$ be the intersection of the line $BN$ and the line parallel to $BN$ that passes through $C$. Let $P$ be the intersection of the angle bisectors of the angles $CAN$ and $ABN$. Show that the lines $DP$ and $AN$ are perpendicular.

positive_text:
Determine all functions $f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ satisfying
$$
f(x f(x) + 2y) = f(x^2) + f(y) + x + y - 1
$$
for every real number $x$ and $y$.

negatives.text:
Find all functions $f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ such that
$$
f(x f(x)+2 y)=f\left(x^{2}\right)+f(y)+x-y-1
$$
for all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$.

Find all functions $f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ such that
$$
f(x f(x)+2 y)=f\left(x^{2}\right)+f(y)+x+y-1
$$
for all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$ where $f$ is continuous.

Find all functions $f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ such that
$$
f(x f(x)+2 y)=f\left(x^{2}\right)+f(y)+x+y-1
$$
for all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$ where $x$ and $y$ are non-negative.

positive_text: \text{Let } a, b, c, d \in \mathbb{R} \text{ with none equal to zero. Suppose } a + b \neq 0, \ c + d \neq 0, \text{ and } a b + c d \geq 0. \text{ Show that} \$$ \left(\frac{a + b}{c + d} + \frac{c + d}{a + b}\right)^{-1} + \frac{1}{2} \geq \left(\frac{a}{c} + \frac{c}{a}\right)^{-1} + \left(\frac{b}{d} + \frac{d}{b}\right)^{-1} \$$

negatives.text: \text{Let } x, y, z, w \in \mathbb{R} \setminus \{0\} \text{ such that } x+y \neq 0, \ z+w \neq 0, \text{ and } x y+z w \geq 0. \text{ Prove the inequality} \$$ \left(\frac{x+y}{z+w}+\frac{z+w}{x+y}\right)^{-1}+\frac{1}{2} \geq \left(\frac{x}{w}+\frac{w}{x}\right)^{-1}+\left(\frac{y}{z}+\frac{z}{y}\right)^{-1} \$$

\text{Let } x, y, z, w \in \mathbb{R} \setminus \{0\} \text{ such that } x+y \neq 0, \ z+w \neq 0, \text{ and } x y+z w \geq 0. \text{ Prove the inequality} \$$ \left(\frac{x+y}{z+w}+\frac{z+w}{x+y}\right)^{-1}+\frac{1}{2} \geq \left(\frac{x}{z}+\frac{z}{x}\right)^{-1}+\left(\frac{y}{w}+\frac{w}{y}\right)^{-1} + \frac{1}{4} \$$

\text{Let } x, y, z, w \in \mathbb{R} \setminus \{0\} \text{ such that } x+y \neq 0, \ z+w \neq 0, \text{ and } x y+z w \geq 0. \text{ Prove the inequality} \$$ \left(\frac{x+y}{z+w}+\frac{z+w}{x+y}\right)^{-1}+\frac{1}{2} \geq \left(\frac{x+y}{z+w}\right)^{-1}+\left(\frac{z+w}{x+y}\right)^{-1} \$$

positive_text: Imagine there are $n \geq 2$ houses on one side of a street. The houses are labeled $1$ to $n$ from left to right. Each house has a sign showing its number. One day, the neighbors play a trick on the mailman by swapping the signs on neighboring houses. Each pair of neighbors swaps signs exactly once during the day. How many different final arrangements of the house numbers are possible at the end of the day?

negatives.text: There are $n \geq 2$ houses on the northern side of a street. Going from the west to the east, the houses are numbered from $1$ to $n$. The number of each house is shown on a plate. One day the inhabitants of the street make fun of the postman by shuffling their number plates in the following way: for each pair of neighbouring houses, the current number plates are swapped at most once during the day. How many different sequences of number plates are possible at the end of the day?

There are $n \geq 2$ houses on the northern side of a street. Going from the west to the east, the houses are numbered from $1$ to $n$. The number of each house is shown on a plate. One day the inhabitants of the street make fun of the postman by shuffling their number plates in the following way: for each pair of neighbouring houses, the current number plates are swapped exactly once during the day, but only for the first $n - 1$ pairs. How many different sequences of number plates are possible at the end of the day?

There are $n \geq 2$ houses on the northern side of a street. Going from the west to the east, the houses are numbered from $1$ to $n$. The number of each house is shown on a plate. One day the inhabitants of the street make fun of the postman by shuffling their number plates in the following way: for each pair of non-neighboring houses, the current number plates are swapped exactly once during the day. How many different sequences of number plates are possible at the end of the day?

positive_text: Consider an acute triangle $ABC$. Construct another triangle $PQR$ such that the side lengths of $PQR$ are exactly half those of $ABC$ (i.e., $PQ = \frac{1}{2}AB$, $QR = \frac{1}{2}BC$, and $RP = \frac{1}{2}CA$), and the lines $PQ$, $QR$, and $RP$ each pass through the points $A$, $B$, and $C$, respectively. Ensure all six points $A, B, C, P, Q$, and $R$ are different.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle. Construct a triangle $PQR$ such that $AB=2PQ$, $BC=2QR$, $CA=2RP$, and the lines $PQ$, $QR$, and $RP$ pass through the points $B$, $C$, and $A$, respectively. (All six points $A, B, C, P, Q$, and $R$ are distinct.)

Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle. Construct a triangle $PQR$ such that $AB=2PQ$, $BC=2QR$, $CA=2RP$, and the lines $PQ$, $QR$, and $RP$ pass through the points $A$, $C$, and $B$, respectively. (All six points $A, B, C, P, Q$, and $R$ are distinct.)

Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle. Construct a triangle $PQR$ such that $AB=2PQ$, $BC=2QR$, $CA=2RP$, and the lines $PQ$, $QR$, and $RP$ pass through the points $A$, $B$, and $A$, respectively. (All six points $A, B, C, P, Q$, and $R$ are distinct.)

positive_text: Let $n \geq 3$ be a whole number. A diagonal is called an inner diagonal of a polygon with $n$ sides if it lies entirely inside the polygon. Let $D(P)$ count all such inner diagonals in a polygon $P$ with $n$ sides, and let $D(n)$ be the smallest possible value of $D(P)$ across all such polygons. Show that no two inner diagonals in $P$ cross each other (except at their endpoints) if and only if $D(P) = D(n)$.

negatives.text: Let $n \geq 3$ be an integer. An inner diagonal of a simple $n$-gon is a diagonal that is contained in the $n$-gon. Denote by $D(P)$ the number of all inner diagonals of a simple $n$-gon $P$ and by $D(n)$ the greatest possible value of $D(Q)$, where $Q$ is a simple $n$-gon. Prove that no two inner diagonals of $P$ intersect (except possibly at a common endpoint) if and only if $D(P)=D(n)$.

Let $n \geq 3$ be an integer. An inner diagonal of a simple $n$-gon is a diagonal that is contained in the $n$-gon. Denote by $D(P)$ the number of all inner diagonals of a simple $n$-gon $P$ and by $D(n)$ the least possible value of $D(Q)$, where $Q$ is a simple $n$-gon. Prove that no two sides of $P$ intersect (except possibly at a common endpoint) if and only if $D(P)=D(n)$.

Let $n \geq 3$ be an integer. An inner diagonal of a simple $n$-gon is a diagonal that is contained in the $n$-gon. Denote by $D(P)$ the number of all inner diagonals of a simple $n$-gon $P$ and by $D(n)$ the least possible value of $D(Q)$, where $Q$ is a simple $n$-gon. Prove that no two inner diagonals of $P$ intersect (except possibly at a common endpoint) if and only if $D(P) \geq D(n)$.

positive_text: Show that for any positive real numbers $x, y, z$ with $xyz = 1$, the inequality $$ \frac{x}{2y + z^2} + \frac{y}{2z + x^2} + \frac{z}{2x + y^2} \leqslant \frac{x^2 + y^2 + z^2}{3} $$ is always true.

negatives.text: Prove that for all positive real numbers $a, b, c$ such that $abc = 1$ the following inequality holds: $$ \frac{a}{2b + c^2} + \frac{b}{2c + a^2} + \frac{c}{2a + b^2} \geqslant \frac{a^2 + b^2 + c^2}{3} $$

Prove that for all positive real numbers $a, b, c$ such that $a + b + c = 1$ the following inequality holds: $$ \frac{a}{2b + c^2} + \frac{b}{2c + a^2} + \frac{c}{2a + b^2} \leqslant \frac{a^2 + b^2 + c^2}{3} $$

Prove that for all positive real numbers $a, b, c$ such that $abc = 1$ the following inequality holds: $$ \frac{a}{b + c^2} + \frac{b}{c + a^2} + \frac{c}{a + b^2} \leqslant \frac{a^2 + b^2 + c^2}{3} $$

positive_text:
Find all functions $f: \mathbb{R} \setminus \{0\} \to \mathbb{R} \setminus \{0\}$ that satisfy the equation
$$
f\left(x^2 y f(x)\right) + f(1) = x^2 f(x) + f(y)
$$
for all real numbers $x$ and $y$ that are not zero.

negatives.text:
Find all functions $f: \mathbb{R} \setminus \{0\} \to \mathbb{R} \setminus \{0\}$ that satisfy the equation
$$
f\left(x y f(x)\right) + f(1) = x f(x) + f(y)
$$
for all real numbers $x$ and $y$ that are not zero.

Find all functions $f: \mathbb{R} \setminus \{0\} \to \mathbb{R} \setminus \{0\}$ that satisfy the equation
$$
f\left(x^2 y f(x)\right) = x^2 f(x) + f(y)
$$
for all real numbers $x$ and $y$ that are not zero.

Find all functions $f: \mathbb{R} \setminus \{0\} \to \mathbb{R} \setminus \{0\}$ that satisfy the equation
$$
f\left(x^2 y f(x)\right) + f(1) = x f(x) + f(y)
$$
for all real numbers $x$ and $y$ that are not zero.

positive_text: Suppose $N$ is a positive whole number. Imagine an $N \times N$ grid made up of $N^2$ small squares. In each square, we draw one of the two diagonals. These diagonals split the entire grid into $K$ regions. For each value of $N$, find the smallest and largest possible numbers of regions $K$.

negatives.text: Let $N$ be a positive integer. In each of the $N^{2}$ unit squares of an $N \times N$ board, one of the two diagonals is drawn. The drawn diagonals divide the $N \times N$ board into $K$ regions. For each $N$, determine the smallest and the largest possible values of the number of diagonals drawn.

Let $N$ be a positive integer. In each of the $N^{2}$ unit squares of an $N \times N$ board, one of the two diagonals is drawn. The drawn diagonals divide the $N \times N$ board into $K$ regions. For each $N$, determine the smallest and the largest possible values of the number of squares that are split by a diagonal.

positive_text: Consider an acute triangle $ABC$ where $AB$ is longer than $AC$. Show that there is a special point $D$ such that for any two different points $X$ and $Y$ inside triangle $ABC$, if the points $B$, $C$, $X$, and $Y$ lie on the same circle and the equation $$\angle AXB - \angle ACB = \angle CYA - \angle CBA$$ is satisfied, then the line connecting $X$ and $Y$ must pass through point $D$.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with $AB > AC$. Prove that there exists a point $D$ with the following property: whenever two distinct points $X$ and $Y$ lie in the interior of $ABC$ such that the points $A$, $C$, $X$, and $Y$ lie on a circle and $$\angle AXB - \angle ACB = \angle CYA - \angle CBA$$ holds, the line $XY$ passes through $D$.

Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with $AB > AC$. Prove that there exists a point $D$ with the following property: whenever two distinct points $X$ and $Y$ lie in the interior of $ABC$ such that the points $B$, $C$, $X$, and $Y$ lie on a circle and $$\angle AXB + \angle ACB = \angle CYA - \angle CBA$$ holds, the line $XY$ passes through $D$.

Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with $AB > AC$. Prove that there exists a point $D$ with the following property: whenever two distinct points $X$ and $Y$ lie in the interior of $ABC$ such that the points $B$, $C$, $X$, and $Y$ lie on a circle and $$\angle AXB - \angle ACB = \angle CYA - \angle CAB$$ holds, the line $XY$ passes through $D$.

positive_text: In triangle $ABC$, let $I$ be the incenter, and suppose $AB > AC$. The line $AI$ meets side $BC$ at $D$. There is a point $P$ on segment $BC$ such that $PI = PD$. Let $J$ be the reflection of $I$ over the perpendicular bisector of $BC$, and let $Q$ be the other point where the circumcircles of triangles $ABC$ and $APD$ meet. Show that $\angle BAQ = \angle CAJ$.

negatives.text: Let $I$ be the incenter of triangle $ABC$ with $AB > AC$ and let the line $AI$ intersect the side $BC$ at $D$. Suppose that point $P$ lies on the segment $BC$ and satisfies $PI = PD$. Further, let $J$ be the point obtained by reflecting $I$ over the perpendicular bisector of $BC$, and let $Q$ be the other intersection of the circumcircles of the triangles $ABC$ and $APC$. Prove that $\angle BAQ = \angle CAJ$.

Let $I$ be the incenter of triangle $ABC$ with $AB > AC$ and let the line $AI$ intersect the side $BC$ at $D$. Suppose that point $P$ lies on the segment $BC$ and satisfies $PI = PD$. Further, let $J$ be the point obtained by reflecting $I$ over the perpendicular bisector of $AC$, and let $Q$ be the other intersection of the circumcircles of the triangles $ABC$ and $APD$. Prove that $\angle BAQ = \angle CAJ$.

positive_text:
Find all pairs of positive whole numbers $(a, b)$ such that
$$
a! + b! = a^{b} + b^{a}
$$

negatives.text:
Find all pairs of positive integers $(a, b)$ such that
$$
a! + b! = a^{b} - b^{a}
$$

Find all pairs of positive integers $(a, b)$ such that
$$
(a!)^2 + (b!)^2 = a^{b} + b^{a}
$$

Find all pairs of positive integers $(a, b)$ such that
$$
a! + b! = a^{a} + b^{b}
$$

positive_text:
Suppose $n \geq 2$ is an integer, and let $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}$ be real numbers such that
(i) each $a_{j} > -1$, and
(ii) $a_{1} + a_{2} + \cdots + a_{n} = n$.
Show that
$$
\sum_{j=1}^{n} \frac{1}{1+a_{j}} \geq \sum_{j=1}^{n} \frac{a_{j}}{1+a_{j}^{2}}
$$
and find when equality occurs.

negatives.text:
Let $n \geqslant 2$ be an integer and $x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{n}$ be real numbers satisfying
(a) $x_{j}>-1$ for $j=1,2, \ldots, n$ and
(b) $x_{1}+x_{2}+\cdots+x_{n}=n$.
Prove the inequality
$$
\sum_{j=1}^{n} \frac{1}{1+x_{j}} \geqslant \sum_{j=1}^{n} \frac{x_{j}}{1+x_{j}}
$$
and determine when equality holds.

Let $n \geqslant 2$ be an integer and $x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{n}$ be real numbers satisfying
(a) $x_{j}>-1$ for $j=1,2, \ldots, n$ and
(b) $x_{1}+x_{2}+\cdots+x_{n}=2n$.
Prove the inequality
$$
\sum_{j=1}^{n} \frac{1}{1+x_{j}} \geqslant \sum_{j=1}^{n} \frac{x_{j}}{1+x_{j}^{2}}
$$
and determine when equality holds.

Let $n \geqslant 2$ be an integer and $x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{n}$ be real numbers satisfying
(a) $x_{j}>0$ for $j=1,2, \ldots, n$ and
(b) $x_{1}+x_{2}+\cdots+x_{n}=n$.
Prove the inequality
$$
\sum_{j=1}^{n} \frac{1}{1+x_{j}} \geqslant \sum_{j=1}^{n} \frac{x_{j}}{1+x_{j}^{2}}
$$
and determine when equality holds.

positive_text: There are $n$ positive whole numbers written on a board, with $n$ being at least 3. You can pick any three numbers $a, b, c$ that can form a triangle (not equilateral) and replace them with $a+b-c$, $b+c-a$, and $c+a-b$. Show that you cannot keep doing this forever.

negatives.text: There are $n \geqslant 3$ positive integers written on a blackboard. A move consists of choosing three numbers $a, b, c$ on the blackboard such that they are the sides of a non-degenerate non-equilateral triangle and replacing them by $a+b+c$, $b+c+a$ and $c+a+b$. Show that an infinite sequence of moves cannot exist.

There are $n \geqslant 3$ positive integers written on a blackboard. A move consists of choosing three numbers $a, b, c$ on the blackboard such that they are the sides of a degenerate triangle and replacing them by $a+b-c$, $b+c-a$ and $c+a-b$. Show that an infinite sequence of moves cannot exist.

There are $n \geqslant 3$ positive integers written on a blackboard. A move consists of choosing three numbers $a, b, c$ on the blackboard such that they are the sides of a non-degenerate non-equilateral triangle and replacing them by $a+b-c$, $b+c-a$ and $c+a-b$. Show that an infinite sequence of moves can exist.

positive_text:
Find all functions $f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ that satisfy the equation
$$
 f(x) f(y) = x f(f(y - x)) + x f(2x) + f\left(x^{2}\right)
$$
for every pair of real numbers $x$ and $y$.

negatives.text:
Find all functions $f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ that satisfy the equation
$$
 f(x) f(y) = x f(f(y + x)) + x f(2x) + f\left(x^{2}\right)
$$
for every pair of real numbers $x$ and $y$.

Find all functions $f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ that satisfy the equation
$$
 f(x) f(y) = x f(f(y - x)) + x f(2x) + f\left(-x^{2}\right)
$$
for every pair of real numbers $x$ and $y$.

Find all functions $f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ that satisfy the equation
$$
 f(x) f(y) = x f(f(y - x)) + x f(3x) + f\left(x^{2}\right)
$$
for every pair of real numbers $x$ and $y$.

positive_text: Let triangle $ABC$ be acute and not isosceles with vertex $A$. Let $O$ be the center of the circle that passes through all three vertices of triangle $ABC$. The line connecting $A$ and $O$ intersects the circle again at a point $D$ and also meets the line $BC$ at point $E$. A new circle passing through $C$, $D$, and $E$ intersects the line $CA$ again at point $P$. The line joining $P$ and $E$ intersects the line $AB$ at point $Q$. Now, draw a line through $O$ that is parallel to $PE$ and let it meet the altitude from $A$ to $BC$ at point $F$. Prove that the distances $FP$ and $FQ$ are equal.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be an acute-angled triangle with $AB \neq AC$, and let $O$ be its circumcenter. The line $AO$ intersects the circumcircle $\omega$ of $ABC$ a second time in point $D$, and the line $BC$ in point $E$. The circumcircle of $BDE$ intersects the line $CA$ a second time in point $P$. The line $PE$ intersects the line $AB$ in point $Q$. The line through $O$ parallel to $PE$ intersects the altitude of the triangle $ABC$ that passes through $A$ in point $F$. Prove that $FP = FQ$.

Let $ABC$ be an acute-angled triangle with $AB \neq AC$, and let $O$ be its circumcenter. The line $AO$ intersects the circumcircle $\omega$ of $ABC$ a second time in point $D$, and the line $BC$ in point $E$. The circumcircle of $CDE$ intersects the line $AB$ a second time in point $P$. The line $PE$ intersects the line $CA$ in point $Q$. The line through $O$ parallel to $PE$ intersects the altitude of the triangle $ABC$ that passes through $A$ in point $F$. Prove that $FP = FQ$.

Let $ABC$ be an acute-angled triangle with $AB \neq AC$, and let $O$ be its circumcenter. The line $AO$ intersects the circumcircle $\omega$ of $ABC$ a second time in point $D$, and the line $BC$ in point $E$. The circumcircle of $CDE$ intersects the line $CA$ a second time in point $P$. The line $PE$ intersects the line $AB$ in point $Q$. The line through $F$ parallel to $PE$ intersects the altitude of the triangle $ABC$ that passes through $A$ in point $O$. Prove that $FP = FQ$.

positive_text:
We are given the equation $a^2 + b^2 + c^2 + n = abc$, where $a$, $b$, and $c$ are positive whole numbers. Show:
(a) There are no such values of $a$, $b$, and $c$ when $n = 2017$.
(b) When $n = 2016$, the number $a$ must always be a multiple of $3$ in any solution.
(c) There are infinitely many triples $(a, b, c)$ that satisfy the equation when $n = 2016$.

negatives.text:
We consider the equation $a^2 + b^2 + c^2 + n = abc$, where $a, b, c$ are positive integers.
Prove:
(a) There are no solutions $(a, b, c)$ for $n=2016$.
(b) For $n=2016$, $a$ must be divisible by $3$ for every solution $(a, b, c)$.
(c) The equation has infinitely many solutions $(a, b, c)$ for $n=2016$.

We consider the equation $a^2 + b^2 + c^2 + n = abc$, where $a, b, c$ are positive integers.
Prove:
(a) There are no solutions $(a, b, c)$ for $n=2017$.
(b) For $n=2016$, $a$ must be divisible by $2$ for every solution $(a, b, c)$.
(c) The equation has infinitely many solutions $(a, b, c)$ for $n=2016$.

We consider the equation $a^2 + b^2 + c^2 + n = abc$, where $a, b, c$ are positive integers.
Prove:
(a) There are no solutions $(a, b, c)$ for $n=2017$.
(b) For $n=2016$, $a$ must be divisible by $3$ for every solution $(a, b, c)$.
(c) The equation has finitely many solutions $(a, b, c)$ for $n=2016$.

positive_text:
Find all real-valued functions $ f $ defined on the real numbers such that
$$
 f\left(x^2 + f(x)f(y)\right) = x f(x + y)
$$
holds for every real $ x $ and $ y $.

negatives.text:
Find all functions $ f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R} $ satisfying
$$
 f\left(x^2 + f(x) + f(y)\right) = x f(x + y)
$$
for all real numbers $ x $ and $ y $.

Determine all functions $ f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R} $ satisfying
$$
 f\left(x^2 + f(x) f(y)\right) = f(x) f(x + y)
$$
for all real numbers $ x $ and $ y $.

Determine all functions $ f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R} $ satisfying
$$
 f\left(x^2 + f(x) f(y)\right) = x f(y)
$$
for all real numbers $ x $ and $ y $.

positive_text:
Let $n$ be an integer greater than or equal to 3. We assign $2n+1$ different integers to the $n$ corners, the $n$ sides, and the center of a regular $n$-gon. This assignment is called memorable if the following two rules are satisfied:

1. The number on each side is the average of the numbers on the two corners it connects.
2. The number in the center is the average of the numbers on all the corners.

Find all values of $n$ with $n \geqslant 3$ for which such a memorable assignment is possible using $2n+1$ consecutive integers.

negatives.text:
Let $n \geqslant 3$ be an integer. A labelling of the $n$ vertices, the $n$ sides and the interior of a regular $n$-gon by $2n+1$ distinct integers is called memorable if the following conditions hold:

1. Each side has a label that is the arithmetic mean of the labels of its endpoints.
2. The interior of the $n$-gon has a label that is the arithmetic mean of the labels of all the sides.

Determine all integers $n \geqslant 3$ for which there exists a memorable labelling of a regular $n$-gon consisting of $2n+1$ consecutive integers.

Let $n \geqslant 3$ be an integer. A labelling of the $n$ vertices, the $n$ sides and the interior of a regular $n$-gon by $2n+1$ distinct integers is called memorable if the following conditions hold:

1. Each vertex has a label that is the arithmetic mean of the labels of the two adjacent sides.
2. The interior of the $n$-gon has a label that is the arithmetic mean of the labels of all the vertices.

Determine all integers $n \geqslant 3$ for which there exists a memorable labelling of a regular $n$-gon consisting of $2n+1$ consecutive integers.

Let $n \geqslant 3$ be an integer. A labelling of the $n$ vertices, the $n$ sides and the interior of a regular $n$-gon by $2n+1$ distinct integers is called memorable if the following conditions hold:

1. Each side has a label that is the geometric mean of the labels of its endpoints.
2. The interior of the $n$-gon has a label that is the arithmetic mean of the labels of all the vertices.

Determine all integers $n \geqslant 3$ for which there exists a memorable labelling of a regular $n$-gon consisting of $2n+1$ consecutive integers.

positive_text:
Find all pairs of polynomials $(P, Q)$ with real coefficients such that
$$
P(x + Q(y)) = Q(x + P(y))
$$
for every real number $x$ and every real number $y$.

negatives.text:
Find all pairs of polynomials $(P, Q)$ with real coefficients such that
$$
P(x + Q(y)) = P(x + P(y))
$$
for every real number $x$ and every real number $y$.

positive_text: Find the smallest real number $ C $ such that the inequality $ \left|x^{3}+y^{3}+z^{3}+1\right| \leq C\left|x^{5}+y^{5}+z^{5}+1\right| $ is true for all real values $ x, y, z $ with the condition that $ x + y + z = -1 $.

negatives.text: Determine the smallest possible real constant $ C $ such that the inequality $ \left|x^{3}+y^{3}+z^{3}+1\right| \leqslant C\left|x^{5}+y^{5}+z^{5}+1\right| $ holds for all real numbers $ x, y, z $ satisfying $ x+y+z=1 $.

Determine the smallest possible real constant $ C $ such that the inequality $ \left|x^{3}+y^{3}+z^{3}+1\right| \leqslant C\left|x^{3}+y^{3}+z^{3}+1\right| $ holds for all real numbers $ x, y, z $ satisfying $ x+y+z=-1 $.

positive_text: Let $n \geq 3$ be an integer. A sequence $P_1, P_2, \ldots, P_n$ of distinct points on a flat surface is called good if: (1) no three points lie on the same straight line, (2) the path formed by connecting the points in order is not self-intersecting, and (3) for every three consecutive points $P_i, P_{i+1}, P_{i+2}$, the triangle they form turns counterclockwise. For each $n \geq 3$, find the largest number $k$ such that there exists a set of $n$ distinct points $A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_n$ for which $k$ different orderings of these points form a good sequence.

negatives.text: Let $n \geq 3$ be an integer. A sequence $P_1, P_2, \ldots, P_n$ of distinct points in the plane is called good if no three of them are collinear, the polyline $P_1 P_2 \ldots P_n$ is non-self-intersecting, and the triangle $P_i P_{i+1} P_{i+2}$ is oriented clockwise for every $i=1,2,\ldots,n-2$. For every integer $n \geq 3$, determine the greatest possible integer $k$ such that there exist $n$ distinct points $A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_n$ in the plane for which there are $k$ distinct permutations $\sigma:\{1,2,\ldots,n\} \rightarrow\{1,2,\ldots,n\}$ such that $A_{\sigma(1)}, A_{\sigma(2)}, \ldots, A_{\sigma(n)}$ is good.

Let $n \geq 3$ be an integer. A sequence $P_1, P_2, \ldots, P_n$ of distinct points in the plane is called good if no three of them are collinear, the polyline $P_1 P_2 \ldots P_n$ is self-intersecting, and the triangle $P_i P_{i+1} P_{i+2}$ is oriented counterclockwise for every $i=1,2,\ldots,n-2$. For every integer $n \geq 3$, determine the greatest possible integer $k$ such that there exist $n$ distinct points $A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_n$ in the plane for which there are $k$ distinct permutations $\sigma:\{1,2,\ldots,n\} \rightarrow\{1,2,\ldots,n\}$ such that $A_{\sigma(1)}, A_{\sigma(2)}, \ldots, A_{\sigma(n)}$ is good.

Let $n \geq 3$ be an integer. A sequence $P_1, P_2, \ldots, P_n$ of distinct points in the plane is called good if no three of them are collinear, the polyline $P_1 P_2 \ldots P_n$ is non-self-intersecting, and the triangle $P_i P_{i+1} P_{i+2}$ is oriented counterclockwise for every $i=1,2,\ldots,n-2$. For every integer $n \geq 3$, determine the greatest possible integer $k$ such that there exist $n$ distinct points $A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_n$ in the plane for which there are $k$ distinct permutations $\sigma:\{1,2,\ldots,n\} \rightarrow\{1,2,\ldots,n\}$ such that $A_{\sigma(1)}, A_{\sigma(2)}, \ldots, A_{\sigma(n)}$ is not good.

positive_text:
Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $AB > AC$ and circumcircle $\Gamma$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of the shorter arc $BC$ in $\Gamma$, and let $D$ be the point where ray $AC$ meets ray $BM$. Let $E$ (not equal to $C$) be the point where the angle bisector of $\angle ACB$ meets the circumcircle of triangle $BDC$. Suppose $E$ lies inside triangle $ABC$, and that the line $DE$ intersects $\Gamma$ again at a point $N$ such that $E$ is the midpoint of segment $DN$.

Prove that $N$ is the midpoint of the segment joining the excenters $I_B$ and $I_C$ of triangle $ABC$ opposite to $B$ and $C$, respectively.

negatives.text:
Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $AB > AC$ and circumcircle $\Gamma$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of the shorter arc $BC$ in $\Gamma$, and let $D$ be the point where ray $AC$ meets ray $BM$. Let $E$ (not equal to $C$) be the point where the angle bisector of $\angle BAC$ meets the circumcircle of triangle $BDC$. Suppose $E$ lies inside triangle $ABC$, and that the line $DE$ intersects $\Gamma$ again at a point $N$ such that $E$ is the midpoint of segment $DN$.

Prove that $N$ is the midpoint of the segment joining the excenters $I_B$ and $I_C$ of triangle $ABC$ opposite to $B$ and $C$, respectively.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $AB > AC$ and circumcircle $\Gamma$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of the shorter arc $BC$ in $\Gamma$, and let $D$ be the point where ray $AC$ meets ray $BM$. Let $E$ (not equal to $C$) be the point where the external bisector of $\angle ACB$ meets the circumcircle of triangle $BDC$. Suppose $E$ lies inside triangle $ABC$, and that the line $DE$ intersects $\Gamma$ again at a point $N$ such that $E$ is the midpoint of segment $DN$.

Prove that $N$ is the midpoint of the segment joining the excenters $I_B$ and $I_C$ of triangle $ABC$ opposite to $B$ and $C$, respectively.

positive_text: Find all integers $n \geq 2$ for which you can rearrange the numbers $0, 1, 2, \ldots, n-1$ into a sequence $x_0, x_1, \ldots, x_{n-1}$ such that the cumulative sums $x_0$, $x_0 + x_1$, $x_0 + x_1 + x_2$, ..., $x_0 + x_1 + \ldots + x_{n-1}$ are all different when taken modulo $n$.

negatives.text: Find all integers $n \geq 2$ for which you can rearrange the numbers $0, 1, 2, \ldots, n-1$ into a sequence $x_0, x_1, \ldots, x_{n-1}$ such that the cumulative sums $x_0$, $x_0 + x_1$, $x_0 + x_1 + x_2$, ..., $x_0 + x_1 + \ldots + x_{n-1}$ are all different when taken modulo $n-1$.

Find all integers $n \geq 2$ for which you can rearrange the numbers $0, 1, 2, \ldots, n-1$ into a sequence $x_0, x_1, \ldots, x_{n-1}$ such that the cumulative sums $x_0$, $x_0 + x_1$, $x_0 + x_1 + x_2$, ..., $x_0 + x_1 + \ldots + x_{n-1}$ are all different when taken modulo $n$, but the sequence is not required to be a permutation of $0, 1, \ldots, n-1$.

Find all integers $n \geq 2$ for which you can rearrange the numbers $0, 1, 2, \ldots, n-1$ into a sequence $x_0, x_1, \ldots, x_{n-1}$ such that the cumulative sums $x_0$, $x_0 + x_1$, $x_0 + x_1 + x_2$, ..., $x_0 + x_1 + \ldots + x_{n-1}$ are all divisible by $n$.

positive_text: Let $ n $ be a whole number greater than or equal to 3. Consider the prime factorization of $ n! $, written as $ n! = p_{1}^{\alpha_{1}} p_{2}^{\alpha_{2}} \ldots p_{k}^{\alpha_{k}} $, where $ p_{1} < p_{2} < \cdots < p_{k} $ are the primes in increasing order. Define the sequence $ \alpha_{1}, \alpha_{2}, \ldots, \alpha_{k} $. Find all values of $ n $ such that this sequence forms a geometric progression.

negatives.text: Let $ n $ be a whole number greater than or equal to 3. Consider the prime factorization of $ n! $, written as $ n! = p_{1}^{\alpha_{1}} p_{2}^{\alpha_{2}} \ldots p_{k}^{\alpha_{k}} $, where $ p_{1} < p_{2} < \cdots < p_{k} $ are the primes in increasing order. Define the sequence $ \alpha_{1}, \alpha_{2}, \ldots, \alpha_{k} $. Find all values of $ n $ such that this sequence forms an arithmetic progression.

Let $ n $ be a whole number greater than or equal to 3. Consider the prime factorization of $ n! $, written as $ n! = p_{1}^{\alpha_{1}} p_{2}^{\alpha_{2}} \ldots p_{k}^{\alpha_{k}} $, where $ p_{1} < p_{2} < \cdots < p_{k} $ are the primes in increasing order. Define the sequence $ \alpha_{1}, \alpha_{2}, \ldots, \alpha_{k} $. Find all values of $ n $ such that this sequence consists of all equal numbers.

Let $ n $ be a whole number greater than or equal to 3. Consider the prime factorization of $ n! $, written as $ n! = p_{1}^{\alpha_{1}} p_{2}^{\alpha_{2}} \ldots p_{k}^{\alpha_{k}} $, where $ p_{1} < p_{2} < \cdots < p_{k} $ are the primes in increasing order. Define the sequence $ \alpha_{1}, \alpha_{2}, \ldots, \alpha_{k} $. Find all values of $ n $ such that this sequence is a constant sequence.

positive_text: Consider an acute triangle $ABC$ with $AB < AC$. Let $D$ be the point where the perpendicular from $A$ to side $BC$ lands. Suppose $R$ and $Q$ are the centroids of triangles $ABD$ and $ACD$, respectively. Let $P$ be a point on segment $BC$, different from $D$, such that $P, Q, R,$ and $D$ all lie on the same circle. Show that the lines $AP$, $BQ$, and $CR$ all meet at one point.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be an acute-angled triangle with $AB < AC$, and let $D$ be the foot of its altitude from $A$. Let $R$ and $Q$ be the centroids of the triangles $ABD$ and $ACD$, respectively. Let $P$ be a point on the line segment $BC$ such that $P \neq D$ and the points $P, Q, R$ and $A$ are concyclic. Prove that the lines $AP, BQ$ and $CR$ are concurrent.

Let $ABC$ be an acute-angled triangle with $AB < AC$, and let $D$ be the foot of its altitude from $A$. Let $R$ and $Q$ be the centroids of the triangles $ABD$ and $ACD$, respectively. Let $P$ be a point on the line segment $BC$ such that $P \neq D$ and the points $P, Q, R$ and $D$ are concyclic. Prove that the lines $AQ, BP$ and $CR$ are concurrent.

Let $ABC$ be an acute-angled triangle with $AB < AC$, and let $D$ be the foot of its altitude from $A$. Let $R$ and $Q$ be the centroids of the triangles $ABD$ and $ACD$, respectively. Let $P$ be a point on the line segment $BC$ such that $P \neq D$ and the points $P, Q, R$ and $D$ are concyclic. Prove that the lines $AP, CQ$ and $BR$ are concurrent.

positive_text: Suppose $n$ is a positive integer and each of the numbers $u_1, u_2, \ldots, u_n$ is a positive integer that is at most $2^k$, where $k$ is an integer greater than or equal to 3. A way to express a non-negative integer $t$ is as a sum $t = a_1 u_1 + a_2 u_2 + \cdots + a_n u_n$, where each $a_i$ is a non-negative integer. Show that if $t$ can be expressed this way, then there is also an expression where fewer than $2k$ of the $a_i$'s are non-zero.

negatives.text:

positive_text: Consider an acute triangle $ABC$ with $AB < AC$. Drop a perpendicular from $A$ to side $BC$, and let the foot of this perpendicular be point $D$. positive_text:
A number $n$ is called Silesian if we can find positive whole numbers $a, b$, and $c$ such that
$$
n = \frac{a^{2} + b^{2} + c^{2}}{ab + bc + ca}
$$

a. Show that there are infinitely many such numbers $n$.

b. Show that not all positive whole numbers are Silesian.

$$

b. Show that all positive whole numbers are Silesian.

positive_text:
Find the minimum and maximum values of the expression

$$
\left(\frac{1}{x^{2}+1}+\frac{1}{y^{2}+1}+\frac{1}{z^{2}+1}\right)\left(\frac{x^{2}}{x^{2}+1}+\frac{y^{2}}{y^{2}+1}+\frac{z^{2}}{z^{2}+1}\right)
$$
where $x$, $y$, and $z$ are non-negative real numbers such that $xy + yz + zx = 1$.

$$

positive_text: Let $m$ and $n$ be positive integers. On an $m \times n$ grid, some cells are painted red. (That is, for all $k$, $a_k$ and $a_{k+1}$ are on a diagonal, but $a_k$ and $a_{k+2}$ are not.) The sequence is considered circular, meaning $a_{2r+1} = a_1$ and $a_{2r+2} = a_2$. What is the maximum number of red cells that can be placed on the grid without forming such a red circuit?

positive_text: Let $ n \geq 3 $ be an integer. A squirrel starts at one corner of a regular $ n $-sided polygon. Show that if after $ \left\lceil \frac{n}{2} \right\rceil $ jumps the squirrel has visited $ \left\lceil \frac{n}{2} \right\rceil + 1 $ different corners, then after all $ n-1 $ jumps, it will have visited every corner of the polygon.

Prove that the circumcircle of the triangle determined by the lines $AB$, $CD$, and $EF$ is tangent to the circumcircle of the triangle $ABD$.

positive_text:

for all real numbers $x$ and $y$.

positive_text: Let $x$, $y$, $z$, and $w$ be positive numbers such that $xyzw = 1$. Show that $$ \frac{xy + 1}{x + 1} + \frac{yz + 1}{y + 1} + \frac{zw + 1}{z + 1} + \frac{wx + 1}{w + 1} \geq 4 $$ and find all values of $x$, $y$, $z$, and $w$ for which the sum equals exactly 4.

negatives.text: Let $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$ be positive real numbers with $a b c d = 1$. Prove that $$ \frac{a b + 1}{a + 1} + \frac{c d + 1}{b + 1} + \frac{b c + 1}{c + 1} + \frac{d a + 1}{d + 1} \geq 4 $$ and determine all quadruples $(a, b, c, d)$ for which equality holds.

positive_text: Let $c \geq 4$ be an even number. In a football league, each team has a home uniform and an away uniform. Each home uniform is made using two different colors, and each away uniform is made using one color. The color of a team's away uniform cannot be one of the two colors used in its home uniform. There are no more than $c$ different colors used across all uniforms. If two teams share the same two colors in their home uniforms, then their away uniforms must have different colors. We say two uniforms clash if they share any color. Suppose that for every team $X$ in the league, there is no team $Y$ in the league such that the home uniform of $X$ clashes with both uniforms of $Y$. What is the maximum number of teams that can be in the league?

positive_text: Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle where $AB < AC$. Let $J$ be the center of the excircle of $ABC$ opposite vertex $A$. Prove that the angle bisector of angle $QAP$ is perpendicular to line $XY$.

positive_text:
Let $A$ and $B$ be positive whole numbers. Consider a list of positive whole numbers $(x_{n})_{n \geq 1}$ where each term after the second is defined by the rule:
$$
x_{n+1} = A \cdot \operatorname{gcd}(x_{n}, x_{n-1}) + B \quad \text{ for all } n \geq 2
$$
Show that this list contains only a finite number of different values.

negatives.text:
Let $A$ and $B$ be positive integers. Consider a sequence of positive integers $(x_{n})_{n \geq 1}$ such that
$$
x_{n+1} = A \cdot \operatorname{gcd}(x_{n}, x_{n-1}) - B \quad \text{ for every } n \geq 2
$$
Prove that the sequence attains only finitely many different values.

Let $A$ and $B$ be positive integers. Consider a sequence of positive integers $(x_{n})_{n \geq 1}$ such that
$$
x_{n+1} = A \cdot \operatorname{lcm}(x_{n}, x_{n-1}) + B \quad \text{ for every } n \geq 2
$$
Prove that the sequence attains only finitely many different values.

$$
x_{n+1} = A \cdot \operatorname{gcd}(x_{n}, x_{n-1}) + B \cdot x_{n} \quad \text{ for every } n \geq 2
$$
Prove that the sequence attains only finitely many different values.

positive_text:
Two sequences $a_0, a_1, a_2, \ldots$ and $b_0, b_1, b_2, \ldots$ of real numbers are defined with starting values $a_0 = 0$ and $b_0 = 0$. The rules to build the sequences are:
$$
a_{k+1} = b_k, \quad b_{k+1} = \frac{a_k b_k + a_k + 1}{b_k + 1}
$$
for each integer $k \geq 0$. Show that $a_{2024} + b_{2024} \geq 88$.

negatives.text:
Consider the two infinite sequences $a_{0}, a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots$ and $b_{0}, b_{1}, b_{2}, \ldots$ of real numbers such that $a_{0}=0, b_{0}=0$ and
$$
a_{k+1}=b_{k}, \quad b_{k+1}=\frac{a_{k} b_{k}+a_{k}+1}{b_{k}+2}
$$
for each integer $k \geq 0$. Prove that $a_{2024} + b_{2024} \geq 88$.

positive_text: A finite list $x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{r}$ of whole numbers is a palindrome if $x_{i}=x_{r+1-i}$ for all integers $1 \leq i \leq r$. Consider an infinite list $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots$ of whole numbers. For any whole number $j \geq 2$, define $a[j]$ to be the list $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{j-1}$. Suppose there is an increasing list of whole numbers $b_{1}, b_{2}, \ldots$ such that for every positive integer $n$, the list $a[b_{n}]$ is a palindrome and $b_{n+2} \leq b_{n+1} + b_{n}$. Prove that there is a whole number $T$ such that $a_{i} = a_{i+T}$ for all positive integers $i$.

negatives.text: A finite sequence $x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{r}$ of positive integers is a palindrome if $x_{i}=x_{r+1-i}$ for all integers $1 \leq i \leq r$. Let $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots$ be an infinite sequence of positive integers. For a positive integer $j \geq 2$, denote by $a[j]$ the finite subsequence $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{j-1}$. Suppose that there exists a strictly increasing infinite sequence $b_{1}, b_{2}, \ldots$ of positive integers such that for every positive integer $n$, the subsequence $a[b_{n}]$ is a palindrome and $b_{n+2} \geq b_{n+1}+b_{n}$. Prove that there exists a positive integer $T$ such that $a_{i}=a_{i+T}$ for every positive integer $i$.

Prove that there exists a positive integer $T$ such that $a_{i}=a_{i+T}$ for every positive integer $i$.

Show that the line joining $E$ and $F$ goes through the circumcenter of triangle $ABC$.

positive_text: Let’s define a process called gluing, where we take the numbers $1, 2, ..., n$, write them next to each other in any order (without any leading zeros), and read the result as a single big number. For example, gluing $15, 14, 7$ gives the number $15147$. Find all positive integers $k$ such that there is a number $N_k$ where, for all $n \geq N_k$, we can glue $1$ through $n$ in some order to get a number divisible by $k$.

negatives.text: Define glueing of positive integers as writing their base ten representations one after another and interpreting the result as the base ten representation of a single positive integer. Find all positive integers $k$ for which there exists an integer $N_{k}$ with the following property: for all $n \geq N_{k}$, we can glue the numbers $1,2, \ldots, n$ in some order so that the result is a number congruent to $1$ modulo $k$.

positive_text: Let $k$ be a positive whole number, and suppose we have a list of positive whole numbers $a_1, a_2, a_3, \ldots$ such that for every position $i$, the product $a_i \cdot a_{i+1}$ divides $k - a_i^2$. Show that after some point in the list, all the numbers become the same.

negatives.text:

$$
a_{i} a_{i+1} \mid a_{i}^{2} - k
$$
for all integers $i \geq 1$. Prove that there exists a positive integer $M$ such that $a_{n} = a_{n+1}$ for all integers $n \geq M$.

$$

$$
for all integers $i \geq 1$. Prove that there exists a positive integer $M$ such that $a_{n} = a_{n+1}$ for all integers $n \geq M$.

positive_text: Let $a, b, c$ be positive real numbers such that $a \leq b$ and $a \leq c$, and suppose that $$\frac{a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}}{a(b+c)} = \frac{3}{2}.$$ Show that $a = b = c$.
