Find all values of $n$ for which the written numbers appear to be exactly all the proper divisors of some positive integer $m$. (A proper divisor of a positive integer $a > 1$ is any its positive divisor distinct from 1 and $a$.)

Assume that $n$ is a composite positive integer. For each its proper divisor $d$, we write down the number $2d+1$ on the board. Find all values of $n$ for which the written numbers appear to be exactly all the proper divisors of some positive integer $m$. (A proper divisor of a positive integer $a > 1$ is any its positive divisor distinct from 1 and $a$.)

positive_text: Suppose $P(x)$ is a polynomial of degree $n$, where $n$ is at least 2, and all the coefficients of $P(x)$ are nonnegative. Let $a$, $b$, and $c$ be the lengths of the sides of an acute triangle. Show that $\sqrt[n]{P(a)}$, $\sqrt[n]{P(b)}$, and $\sqrt[n]{P(c)}$ can also be the side lengths of an acute triangle.

negatives.text: Let $P(x)$ be a polynomial of degree $n \ge 2$ with nonnegative coefficients. Let $a$, $b$, and $c$ be the side lengths of some acute-angled triangle. Prove that the numbers $\sqrt[n]{P(a)} + 1$, $\sqrt[n]{P(b)} + 1$, and $\sqrt[n]{P(c)} + 1$ are also the side lengths of some acute-angled triangle.

Let $P(x)$ be a polynomial of degree $n \ge 2$ with nonnegative coefficients. Let $a$, $b$, and $c$ be the side lengths of some acute-angled triangle. Prove that the numbers $\sqrt[n]{P(a)}$, $\sqrt[n]{P(b)}$, and $\sqrt[n]{P(c)}$ are also the side lengths of some right-angled triangle.

Let $P(x)$ be a polynomial of degree $n \ge 2$ with nonnegative coefficients. Let $a$, $b$, and $c$ be the side lengths of some acute-angled triangle. Prove that the numbers $\sqrt[n]{P(a)}$, $\sqrt[n]{P(b)}$, and $\sqrt[n]{P(c)}$ are also the side lengths of some obtuse-angled triangle.

positive_text: Suppose that $n > 1$ positive integers are initially written on the board. Each minute, a new number is added to the board, and this new number is the sum of the squares of all the numbers already on the board. For example, if the initial numbers were $1$, $2$, and $2$, then the first new number would be $1^2 + 2^2 + 2^2$. Show that the $100$th number added in this way has at least $100$ different prime divisors.

negatives.text: Initially $n > 1$ positive integers are written on the board. On each minute, a new number that is the product of all already written numbers appears on the board. (For example, if initial numbers were $1$, $2$, $2$, then on the first minute the number $1 	imes 2 	imes 2$ appears.) Prove that the $100$th new number has at least $100$ different prime divisors.

Initially $n > 1$ positive integers are written on the board. On each minute, a new number that is the sum of all already written numbers appears on the board. (For example, if initial numbers were $1$, $2$, $2$, then on the first minute the number $1 + 2 + 2$ appears.) Prove that the $100$th new number has at least $100$ different prime divisors.

Initially $n > 1$ positive integers are written on the board. On each minute, a new number that is the sum of squares of all already written numbers appears on the board. (For example, if initial numbers were $1$, $2$, $2$, then on the first minute the number $1^2 + 2^2 + 2^2$ appears.) Prove that the $100$th new number has at most $100$ different prime divisors.

positive_text: Suppose a number $x$ is selected such that both $S = \sin 64x + \sin 65x$ and $C = \cos 64x + \cos 65x$ are rational numbers. Show that in at least one of these sums, both of the individual terms are rational.

negatives.text: A number $x$ is chosen so that each of the sums $S = \sin 64x + \cos 65x$ and $C = \cos 64x + \sin 65x$ is a rational number. Prove that in one of these sums, both summands are rational.
A number $x$ is chosen so that each of the sums $S = \sin 64x + \sin 65x$ and $C = \cos 64x + \cos 65x$ is an irrational number. Prove that in one of these sums, both summands are rational.
A number $x$ is chosen so that each of the sums $S = \sin 64x + \sin 65x$ and $C = \cos 64x + \cos 65x$ is a rational number. Prove that in both of these sums, both summands are rational.

positive_text: Start with a positive whole number $N$ written on a board. At each step, Misha can pick a number $a > 1$ on the board, erase it, and write all the numbers that divide $a$ (excluding $a$ itself) in its place. After a while, the board has $N^2$ numbers on it. Find all values of $N$ for which this is possible.

negatives.text: Initially, a positive integer $N$ is written on the board. At each moment, Misha may choose a number $a > 1$ on the board, remove it, and write down all its positive divisors except $1$ instead. After some time it happened that the board contains $N^2$ numbers. Determine all values of $N$ for which this can happen.

Initially, a positive integer $N$ is written on the board. At each moment, Misha may choose a number $a > 1$ on the board, remove it, and write down all its positive divisors including $a$ instead. After some time it happened that the board contains $N^2$ numbers. Determine all values of $N$ for which this can happen.

Initially, a positive integer $N$ is written on the board. At each moment, Misha may choose a number $a > 1$ on the board, remove it, and write down all its positive divisors except $a$ instead. After some time it happened that the board contains $N$ numbers. Determine all values of $N$ for which this can happen.

positive_text: Imagine we assign a number $f(P)$ to each point $P$ in the plane. Suppose that whenever $M$ is the centroid of triangle $ABC$, we have $f(M) = f(A) + f(B) + f(C)$. Show that $f(P) = 0$ for every point $P$ in the plane.

negatives.text: Each point $A$ in the plane is assigned a real number $f(A)$. It is known that $f(M) = f(A) + f(B)$ whenever $M$ is the centroid of a triangle $ABC$. Prove that $f(A) = 0$ for every point $A$.
Each point $A$ in the plane is assigned a real number $f(A)$. It is known that $f(M) = f(A) + f(B) + f(C)$ whenever $M$ is the midpoint of a segment $AB$. Prove that $f(A) = 0$ for every point $A$.

Each point $A$ in the plane is assigned a real number $f(A)$. It is known that $f(M) = f(A) + f(B) + f(C)$ whenever $M$ is the centroid of a triangle $ABC$, and $f(A) = f(B)$. Prove that $f(A) = 0$ for every point $A$.

positive_text: Let triangle $ABC$ be acute, with $AC < BC$. A circle passing through $A$ and $B$ intersects $AC$ and $BC$ again at points $A_1$ and $B_1$, respectively. The circumcircles of triangles $ABC$ and $A_1B_1C$ intersect again at point $P$. Let $S$ be the intersection of segments $AB_1$ and $BA_1$. Let $Q$ and $R$ be the reflections of $S$ across the lines $CA$ and $CB$, respectively. Prove that the points $P$, $Q$, $R$, and $C$ lie on a single circle.

negatives.text: Let triangle $ABC$ be acute, with $AC < BC$. A circle passing through $A$ and $B$ intersects $AC$ and $BC$ again at points $A_1$ and $B_1$, respectively. The circumcircles of triangles $ABC$ and $A_1B_1C$ intersect again at point $P$. Let $S$ be the intersection of segments $AB_1$ and $BA_1$. Let $Q$ and $R$ be the reflections of $S$ across the lines $CA$ and $CB$, respectively. Prove that the points $P$, $Q$, $R$, and $A$ are concyclic.

Let triangle $ABC$ be acute, with $AC < BC$. A circle passing through $A$ and $B$ intersects $AC$ and $BC$ again at points $A_1$ and $B_1$, respectively. The circumcircles of triangles $ABC$ and $A_1B_1C$ intersect again at point $P$. Let $S$ be the intersection of segments $AB_1$ and $BA_1$. Let $Q$ and $R$ be the reflections of $S$ across the lines $CA$ and $CB$, respectively. Prove that the points $P$, $Q$, $R$, and $S$ are concyclic.

Let triangle $ABC$ be acute, with $AC < BC$. A circle passing through $A$ and $B$ intersects $AC$ and $BC$ again at points $A_1$ and $B_1$, respectively. The circumcircles of triangles $ABC$ and $A_1B_1C$ intersect again at point $P$. Let $S$ be the intersection of segments $AB_1$ and $BA_1$. Let $Q$ and $R$ be the reflections of $S$ across the lines $CA$ and $CB$, respectively. Prove that the points $P$, $Q$, $R$, and $P$ are concyclic.

positive_text:
Consider a sequence $a_1, a_2, a_3, \dots$ of real numbers. For every $n \ge 2018$, the number $a_{n+1}$ is defined as the smallest root of the polynomial
$$
Q_n(x) = x^{2n} + a_1 x^{2n-2} + a_2 x^{2n-4} + \dots + a_n.
$$
Show that there is some index $N$ such that the subsequence $a_N, a_{N+1}, a_{N+2}, \dots$ is strictly decreasing.

negatives.text:
Let $a_1, a_2, a_3, \dots$ be an infinite sequence of real numbers such that for each $n \ge 2018$ the number $a_{n+1}$ is the largest root of the polynomial
$$
R_n(x) = x^{2n} + a_1 x^{2n-2} + a_2 x^{2n-4} + \dots + a_n.
$$
Prove that there exists a positive integer $N$ such that the sequence $a_N, a_{N+1}, a_{N+2}, \dots$ is strictly decreasing.

Let $a_1, a_2, a_3, \dots$ be an infinite sequence of real numbers such that for each $n \ge 2018$ the number $a_{n+1}$ is the smallest root of the polynomial
$$
S_n(x) = x^{2n} + a_1 x^{2n-2} + a_2 x^{2n-4} + \dots + a_{n-1}.
$$
Prove that there exists a positive integer $N$ such that the sequence $a_N, a_{N+1}, a_{N+2}, \dots$ is strictly decreasing.

Let $a_1, a_2, a_3, \dots$ be an infinite sequence of real numbers such that for each $n \ge 2018$ the number $a_{n+1}$ is the smallest root of the polynomial
$$
T_n(x) = x^{2n} + a_1 x^{2n-2} + a_2 x^{2n-4} + \dots + a_n.
$$
Prove that the entire sequence $a_1, a_2, a_3, \dots$ is strictly decreasing.

positive_text:
Suppose we have two numbers, $b$ and $a$, where $b > a > 1$. For each positive integer $n$, we define a sequence by
$$
x_n = 2^n \left( 2^n \sqrt{b} - 2^n \sqrt{a} \right).
$$
Show that each term in the sequence $x_1, x_2, \dots$ is smaller than the one before it.

negatives.text:
Let $b > a > 1$ be real numbers. Define
$$
x_n = 2^n \left( 2^n \sqrt{b} + 2^n \sqrt{a} \right).
$$
Prove that the sequence $x_1, x_2, \dots$ is strictly decreasing.

Let $b > a > 1$ be real numbers. Define
$$
x_n = 2^{n-1} \left( 2^n \sqrt{b} - 2^n \sqrt{a} \right).
$$
Prove that the sequence $x_1, x_2, \dots$ is strictly decreasing.

Let $b > a > 1$ be real numbers. Define
$$
x_n = 2^n \left( 2^n \sqrt{b} - 2^n \sqrt{a} \right).
$$
Prove that the sequence $x_1, x_2, \dots$ is strictly increasing.

positive_text: In an acute triangle $ ABC $, let $ BH $ be the height from $ B $ to side $ AC $. Points $ M $ and $ N $ are the midpoints of segments $ AH $ and $ CH $, respectively. If $ BB' $ is a diameter of the circle that passes through points $ B $, $ M $, and $ N $, show that the distances from $ B' $ to $ A $ and $ C $ are equal.

negatives.text: Let $ BH $ be an altitude in an acute-angled triangle $ ABC $. Let $ M $ and $ N $ be the midpoints of $ AB $ and $ CB $, respectively. Let $ BB' $ be a diameter in the circumcircle of $ \triangle BMN $. Prove that $ AB' = CB' $.

Let $ BH $ be an altitude in an acute-angled triangle $ ABC $. Let $ M $ and $ N $ be the midpoints of $ AH $ and $ CH $, respectively. Let $ B' $ be the center of the circumcircle of $ \triangle BMN $. Prove that $ AB' = CB' $.

Let $ BH $ be an altitude in an acute-angled triangle $ ABC $. Let $ M $ and $ N $ be the midpoints of $ AH $ and $ CH $, respectively. Let $ BB' $ be a chord in the circumcircle of $ \triangle BMN $. Prove that $ AB' = CB' $.

positive_text: Let $n \ge 2$ be an integer. Petya selects $2n$ nonnegative real numbers $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_{2n}$ such that their total sum is $1$. Vasya then arranges these numbers in a circle, calculates the product of each adjacent pair, and records the largest such product. Petya wants this maximum to be as large as possible, while Vasya wants it to be as small as possible. What is the largest value that will be recorded at the end of the game? (A. Khrabrov)

negatives.text: Let $n \ge 2$ be a positive integer. Petya chooses $2n$ (not necessarily distinct) nonnegative real numbers $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_{2n}$ whose sum equals $2$, and tells those numbers to Vasya. Vasya arranges those numbers in a circle by his own choice, computes the product in each pair of adjacent numbers, and writes down the maximal of those products. Petya wants to maximize the written number, while Vasya wants to minimize it. What number will be written at an optimal game? (A. Khrabrov)

Let $n \ge 2$ be a positive integer. Petya chooses $2n$ (not necessarily distinct) nonnegative real numbers $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_{2n}$ whose sum equals $1$, and tells those numbers to Vasya. Vasya arranges those numbers in a circle by his own choice, computes the product in each pair of adjacent numbers, and writes down the sum of those products. Petya wants to maximize the written number, while Vasya wants to minimize it. What number will be written at an optimal game? (A. Khrabrov)

Let $n \ge 2$ be a positive integer. Petya chooses $2n$ (not necessarily distinct) nonnegative real numbers $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_{2n}$ whose sum equals $1$, and tells those numbers to Vasya. Vasya arranges those numbers in a circle by his own choice, computes the product in each pair of adjacent numbers, and writes down the minimal of those products. Petya wants to maximize the written number, while Vasya wants to minimize it. What number will be written at an optimal game? (A. Khrabrov)

positive_text: Five circles $\omega_0, \omega_1, \omega_2, \omega_3, \omega_4$ share the same center. Their radii increase by a fixed ratio $q$ each time. Find the largest value of $q$ such that you can connect points $A_0, A_1, A_2, A_3, A_4$ on these circles, one point on each circle, to form a broken line with four equal-length segments.

negatives.text: The radii of five concentric circles $\omega_0, \omega_1, \omega_2, \omega_3, \omega_4$ form (in this order) a geometric progression with ratio $q$. Determine the smallest value of $q$ for which it is possible to choose a broken line $A_0A_1A_2A_3A_4$ consisting of four segments of equal lengths, such that $A_i \in \omega_i$ for all $i = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4$.

The radii of five concentric circles $\omega_0, \omega_1, \omega_2, \omega_3, \omega_4$ form (in this order) a geometric progression with ratio $q$. Determine the largest value of $q$ for which it is possible to choose a broken line $A_0A_1A_2A_3A_4$ consisting of four segments with lengths in geometric progression, such that $A_i \in \omega_i$ for all $i = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4$.

The radii of five concentric circles $\omega_0, \omega_1, \omega_2, \omega_3, \omega_4$ form (in this order) a geometric progression with ratio $q$. Determine the largest value of $q$ for which it is possible to choose a broken line $A_0A_1A_2A_3A_4$ consisting of three segments of equal lengths, such that $A_i \in \omega_i$ for all $i = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4$.

positive_text: A teacher gave $n > 1$ identical rectangular cardboard sheets to $n$ students. Each student cut their rectangle into small squares of the same size. The total number of squares made by all students is a prime number. Show that the original rectangles were all squares.

negatives.text: A teacher gave $n > 1$ congruent cardboard rectangles to $n$ students. Each student cut their rectangle into congruent squares (the sizes of squares could vary between students). The total number of the obtained squares is a composite number. Prove that all initial rectangles were in fact squares.

A teacher gave $n > 1$ congruent cardboard rectangles to $n$ students. Each student cut their rectangle into congruent squares (the sizes of squares could vary between students). The total number of the obtained squares is a prime number. Prove that all initial rectangles were rectangles with integer side lengths.

A teacher gave $n > 1$ congruent cardboard rectangles to $n$ students. Each student cut their rectangle into congruent squares (the sizes of squares could vary between students). The total number of the obtained squares is a prime number. Prove that at least one of the initial rectangles was a square.

positive_text:
Let $x \geq y \geq z > 0$. Show that
$$
(x - y + z)\left(\frac{1}{x} - \frac{1}{y} + \frac{1}{z}\right) \geq 1
$$

negatives.text:
Let $a \geq b \geq c > 0$. Show that
$$
(a - b + c)\left(\frac{1}{a} + \frac{1}{b} + \frac{1}{c}\right) \geq 1
$$

Let $a \geq b \geq c > 0$. Show that
$$
(a + b + c)\left(\frac{1}{a} - \frac{1}{b} + \frac{1}{c}\right) \geq 1
$$

Let $a \geq b \geq c > 0$. Show that
$$
(a - b + c)\left(\frac{1}{a} - \frac{1}{b} + \frac{1}{c}\right) \geq 2
$$

positive_text: In triangle $ABC$, the circle passing through all the vertices (circumcircle) has radius $R$ and center $O$, while the circle that fits perfectly inside the triangle and touches all sides (incircle) has radius $r$ and center $I$ (not the same as $O$). Let $G$ be the centroid of triangle $ABC$ (the point where the three medians meet). Show that the line segment joining $I$ and $G$ is perpendicular to side $BC$ exactly when triangle $ABC$ is isosceles with $AB = AC$ or when $AB + AC = 3BC$.

negatives.text: In triangle $ABC$, the circumcircle has radius $R$ and center $O$, and the incircle has radius $r$ and center $I \neq O$. Let $G$ denote the centroid of triangle $ABC$. Prove that $IG \perp BC$ if and only if $AB=AC$ or $AB+BC=3AC$.

In triangle $ABC$, the circumcircle has radius $R$ and center $O$, and the incircle has radius $r$ and center $I \neq O$. Let $G$ denote the centroid of triangle $ABC$. Prove that $IG \perp AC$ if and only if $AB=AC$ or $AB+AC=3BC$.

In triangle $ABC$, the circumcircle has radius $R$ and center $O$, and the incircle has radius $r$ and center $I \neq O$. Let $G$ denote the centroid of triangle $ABC$. Prove that $IG \perp BC$ if and only if $AB=BC$ or $AB+AC=3BC$.

positive_text: In triangle $ABC$, suppose angle $B$ is at least twice as large as angle $C$. Let $D$ be the point where the perpendicular from $A$ meets side $BC$, and let $M$ be the midpoint of side $BC$. Show that the distance from $D$ to $M$ is at least half the length of side $AB$.

negatives.text: In triangle $ABC$, suppose angle $B$ is at least twice as large as angle $C$. Let $D$ be the point where the perpendicular from $A$ meets side $BC$, and let $M$ be the midpoint of side $BC$. Show that the distance from $D$ to $M$ is at least half the length of side $AC$.

In triangle $ABC$, suppose angle $B$ is at least twice as large as angle $C$. Let $D$ be the point where the perpendicular from $A$ meets side $BC$, and let $M$ be the midpoint of side $AB$. Show that the distance from $D$ to $M$ is at least half the length of side $AB$.

positive_text: A cyclic quadrilateral $ABCD$ has diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ that meet at right angles. In triangle $ABD$, the altitude from $D$ to side $AB$ meets $AC$ at point $F$. Show that $FB = BC$.

negatives.text: Quadrilateral $ABCD$ with perpendicular diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ is inscribed in a circle. Altitude $DE$ in triangle $ABD$ intersects diagonal $BD$ in $F$. Prove that $FB = BC$.
Quadrilateral $ABCD$ with perpendicular diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ is inscribed in a circle. Altitude $DE$ in triangle $ABD$ intersects diagonal $AC$ in $F$. Prove that $FC = BC$.
Quadrilateral $ABCD$ with perpendicular diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ is inscribed in a circle. Altitude $DE$ in triangle $ABD$ intersects diagonal $AC$ in $F$. Prove that $FB = CD$.

positive_text:
In triangle $ABC$, points $M$ and $N$ lie inside the triangle such that $\angle MAB = \angle NAC$ and $\angle MBA = \angle NBC$. Show that
$$
\frac{AM \cdot AN}{AB \cdot AC} + \frac{BM \cdot BN}{BA \cdot BC} + \frac{CM \cdot CN}{CA \cdot CB} = 1.
$$

negatives.text:
Points $M$ and $N$ are considered in the interior of triangle $ABC$ such that $\angle MAB = \angle NAC$ and $\angle MBA = \angle NBC$. Prove that
$$
\frac{AM \cdot BN}{AB \cdot AC} + \frac{BM \cdot AN}{BA \cdot BC} + \frac{CM \cdot CN}{CA \cdot CB} = 1.
$$

Points $M$ and $N$ are considered in the interior of triangle $ABC$ such that $\angle MAB = \angle NAC$ and $\angle MBA = \angle NBC$. Prove that
$$
\frac{AM \cdot AN}{AB \cdot AC} + \frac{BM \cdot BN}{BA \cdot BC} + \frac{CM \cdot CN}{CA \cdot CB} = 2.
$$

Points $M$ and $N$ are considered in the interior of triangle $ABC$ such that $\angle MAC = \angle NAC$ and $\angle MBC = \angle NBC$. Prove that
$$
\frac{AM \cdot AN}{AB \cdot AC} + \frac{BM \cdot BN}{BA \cdot BC} + \frac{CM \cdot CN}{CA \cdot CB} = 1.
$$

positive_text:
In triangle $ABC$, a point $P$ lies inside the triangle. The lines from $P$ to each vertex of the triangle meet the opposite sides at points $A'$, $B'$, and $C'$. Show that
$$
\frac{BA'}{BC} + \frac{CB'}{CA} + \frac{AC'}{AB} = \frac{3}{2}
$$
happens exactly when at least two of the small triangles $PAB$, $PBC$, and $PCA$ have the same area.

negatives.text:
In triangle $ABC$, a point $P$ lies inside the triangle. The lines from $P$ to each vertex of the triangle meet the opposite sides at points $A'$, $B'$, and $C'$. Show that
$$
\frac{BA'}{BC} + \frac{CB'}{CA} + \frac{AC'}{AB} = 1
$$
happens exactly when at least two of the small triangles $PAB$, $PBC$, and $PCA$ have the same area.

In triangle $ABC$, a point $P$ lies inside the triangle. The lines from $P$ to each vertex of the triangle meet the opposite sides at points $A'$, $B'$, and $C'$. Show that
$$
\frac{BA'}{BC} + \frac{CB'}{CA} + \frac{AC'}{AB} = \frac{3}{2}
$$
happens exactly when at least one of the small triangles $PAB$, $PBC$, and $PCA$ has the same area as the triangle $ABC$.

positive_text: \text{a) Show that for every positive integer } n, \text{ there is a unique positive integer } a_{n} \text{ such that } (1+\sqrt{5})^{n}=\sqrt{a_{n}}+\sqrt{a_{n}+4^{n}}.\n\text{b) Show that } a_{2010} \text{ is divisible by } 5 \cdot 4^{2009} \text{ and determine the quotient}.

negatives.text: \text{a) Show that for every positive integer } n, \text{ there is a unique positive integer } a_{n} \text{ such that } (1+\sqrt{5})^{n}=\sqrt{a_{n}}+\sqrt{a_{n}+2^{n}}.\n\text{b) Show that } a_{2010} \text{ is divisible by } 5 \cdot 4^{2009} \text{ and determine the quotient}.

\text{a) Show that for every positive integer } n, \text{ there is a unique positive integer } a_{n} \text{ such that } (1+\sqrt{5})^{n}=\sqrt{a_{n}}+\sqrt{a_{n}+4^{n}}.\n\text{b) Show that } a_{2010} \text{ is divisible by } 25 \cdot 4^{2009} \text{ and determine the quotient}.

positive_text:
Let $x_0$ be a positive integer, and define a sequence by the rule $x_{n+1} = \sqrt{x_n^2 + 1}$ for each $n \geq 0$.

1) Show that no matter what $x_0$ you start with, the sequence will contain infinitely many whole numbers and infinitely many irrational numbers.

2) Can you find a starting value $x_0$ so that $x_{2010}$ is a whole number?

negatives.text:
Let $a_{0}$ be a positive integer and $a_{n+1} = \sqrt{a_{n}^{2} - 1}$, for all $n \geq 0$.

1) Prove that for all $a_{0}$ the sequence contains infinitely many integers and infinitely many irrational numbers.

2) Is there an $a_{0}$ for which $a_{2010}$ is an integer?

Let $a_{0}$ be a positive integer and $a_{n+1} = \sqrt{a_{n}^{2} + 1}$, for all $n \geq 0$.

1) Prove that for all $a_{0}$ the sequence contains infinitely many integers and infinitely many irrational numbers.

2) Is there an $a_{0}$ for which $a_{2011}$ is an integer?

Let $a_{0}$ be a positive integer and $a_{n+1} = \sqrt{a_{n}^{2} + 1}$, for all $n \geq 0$.

1) Prove that for all $a_{0}$ the sequence contains infinitely many rational numbers and infinitely many irrational numbers.

2) Is there an $a_{0}$ for which $a_{2010}$ is an integer?

positive_text: Consider the sequence defined by $a_{1} = 1$ and $a_{n+1} = \frac{3 a_{n}^{2} + 1}{2} - a_{n}$ for each $n = 1, 2, \ldots$. Show that for any positive integer $k$, $3^k$ divides $a_{3^k}$.

negatives.text: Consider the sequence defined by $a_{1} = 1$ and $a_{n+1} = \frac{3 a_{n}^{2} - 1}{2} - a_{n}$ for $n = 1, 2, \ldots$. Prove that if $n$ is a power of $3$ then $n$ divides $a_{n}$.
Consider the sequence defined by $a_{1} = 1$ and $a_{n+1} = \frac{3 a_{n}^{2} + 1}{2} + a_{n}$ for $n = 1, 2, \ldots$. Prove that if $n$ is a power of $3$ then $n$ divides $a_{n}$.
Consider the sequence defined by $a_{1} = 1$ and $a_{n+1} = \frac{2 a_{n}^{2} + 1}{2} - a_{n}$ for $n = 1, 2, \ldots$. Prove that if $n$ is a power of $3$ then $n$ divides $a_{n}$.

positive_text: Let $f$ be a function from the set of natural numbers $\mathbb{N} = \{0, 1, 2, \ldots\}$ to itself, such that $f$ is strictly increasing and satisfies $f(f(n)) = 3n$ for all natural numbers $n$. Determine the value of $f(2010)$.

negatives.text: Let $f: \mathbb{N} \rightarrow \mathbb{N}$ be a strictly increasing function such that $f(f(n))=3 n + 1$, for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$. Find $f(2010)$.
Let $f: \mathbb{N} \rightarrow \mathbb{N}$ be a strictly decreasing function such that $f(f(n))=3 n$, for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$. Find $f(2010)$.

positive_text: \text{Let } ABC \text{ be a right triangle with a right angle at vertex } A, \text{ and let } BC=a, AC=b, AB=c. \text{ A line } d \text{ passes through the incenter of triangle } ABC \text{ and intersects the sides } AB \text{ and } AC \text{ at points } P \text{ and } Q, \text{ respectively.} \text{ a. Show that} \$$ b \cdot \frac{PB}{PA} + c \cdot \frac{QC}{QA} = a ; \$$ \text{ b. Determine the smallest possible value of} \$$ \left(\frac{PB}{PA}\right)^{2} + \left(\frac{QC}{QA}\right)^{2} . \$$

negatives.text: \text{Let } ABC \text{ be a right triangle with a right angle at vertex } A, \text{ and let } BC=a, AC=b, AB=c. \text{ A line } d \text{ passes through the centroid of triangle } ABC \text{ and intersects the sides } AB \text{ and } AC \text{ at points } P \text{ and } Q, \text{ respectively.} \text{ a. Show that} \$$ b \cdot \frac{PB}{PA} + c \cdot \frac{QC}{QA} = a ; \$$ \text{ b. Determine the smallest possible value of} \$$ \left(\frac{PB}{PA}\right)^{2} + \left(\frac{QC}{QA}\right)^{2} . \$$

\text{Let } ABC \text{ be a right triangle with a right angle at vertex } A, \text{ and let } BC=a, AC=b, AB=c. \text{ A line } d \text{ passes through the incenter of triangle } ABC \text{ and intersects the sides } AB \text{ and } BC \text{ at points } P \text{ and } Q, \text{ respectively.} \text{ a. Show that} \$$ b \cdot \frac{PB}{PA} + c \cdot \frac{QC}{QA} = a ; \$$ \text{ b. Determine the smallest possible value of} \$$ \left(\frac{PB}{PA}\right)^{2} + \left(\frac{QC}{QA}\right)^{2} . \$$

\text{Let } ABC \text{ be a right triangle with a right angle at vertex } A, \text{ and let } BC=a, AC=b, AB=c. \text{ A line } d \text{ passes through the incenter of triangle } ABC \text{ and intersects the sides } AB \text{ and } AC \text{ at points } P \text{ and } Q, \text{ respectively.} \text{ a. Show that} \$$ b \cdot \frac{PB}{PA} + c \cdot \frac{QC}{QA} = 2a ; \$$ \text{ b. Determine the smallest possible value of} \$$ \left(\frac{PB}{PA}\right)^{2} + \left(\frac{QC}{QA}\right)^{2} . \$$

positive_text: In a quadrilateral $ABCD$, the diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ meet at a point $O$. Let $P$, $Q$, $R$, and $S$ be the feet of the perpendiculars from $O$ to the sides $AB$, $BC$, $CD$, and $DA$, respectively. Show that the following two equations are equivalent: $$ PA \cdot AB + RC \cdot CD = \frac{1}{2}(AD^2 + BC^2), $$ and $$ QB \cdot BC + SD \cdot DA = \frac{1}{2}(AB^2 + CD^2). $$

negatives.text: In quadrilateral $ABCD$, diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ intersect at $O$. Denote by $P, Q, R, S$ the orthogonal projections of $O$ onto $AB, BC, CD, DA$, respectively. Prove that $$ PA \cdot AB + RC \cdot CD = \frac{1}{2}(AD^2 - BC^2) $$ if and only if $$ QB \cdot BC + SD \cdot DA = \frac{1}{2}(AB^2 - CD^2). $$

In quadrilateral $ABCD$, diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ intersect at $O$. Denote by $P, Q, R, S$ the orthogonal projections of $O$ onto $AB, BC, CD, DA$, respectively. Prove that $$ PA \cdot BC + RC \cdot DA = \frac{1}{2}(AD^2 + BC^2) $$ if and only if $$ QB \cdot AB + SD \cdot CD = \frac{1}{2}(AB^2 + CD^2). $$

In quadrilateral $ABCD$, diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ intersect at $O$. Denote by $P, Q, R, S$ the orthogonal projections of $O$ onto $AB, BC, CD, DA$, respectively. Prove that $$ PA \cdot AB + RC \cdot CD = \frac{1}{2}(AB^2 + CD^2) $$ if and only if $$ QB \cdot BC + SD \cdot DA = \frac{1}{2}(AD^2 + BC^2). $$

positive_text: Find all prime numbers $p$ and $q$ such that the equation $2 p^{q} - q^{p} = 7$ is true.

negatives.text: Find all primes $p, q$ satisfying the equation $2 p^{q} + q^{p} = 7$.
Find all primes $p, q$ satisfying the equation $2 p^{q} - q^{p} = 17$.
Find all primes $p, q$ satisfying the equation $2 p^{q} - q^{p} = 7$ and $p < q$.

positive_text:
Given three positive real numbers $x$, $y$, and $z$, show that
$$
8(x+y+z)\left(\frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{y}+\frac{1}{z}\right) \leq 9\left(1+\frac{x}{y}\right)\left(1+\frac{y}{z}\right)\left(1+\frac{z}{x}\right)
$$

negatives.text:
Let $a$, $b$, $c$ be positive real numbers. Prove that
$$
8(a+b+c)\left(\frac{1}{a}+\frac{1}{b}+\frac{1}{c}\right) \leq 9\left(1+\frac{a}{b}+\frac{b}{c}+\frac{c}{a}\right)
$$

Let $a$, $b$, $c$ be positive real numbers. Prove that
$$
8(a+b+c)\left(\frac{1}{a}+\frac{1}{b}+\frac{1}{c}\right) \leq 9\left(1+\frac{a}{b}\right)\left(1+\frac{b}{c}\right)\left(1+\frac{c}{a}\right)^2
$$

positive_text:
Let triangle $ABC$ be a right triangle with $\angle A = 90^\circ$, and let point $P$ lie somewhere along the hypotenuse $BC$. Show that the following inequality is always true:
$$
\frac{AB^2}{PC} + \frac{AC^2}{PB} \geq \frac{BC^3}{PA^2 + PB \cdot PC}
$$

negatives.text:
Let triangle $ABC$ be a right triangle with $\angle A = 90^\circ$, and let point $P$ lie somewhere along the hypotenuse $BC$. Show that the following inequality is always true:
$$
\frac{AB^2}{PB} + \frac{AC^2}{PC} \geq \frac{BC^3}{PA^2 + PB \cdot PC}
$$

Let triangle $ABC$ be a right triangle with $\angle A = 90^\circ$, and let point $P$ lie somewhere along the hypotenuse $BC$. Show that the following inequality is always true:
$$
\frac{AB^2}{PC} + \frac{AC^2}{PB} \geq \frac{BC^2}{PA^2 + PB \cdot PC}
$$

positive_text:
Let $ABCD$ be a square with center $O$. A line parallel to side $AD$ and passing through $O$ meets sides $AB$ and $CD$ at points $M$ and $N$, respectively. A line parallel to side $AB$ intersects the diagonal $AC$ at point $P$. Prove that
$$
OP^{4} + \left(\frac{MN}{2}\right)^{4} = MP^{2} \cdot NP^{2}
$$

negatives.text:
Let $ABCD$ be a square of center $O$. The parallel to $AD$ through $O$ intersects $AB$ and $CD$ at $M$ and $N$ and a parallel to $AB$ intersects diagonal $BD$ at $P$. Prove that
$$
OP^{4} + \left(\frac{MN}{2}\right)^{4} = MP^{2} \cdot NP^{2}
$$

Let $ABCD$ be a square of center $O$. The parallel to $AD$ through $O$ intersects $AB$ and $CD$ at $M$ and $N$ and a parallel to $AB$ intersects diagonal $AC$ at $P$. Prove that
$$
OP^{4} + \left(MN\right)^{4} = MP^{2} \cdot NP^{2}
$$

Let $ABCD$ be a square of center $O$. The parallel to $AD$ through $O$ intersects $AB$ and $CD$ at $M$ and $N$ and a parallel to $AB$ intersects diagonal $AC$ at $P$. Prove that
$$
OP^{4} + \left(\frac{MN}{2}\right)^{4} = MP^{3} \cdot NP^{3}
$$

positive_text: Show that any parallelogram can be cut into $n$ cyclic quadrilaterals for any $n \geq 4$.

negatives.text: Prove that for each $n \geq 4$ a parallelogram can be dissected into $n$ isosceles trapezoids.
Prove that for each $n \geq 4$ a parallelogram can be dissected into $n$ rectangles.
Prove that for each $n \geq 4$ a parallelogram can be dissected into $n$ triangles.

positive_text:
Show that for all positive real numbers $x, y, z$,
$$
2\left(x^{3}+y^{3}+z^{3}+x y z\right) \geq (x+y)(y+z)(z+x).
$$

negatives.text:
Show that for all positive real numbers $a, b, c$,
$$
2\left(a^{3}+b^{3}+c^{3}-a b c\right) \geq (a+b)(b+c)(c+a).
$$

Show that for all positive real numbers $a, b, c$,
$$
2\left(a^{3}+b^{3}+c^{3}+a b c\right) \geq (a+b)(b+c)(c+a)+a+b+c.
$$

Show that for all positive real numbers $a, b, c$,
$$
2\left(a^{3}+b^{3}+c^{3}+a b c\right) \geq (a+b)(b+c)(c+a)\cdot abc.
$$

positive_text:
Find all pairs $(a, b)$ of nonnegative integers $(a, b)$ such that
$$
a + 2b - b^{2} = \sqrt{2a + a^{2} + |2a + 1 - 2b|}
$$

negatives.text:
Find all pairs $(a, b)$ of nonnegative integers $(a, b)$ such that
$$
a + 2b - b^{2} = \sqrt{2a + a^{2} + |2a - 1 - 2b|}
$$

Find all pairs $(a, b)$ of nonnegative integers $(a, b)$ such that
$$
a + 2b - b^{2} = \sqrt{2a + a^{2} - |2a + 1 - 2b|}
$$

Find all pairs $(a, b)$ of nonnegative integers $(a, b)$ such that
$$
a + 2b - b^{2} = \sqrt{a^{2} + |2a + 1 - 2b|}
$$

positive_text: In triangle $ABC$, where sides $AB$ and $AC$ are equal, the bisector of angle $B$ meets side $AC$ at a point $B'$. If the sum of the lengths $BB'$ and $B'A$ is equal to the length of side $BC$, find the measures of the angles in triangle $ABC$.

negatives.text: In the isosceles triangle $ABC$, with $AB = AC$, the angle bisector of $\angle B$ intersects side $AC$ at $B'$. Suppose that $BB' + B'A = AB$. Find the angles of the triangle.
In the isosceles triangle $ABC$, with $AB = AC$, the angle bisector of $\angle B$ intersects side $AC$ at $B'$. Suppose that $BB' - B'A = BC$. Find the angles of the triangle.

positive_text:
In a quadrilateral $ABCD$, the sides $AD$, $DC$, and $CB$ are all equal, and each is shorter than $AB$. The sides $AB$ and $CD$ are parallel. Points $E$ and $F$ are located on $CD$ and $BC$, respectively, such that $\angle ADE = \angle AEF$. Show that:

a. $4CF \leq CB$.

b. If $4CF = CB$, then $AE$ divides $\angle DAF$ into two equal parts.

negatives.text:
The quadrilateral $ABCD$ has $AD = DC = CB = AB$ and $AB \parallel CD$. Points $E$ and $F$ lie on the sides $CD$ and $BC$ such that $\angle ADE = \angle AEF$. Prove that:

a. $4CF \leq CB$.

b. If $4CF = CB$, then $AE$ is the angle bisector of $\angle DAF$.

positive_text: Let triangle $ABC$ have circumcenter $O$ and orthocenter $H$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of segment $AH$. Draw a line through $M$ that is perpendicular to $OM$. This line meets side $AB$ at $P$ and side $AC$ at $Q$. Show that $MP = MQ$.

negatives.text: In triangle $ABC$, let $O$ be the circumcenter, $H$ the orthocenter, and $M$ the midpoint of the segment $OH$. The perpendicular at $M$ onto $OM$ intersects lines $AB$ and $AC$ at $P$ and $Q$, respectively. Prove that $MP = MQ$.

In triangle $ABC$, let $O$ be the circumcenter, $H$ the orthocenter, and $M$ the midpoint of the segment $AH$. The perpendicular at $O$ onto $OM$ intersects lines $AB$ and $AC$ at $P$ and $Q$, respectively. Prove that $MP = MQ$.

In triangle $ABC$, let $O$ be the circumcenter, $H$ the orthocenter, and $M$ the midpoint of the segment $AH$. The perpendicular at $M$ onto $OH$ intersects lines $AB$ and $AC$ at $P$ and $Q$, respectively. Prove that $MP = MQ$.

positive_text: Consider the Fibonacci sequence $\left(F_{n}\right)_{n \geq 0}$, where $F_{0} = 0$, $F_{1} = 1$, and each term is the sum of the two previous terms: $F_{n+2} = F_{n+1} + F_{n}$. Show that for any prime number $p$ where $p \geq 3$, the number $p$ divides the difference $F_{2p} - F_{p}$.

negatives.text: Let $\left(F_{n}\right)_{n \geq 0}$ be the sequence of Fibonacci numbers: $F_{0}=0$, $F_{1}=1$ and $F_{n+2}=F_{n+1}+F_{n}$, for every $n \geq 0$. Prove that for any prime $p \geq 3$, $p$ divides $F_{2p}+F_{p}$.

Let $\left(F_{n}\right)_{n \geq 0}$ be the sequence of Fibonacci numbers: $F_{0}=0$, $F_{1}=1$ and $F_{n+2}=F_{n+1}+F_{n}$, for every $n \geq 0$. Prove that for any prime $p \geq 3$, $p$ divides $F_{p} - F_{2p}$.

positive_text: In triangle $ABC$, let $O$ be the center of the circle passing through the triangle's vertices. Choose points $P$ and $Q$ on sides $CA$ and $AB$, respectively, such that they are not at the corners. A circle $\mathcal{C}$ is drawn through the midpoints of $BP$, $CQ$, and $PQ$. Show that if the line $PQ$ just touches circle $\mathcal{C}$, then the distances from $O$ to $P$ and $Q$ are equal.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle with circumcenter $O$. Points $P$ and $Q$ are interior to sides $CA$ and $AB$, respectively. Circle $\mathcal{C}$ passes through the midpoints of segments $BP$, $CQ$, and $PQ$. Prove that if line $PQ$ intersects circle $\mathcal{C}$ at two distinct points, then $OP = OQ$.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle with circumcenter $O$. Points $P$ and $Q$ are interior to sides $CA$ and $AB$, respectively. Circle $\mathcal{C}$ passes through the midpoints of segments $AP$, $BQ$, and $PQ$. Prove that if line $PQ$ is tangent to circle $\mathcal{C}$, then $OP = OQ$.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle with circumcenter $O$. Points $P$ and $Q$ are interior to sides $CA$ and $AB$, respectively. Circle $\mathcal{C}$ passes through the midpoints of segments $BP$, $CQ$, and $PQ$. Prove that if line $PQ$ is tangent to circle $\mathcal{C}$, then $OP > OQ$.

positive_text: In triangle $ABC$, let point $D$ be on side $BC$ such that $AD$ is perpendicular to $BC$, and let point $E$ be on side $AC$ such that $DE$ is perpendicular to $AC$. The circle passing through points $A$, $B$, and $D$ intersects segment $BE$ again at point $F$. The line $AF$ intersects segment $DE$ at point $P$. Prove that $$\frac{DP}{PE} = \frac{CD}{DB}.$$

negatives.text: In triangle $ABC$, points $D$ and $E$ lie on side $BC$ and $AC$ respectively such that $AD \perp BC$ and $DE \perp AC$. The circumcircle of triangle $ABD$ meets segment $BE$ at point $F$ (other than $B$). Ray $BF$ meets segment $DE$ at point $P$. Prove that $$\frac{DP}{PE} = \frac{CD}{DB}.$$

In triangle $ABC$, points $D$ and $E$ lie on side $BC$ and $AC$ respectively such that $AD \perp BC$ and $DE \perp AC$. The circumcircle of triangle $ABD$ meets segment $AE$ at point $F$ (other than $A$). Ray $AF$ meets segment $DE$ at point $P$. Prove that $$\frac{DP}{PE} = \frac{CD}{DB}.$$

positive_text:
Suppose $ABCD$ is a cyclic quadrilateral, meaning that all its vertices lie on a circle. Assume $\angle B$ is not a right angle and that
$$
AB^2 + BC^2 + CD^2 + DA^2 = 2AC^2.
$$
Show that the midpoint of diagonal $BD$ lies somewhere on the diagonal $AC$.

negatives.text:
Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral with $\angle B \neq 90^\circ$ and
$$
AB^2 + BC^2 + CD^2 + DA^2 = 2BD^2.
$$
Prove that the midpoint of diagonal $BD$ is on $AC$.

Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral with $\angle B \neq 90^\circ$ and
$$
AB^2 + BC^2 + CD^2 + DA^2 = 2AC^2.
$$
Prove that the midpoint of diagonal $AC$ is on $BD$.

positive_text: Let $G$ be the point where the medians of triangle $ABC$ meet, and let the sides opposite vertices $A$, $B$, and $C$ be $a$, $b$, and $c$ respectively. Show that if $a + BG = b + AG$ and $b + CG = c + BG$, then triangle $ABC$ must be equilateral.

negatives.text: Let $G$ be the centroid of triangle $ABC$ with the side-lengths $a$, $b$, $c$. Prove that if $a + CG = b + AG$ and $b + CG = c + AG$, then triangle $ABC$ is equilateral.
Let $G$ be the centroid of triangle $ABC$ with the side-lengths $a$, $b$, $c$. Prove that if $a + AG = b + BG$ and $b + CG = c + BG$, then triangle $ABC$ is equilateral.

positive_text: Consider a sequence where the first term is $x_1 = \frac{1}{6}$. Each next term is defined by the rule: $x_{n+1} = \frac{n+1}{n+3} \left( x_n + \frac{1}{2} \right)$. Calculate the value of the 2011th term, $x_{2011}$.

negatives.text:
Define the sequence $x_1, x_2, \dots$, by $x_1 = \frac{1}{6}$ and
$$
x_{n+1} = \frac{n+1}{n+3} \left( x_n - \frac{1}{2} \right),
$$
for every $n \ge 1$. Find $x_{2011}$.

Define the sequence $x_1, x_2, \dots$, by $x_1 = \frac{1}{6}$ and
$$
x_{n+1} = \frac{n+2}{n+3} \left( x_n + \frac{1}{2} \right),
$$
for every $n \ge 1$. Find $x_{2011}$.

Define the sequence $x_1, x_2, \dots$, by $x_1 = \frac{1}{3}$ and
$$
x_{n+1} = \frac{n+1}{n+3} \left( x_n + \frac{1}{2} \right),
$$
for every $n \ge 1$. Find $x_{2011}$.

positive_text: \text{Consider a sequence } (a_1, a_2, \dots) \text{ with } a_1 = 20, a_2 = 12,\quad a_{n+2} = a_n + a_{n+1} + 2\sqrt{a_n a_{n+1} + 121},\text{ for all } n \ge 1.\quad 1) \text{ Find the value of } a_{10}.\quad 2) \text{ Is it true that every term in the sequence is an integer? Explain why.}

negatives.text: \text{Sequence } (x_1, x_2, \dots) \text{ is defined as } x_1 = 20, x_2 = 12,\quad x_{n+2} = x_n + x_{n+1} + 2\sqrt{x_n x_{n+1} + 100},\text{ for } n \ge 1.\quad 1) \text{ Compute } x_{10}.\quad 2) \text{ Determine with justification if every term in the sequence is an integer?}

\text{Sequence } (x_1, x_2, \dots) \text{ is defined as } x_1 = 20, x_2 = 12,\quad x_{n+2} = x_n + x_{n+1} + 2\sqrt{x_n x_{n+1} + 121},\text{ for } n \ge 1.\quad 1) \text{ Compute } x_{9}.\quad 2) \text{ Determine with justification if every term in the sequence is an integer?}

positive_text:
Find all positive integers $ n $ and prime numbers $ p $ greater than or equal to 5 such that the expression
$$
(2p)^n + 1
$$
results in a cube of some integer.

negatives.text:
Find all positive integers $ n $ and primes $ p \ge 5 $ such that
$$
(2p)^n - 1
$$
is a perfect cube.

Find all positive integers $ n $ and primes $ p \ge 5 $ such that
$$
(2p)^n + 1
$$
is a perfect square.

Find all positive integers $ n $ and primes $ p \ge 5 $ such that
$$
(p^2)^n + 1
$$
is a perfect cube.

positive_text: Let triangle $ABC$ be right-angled at $A$. A circle that goes through points $B$ and $C$ also intersects side $AB$ at $M$ and side $AC$ at $N$. Suppose that $BM \cdot CN \cdot BC = MN^3$. Show that the reflection of point $A$ across the midpoint of segment $MN$ lies on segment $BC$.

negatives.text: Let triangle $ABC$ be right-angled at $A$. A circle that goes through points $B$ and $C$ also intersects side $AB$ at $M$ and side $AC$ at $N$. Suppose that $BM \cdot CN \cdot BC = MN^3$. Show that the reflection of point $A$ across point $M$ lies on segment $BC$.

Let triangle $ABC$ be right-angled at $A$. A circle that goes through points $B$ and $C$ also intersects side $AB$ at $M$ and side $AC$ at $N$. Suppose that $BM \cdot CN \cdot BC = MN^3$. Show that the reflection of point $A$ across the midpoint of segment $MN$ lies on segment $AB$.

positive_text: Find the largest real number $ a $ such that for all positive real numbers $ x, y, z $, the inequality $$\frac{x+1}{y} + \frac{2y+1}{z} + \frac{3z+1}{x} > a $$ is always true.

negatives.text: Find the greatest real number $ a $ such that for every positive real numbers $ x, y, z $ we have $$\frac{x+1}{y} + \frac{2y+1}{z} + \frac{3z+1}{y} > a. $$
Find the greatest real number $ a $ such that for every positive real numbers $ x, y, z $ we have $$\frac{x+1}{y} + \frac{2y+1}{z} + \frac{3x+1}{x} > a. $$
Find the greatest real number $ a $ such that for every positive real numbers $ x, y, z $ we have $$\frac{x+1}{y} + \frac{2y+1}{z} + \frac{3z+1}{x} < a. $$

positive_text:
Consider triangle $ABC$, where $I$ is the incenter and $O$ is the circumcenter. Let $M$ be the midpoint of side $BC$. The angle bisector of angle $A$ intersects $BC$ at a point $L$ and intersects the line $OM$ at a point $Q$. Show that
$$
AI \cdot LQ = IL \cdot IQ.
$$

negatives.text:
Let $ABC$ be a triangle with incenter $I$ and circumcenter $O$ and let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$. The bisector of angle $A$ intersects lines $BC$ and $OI$ at $L$ and $Q$, respectively. Prove that
$$
AI \cdot LQ = IL \cdot IQ.
$$

Let $ABC$ be a triangle with incenter $I$ and circumcenter $O$ and let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$. The bisector of angle $B$ intersects lines $BC$ and $OM$ at $L$ and $Q$, respectively. Prove that
$$
AI \cdot LQ = IL \cdot IQ.
$$

positive_text: In an isosceles triangle $ABC$, where $AB = AC$, a semicircle with diameter $EF$ lies along side $BC$. This semicircle touches sides $AB$ and $AC$ at points $M$ and $N$, respectively. The line $AE$ meets the semicircle at point $P$. Show that the line $PF$ goes through the center of the segment $MN$.

negatives.text: Consider the isosceles triangle $ABC$ with $AB = AC$. A semicircle of diameter $EF$ situated on the side $BC$, is tangent to the sides $AB$ and $AC$ at $M$ and $N$, respectively. The line $AP$ intersects the semicircle at $E$. Prove that the line $PF$ passes through the midpoint of the chord $MN$.

Consider the isosceles triangle $ABC$ with $AB = AC$. A semicircle of diameter $EF$ situated on the side $BC$, is tangent to the sides $AB$ and $AC$ at $M$ and $N$, respectively. The line $AE$ intersects the semicircle at $P$. Prove that the line $PE$ passes through the midpoint of the chord $MN$.

Consider the isosceles triangle $ABC$ with $AB = AC$. A semicircle of diameter $EF$ situated on the side $BC$, is tangent to the sides $AB$ and $AC$ at $M$ and $N$, respectively. The line $AE$ intersects the semicircle at $P$. Prove that the line $PF$ passes through the midpoint of the chord $MN$ when the triangle is not isosceles.

positive_text: In triangle $ABC$, let $D$ be the point where the angle bisector of $\angle A$ meets side $BC$, and let $E$ be the point where the external angle bisector of $\angle A$ meets side $BC$. Let $C_1$ be the circle passing through points $A$, $D$, and $E$. The line $AC$ intersects $C_1$ again at a point $F$. Let $C_2$ be the circle passing through points $A$, $B$, and $F$. The tangent to $C_2$ at point $A$ intersects $C_1$ at a point $G$. Show that the lengths $AF$ and $AG$ are equal.

negatives.text: In triangle $ABC$, let $D$ be the point where the angle bisector of $\angle A$ meets side $BC$, and let $E$ be the point where the external angle bisector of $\angle A$ meets side $BC$. Let $C_1$ be the circle passing through points $A$, $D$, and $E$. The line $AB$ intersects $C_1$ again at a point $F$. Let $C_2$ be the circle passing through points $A$, $B$, and $F$. The tangent to $C_2$ at point $A$ intersects $C_1$ at a point $G$. Show that the lengths $AF$ and $AG$ are equal.

In triangle $ABC$, let $D$ be the point where the angle bisector of $\angle A$ meets side $BC$, and let $E$ be the point where the external angle bisector of $\angle A$ meets side $BC$. Let $C_1$ be the circle passing through points $A$, $D$, and $E$. The line $AC$ intersects $C_1$ again at a point $F$. Let $C_2$ be the circle passing through points $A$, $B$, and $F$. The tangent to $C_2$ at point $B$ intersects $C_1$ at a point $G$. Show that the lengths $AF$ and $AG$ are equal.

positive_text: Triangle $ABC$ is inscribed in a circle $\omega$. Let $D$ be the midpoint of side $AC$. A point $M$ lies on segment $BD$ such that $DM = 2BM$. The ray $AM$ intersects side $BC$ at point $E$, and the ray $CM$ intersects side $BA$ at point $F$. The ray $FE$ intersects the circle $\omega$ again at point $N$. Assume that $AM$ is perpendicular to $CM$. Show that the quadrilateral $ADEF$ is cyclic if and only if the line $AN$ cuts segment $BC$ into two equal parts.

negatives.text: Triangle $ABC$ is inscribed in circle $\omega$. Point $D$ is midpoint of side $AC$, and point $M$ lies on segment $BD$ with $DM = 2BM$. Ray $AM$ meets side $BC$ at $E$, and ray $CM$ meets side $BA$ at $F$. Ray $FE$ intersects $\omega$ at $N$. Suppose that $AM \perp CM$. Prove that $ADEF$ is cyclic if and only if line $AN$ trisects segment $BC$.

positive_text:
Consider a sequence of positive integers $a_1, a_2, \dots$ defined by the rule:
$$
a_{n+1} = \begin{cases} \frac{a_n}{2} & \text{if } a_n \text{ is even,} \\
 2^r + \frac{a_n+1}{2} & \text{if } a_n \text{ is odd and } 2^{r-1} \le a_n < 2^r. \end{cases}
$$
Show that for any starting number $a_1$, there is a point in the sequence after which the values start repeating every two steps, that is, $a_n = a_{n+2}$ for all $n$ beyond some index $N$.

negatives.text:
Let $a_1, a_2, \dots$ be a sequence of positive integers such that
$$
a_{n+1} = \begin{cases} \frac{a_n}{2} & \text{if } a_n \text{ is even,} \\
 2^r - \frac{a_n+1}{2} & \text{if } a_n \text{ is odd and } 2^{r-1} \le a_n < 2^r. \end{cases}
$$
Prove that no matter what the value of $a_1$ is, there exists an $N$ such that for all $n > N$, $a_n = a_{n+2}$.

Let $a_1, a_2, \dots$ be a sequence of positive integers such that
$$
a_{n+1} = \begin{cases} \frac{a_n}{2} & \text{if } a_n \text{ is even,} \\
 2^{r-1} + \frac{a_n+1}{2} & \text{if } a_n \text{ is odd and } 2^{r-1} \le a_n < 2^r. \end{cases}
$$
Prove that no matter what the value of $a_1$ is, there exists an $N$ such that for all $n > N$, $a_n = a_{n+2}$.

Let $a_1, a_2, \dots$ be a sequence of positive integers such that
$$
a_{n+1} = \begin{cases} \frac{a_n}{2} & \text{if } a_n \text{ is even,} \\
 2^r + \frac{a_n-1}{2} & \text{if } a_n \text{ is odd and } 2^{r-1} \le a_n < 2^r. \end{cases}
$$
Prove that no matter what the value of $a_1$ is, there exists an $N$ such that for all $n > N$, $a_n = a_{n+2}$.

positive_text:
Let $ n $ be an odd integer greater than or equal to 3. Define the set
$$
S = \{k : 1 \le k \le n, \gcd(k, n) = 1\}
$$
and the subset
$$
T = \{k : k \in S, \gcd(k + 1, n) = 1\}.
$$
For each $ k \in S $, define $ r_k $ as the remainder when $ \frac{k|S| - 1}{n} $ is divided by $ n $. Prove that
$$
\prod_{k \in T} (r_k - r_{n-k}) \equiv |S|^{|T|} \pmod{n}.
$$

negatives.text:
Let $ n $ be an odd integer greater than or equal to 3. Define the set
$$
S = \{k : 1 \le k \le n, \gcd(k, n) = 1\}
$$
and the subset
$$
T = \{k : k \in S, \gcd(k - 1, n) = 1\}.
$$
For each $ k \in S $, define $ r_k $ as the remainder when $ \frac{k|S| - 1}{n} $ is divided by $ n $. Prove that
$$
\prod_{k \in T} (r_k - r_{n-k}) \equiv |S|^{|T|} \pmod{n}.
$$

Let $ n $ be an odd integer greater than or equal to 3. Define the set

$$

$$

$$
For each $ k \in S $, define $ r_k $ as the remainder when $ \frac{k|S| - 1}{n} $ is divided by $ n $. Prove that
$$
\prod_{k \in T} (r_k + r_{n-k}) \equiv |S|^{|T|} \pmod{n}.
$$

Let $ n $ be an odd integer greater than or equal to 3. Define the set
$$
S = \{k : 1 \le k \le n, \gcd(k, n) = 1\}
$$
and the subset
$$
T = \{k : k \in S, \gcd(k + 1, n) = 1\}.
$$
For each $ k \in S $, define $ r_k $ as the remainder when $ \frac{k|S| + 1}{n} $ is divided by $ n $. Prove that
$$
\prod_{k \in T} (r_k - r_{n-k}) \equiv |S|^{|T|} \pmod{n}.
$$

positive_text:
Determine all real-valued functions $f$ defined on $\mathbb{R}$ such that for every real number $x$ and $y$, the equation
$$
f(f(f(x)+y)+y) = x + y + f(y)
$$
holds true.

negatives.text:
Find all functions $f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ which satisfy for all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$ the relation
$$
f(f(f(x)+y)+y) = x + y - f(y) .
$$

Find all functions $f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ which satisfy for all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$ the relation
$$
f(f(f(x)+y)+y) = x - y + f(y) .
$$

Find all functions $f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ which satisfy for all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$ the relation
$$
f(f(f(x)+y)+y) = x + y + f(x) .
$$

positive_text: We are given a positive integer $ n $. We list all the numbers that divide $ n $ evenly, including $ 1 $ and $ n $ itself. We then count how many of these numbers end in the digit $ 3 $, and express this as a percentage of the total number of divisors. For instance, if $ n = 117 $, the divisors are $ 1, 3, 9, 13, 39, 117 $, and two of them end in $ 3 $, so the percentage is $ 33.33\cdots $%. What is the largest possible value of this percentage, for any positive integer $ n $?

negatives.text: For a positive integer $ n $, we consider all its divisors (including $ 1 $ and itself). Suppose that $ p\% $ of these divisors have their unit digit equal to $ 7 $ (For example $ n = 117 $, has six divisors, namely $ 1, 3, 9, 13, 39, 117 $. None of these divisors have a unit digit equal to $ 7 $. Hence for $ n = 117 $, $ p = 0 $). Find, when $ n $ is any positive integer, the maximum possible value of $ p $.

For a positive integer $ n $, we consider all its divisors (including $ 1 $ and itself). Suppose that $ p\% $ of these divisors have their unit digit equal to $ 3 $. For example $ n = 117 $, has six divisors, namely $ 1, 3, 9, 13, 39, 117 $. Two of these divisors, namely $ 3 $ and $ 13 $, have unit digits equal to $ 3 $. Hence for $ n = 117 $, $ p = 33.33\cdots $%. Find, when $ n $ is any positive integer, the minimum possible value of $ p $.
