Additionally, for any two cities $A$ and $B$ that are not the capital, if there is no round-trip flight between them, then $d_A + d_B \leq n$. The capital has no such limits. Find the maximum number of round-trip flights that can be arranged in one day, and describe all such arrangements that achieve this maximum.

negatives.text: In a country with $n+1$ cities, there are two-way flights between some of these cities. A two-way flight between cities $A$ and $B$ means that within the same day there is a flight from $A$ to $B$ as well as one from $B$ to $A$, while there is no one-way flight from a city to another. There may be more than one two-way flight between two cities. We denote the total number of take-offs from city $A$ within one day by $d_A$. For all cities $A$ except for the capital, one has $d_A \leq n$. Moreover, for any two cities $A$, $B$ both different than the capital, one has $d_A + d_B \leq n$, if there is no two-way flight between $A$ and $B$. There is no restriction on the number of flights from the capital, which is naturally included among the $n+1$ cities. Find the maximal number of one-way flights that can be made within a day in this country and determine all flight schedules with this maximal number of one-way flights.

positive_text: Two distinct points, $A$ and $B$, lie on a circle $\Gamma$. For any point $P$ on $\Gamma$ that is not $A$ or $B$, let $M$ be the point such that $PM$ lies in the opposite direction of the bisector of $\angle APB$, and the distance from $M$ to $P$ is equal to the sum of the distances from $A$ to $P$ and from $P$ to $B$. Determine the set of all such points $M$ as $P$ moves around the circle.

negatives.text: Let $A$ and $B$ be distinct points on a circle $\Gamma$. For a variable point $P$ different from $A$ and $B$ on $\Gamma$, find the geometric locus of the point $M$ such that $PM$ is the opposite ray to the angle bisector of $\angle APB$ and $MP = |AP - PB|$.

Let $A$ and $B$ be distinct points on a circle $\Gamma$. For a variable point $P$ different from $A$ and $B$ on $\Gamma$, find the geometric locus of the point $M$ such that $PM$ is the angle bisector of $\angle APB$ and $MP = AP + PB$.

positive_text: Let $k$ be a positive integer such that $p = 6k + 1$ is a prime. Define $m = 2^p - 1$. Show that the expression $$\frac{2^m - 1}{127m}$$ is always a whole number.

negatives.text: Let $k > 1$ be an integer and $p = 6k + 1$ be a prime number. Define $m = 2^p + 1$. Prove that for each $m$ $$\frac{2^m - 1}{127m}$$ is an integer.
Let $k > 1$ be an integer and $p = 6k + 1$ be a prime number. Define $m = 2^p - 1$. Prove that for each $m$ $$\frac{2^m - 1}{127(m - 1)}$$ is an integer.
Let $k > 1$ be an integer and $p = 6k + 1$ be a prime number. Define $m = 2^p - 1$. Prove that for each $m$ $$\frac{2^{m - 1} - 1}{127m}$$ is an integer.

positive_text:
In a network of $2008$ computers, each computer is part of one cycle, and no cycles overlap. At time $t = 0$, a hacker starts by hacking one computer. At time $t = 1$, a technician protects a different computer that has not been hacked. Then, for each positive integer $k$, at time $t = 2k$, the hacker tries to hack a new computer that is directly connected to an already hacked one and not protected; and at time $t = 2k + 1$, the technician protects a new computer that is directly connected to an already protected one and not hacked. Determine the maximum number of computers the hacker can be certain to hack, regardless of the structure of the network.

[For $m \ge 3$, $\{C_1, C_2, \dots, C_m\}$ is a cycle if $C_1$ is connected to $C_2$, $C_2$ to $C_3$, ..., $C_{m-1}$ to $C_m$, and $C_m$ to $C_1$.]

negatives.text:
In a computer network consisting of $2008$ computers no two cycles intersect. At time $t = 0$, a hacker hacks into a computer in this network; and at time $t = 1$, the network administrator installs a protective software to an unhacked computer. For each positive integer $k$, at time $t = 2k$, the hacker hacks into another computer, if there is one, that is not protected and that is directly connected to a hacked computer; and at time $t = 2k + 1$, the administrator installs the protective software to another computer, if there is one, that is not hacked and that is directly connected to a hacked computer. Determine the maximum number of computers the hacker can guarantee to hack into no matter how the network is configured.

[For $m \ge 3$, $\{C_1, C_2, \dots, C_m\}$ is a cycle if the computers $C_1$ and $C_m$ and, for all $2 \le i \le m$, the computers $C_{i-1}$ and $C_i$ are directly connected.]

In a computer network consisting of $2008$ computers no two cycles intersect. At time $t = 0$, a hacker hacks into a computer in this network; and at time $t = 1$, the network administrator installs a protective software to a hacked computer. For each positive integer $k$, at time $t = 2k$, the hacker hacks into another computer, if there is one, that is not protected and that is directly connected to a hacked computer; and at time $t = 2k + 1$, the administrator installs the protective software to another computer, if there is one, that is not hacked and that is directly connected to a protected computer. Determine the maximum number of computers the hacker can guarantee to hack into no matter how the network is configured.

[For $m \ge 3$, $\{C_1, C_2, \dots, C_m\}$ is a cycle if the computers $C_1$ and $C_m$ and, for all $2 \le i \le m$, the computers $C_{i-1}$ and $C_i$ are directly connected.]

In a computer network consisting of $2008$ computers no two cycles intersect. At time $t = 0$, a hacker hacks into a computer in this network; and at time $t = 1$, the network administrator installs a protective software to an unhacked computer. For each positive integer $k$, at time $t = 2k$, the hacker hacks into another computer, if there is one, that is not protected and that is directly connected to a protected computer; and at time $t = 2k + 1$, the administrator installs the protective software to another computer, if there is one, that is not hacked and that is directly connected to a hacked computer. Determine the maximum number of computers the hacker can guarantee to hack into no matter how the network is configured.

[For $m \ge 3$, $\{C_1, C_2, \dots, C_m\}$ is a cycle if the computers $C_1$ and $C_m$ and, for all $2 \le i \le m$, the computers $C_{i-1}$ and $C_i$ are directly connected.]

positive_text: In a tangential quadrilateral $ABCD$, the incircle has center $O$ and radius $r$. The lines $AB$ and $CD$ intersect at point $P$, the lines $AD$ and $BC$ intersect at point $Q$, and the diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ intersect at point $E$. Prove that the product of the distance from $O$ to $E$ and the distance from $O$ to the line $PQ$ is equal to $r^2$.

negatives.text: Let $ O $ be the center and $ r $ be the radius of the incircle of a tangential quadrilateral $ ABCD $. Let $ P $ be the point of intersection of the lines $ AB $ and $ CD $, $ Q $ be the point of intersection of the lines $ AD $ and $ BC $, and $ E $ be the point of intersection of the diagonals $ AC $ and $ BD $. Show that $ |OE| \cdot d = r^2 $, where $ d $ is the distance from the point $ O $ to the line $ PQ $, assuming $ ABCD $ is a cyclic quadrilateral instead of a tangential one.

positive_text:
Prove that
$$
\sqrt{|AB_1|} + \sqrt{|BC_1|} + \sqrt{|CA_1|} \le \frac{3}{\sqrt{2}}
$$
where $A_1$, $B_1$, and $C_1$ are the points where the incircle of triangle $ABC$ touches the sides $BC$, $AC$, and $AB$, respectively.

negatives.text:
Show that
$$
\sqrt{|AB_1|} + \sqrt{|BC_1|} + \sqrt{|CA_1|} \le \frac{3}{\sqrt{2}}
$$
if the excircle of a triangle $ABC$ touches the sides $BC$, $AC$ and $AB$ at the points $A_1$, $B_1$ and $C_1$, respectively.

positive_text: In a class with at least 4 students, some students are friends. If you remove any one student, the remaining students can always be arranged in a circle so that every pair of neighbors in the circle are friends. However, if all the students are included, such a circle cannot be formed. What is the smallest number of students in the class?

negatives.text: Some of $n \ge 4$ students in a class are friends. Any $n-1$ students in this class can form a line so that any two students next to each other in the line are friends, but all $n$ students cannot form a similar line. Find the smallest possible value of $n$.

Some of $n \ge 4$ students in a class are friends. Any $n-2$ students in this class can form a circle so that any two students next to each other on the circle are friends, but all $n$ students cannot form a similar circle. Find the smallest possible value of $n$.

Some of $n \ge 4$ students in a class are friends. Any $n-1$ students in this class can form a circle so that any two students next to each other on the circle are friends, but all $n$ students cannot form a similar circle. Find the largest possible value of $n$.

positive_text: \text{In triangle } ABC, \text{ points } D, E, F \text{ lie on the sides } AB, BC, CA, \text{ respectively. These points satisfy the following: } AD = AF, BD = BE, \text{ and } DE = DF. \text{ Let } I \text{ be the center of the incircle of triangle } ABC, \text{ and let } K \text{ be the point where the line } BI \text{ meets the tangent to the circumcircle of triangle } ABI \text{ at point } A. \text{ Prove that } AK = EK, \text{ given that } AK = AD.

negatives.text: \text{Let } D, E, F \text{ be points on the sides } AB, BC, CA \text{ respectively of a triangle } ABC \text{ such that } AD = AF, BD = BE \text{ and } DE = DF. \text{ Let } I \text{ be the incenter of triangle } ABC, \text{ and let } K \text{ be the point of intersection of the line } CI \text{ and the tangent line through } A \text{ to the circumcircle of triangle } ABI. \text{ Show that } AK = EK \text{ if } AK = AD.

\text{Let } D, E, F \text{ be points on the sides } AB, BC, CA \text{ respectively of a triangle } ABC \text{ such that } AD = AF, BD = BE \text{ and } DE = DF. \text{ Let } I \text{ be the incenter of triangle } ABC, \text{ and let } K \text{ be the point of intersection of the line } BI \text{ and the tangent line through } B \text{ to the circumcircle of triangle } ABI. \text{ Show that } AK = EK \text{ if } AK = AD.

\text{Let } D, E, F \text{ be points on the sides } AB, BC, CA \text{ respectively of a triangle } ABC \text{ such that } AD = AF, BD = BE \text{ and } DE = DF. \text{ Let } I \text{ be the incenter of triangle } ABC, \text{ and let } K \text{ be the point of intersection of the line } BI \text{ and the tangent line through } A \text{ to the circumcircle of triangle } AIC. \text{ Show that } AK = EK \text{ if } AK = AD.

positive_text: Prove that $$\sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{x_i}{\sqrt{x_i^4 + 3}} \le \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{1}{x_i}$$ for all positive integers $n$ and positive real numbers $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n$ such that the product $x_1 x_2 \cdots x_n = 1$.

negatives.text: Prove that $$\sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{a_i}{\sqrt{a_i^4 + 3}} \ge \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{1}{a_i}$$ for all positive integers $n$ and positive real numbers $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$ satisfying the condition $a_1 a_2 \cdots a_n = 1$.

Prove that $$\sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{a_i}{\sqrt{a_i^4 + 3}} \le \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i$$ for all positive integers $n$ and positive real numbers $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$ satisfying the condition $a_1 a_2 \cdots a_n = 1$.

Prove that $$\sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{a_i}{\sqrt{a_i^4 + 3}} \le \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{1}{a_i}$$ for all positive integers $n$ and positive real numbers $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$ satisfying the condition $a_1 + a_2 + \cdots + a_n = 1$.

positive_text: Show that for all positive real numbers $x$ and $y$, the inequality $x^2 y^2 (x^2 + y^2 - 2) \geq (x + y)(xy - 1)$ holds true.

negatives.text: Prove that $a^2 b^2 (a^2 + b^2 + 2) \geq (a + b)(ab - 1)$ for all positive real numbers $a$ and $b$.
Prove that $a^2 b^2 (a^2 + b^2 - 2) \leq (a + b)(ab - 1)$ for all positive real numbers $a$ and $b$.
Prove that $a^2 b^2 (a^2 + b^2 - 2) \geq (a + b)(ab + 1)$ for all positive real numbers $a$ and $b$.

positive_text: Suppose $n$ is an integer greater than or equal to 2 and let $E = \{1, 2, \dots, n\}$. Consider a list of subsets $A_1, A_2, \dots, A_k$ of $E$. For any two different subsets $A_i$ and $A_j$, exactly one of the following four sets is empty: $A_i \cap A_j$, $A_i' \cap A_j$, $A_i \cap A_j'$, or $A_i' \cap A_j'$. Find the largest possible number $k$ for which such a list of subsets can exist.\\n\\n[Here, $A'$ represents the set of all elements in $E$ that are not in $A$.]

negatives.text: Let $n \ge 2$ be an integer and $E = \{1, 2, \dots, n\}$. If $A_1, A_2, \dots, A_k$ are subsets of $E$ and at least one of $A_i \cap A_j$, $A'_i \cap A_j$, $A_i \cap A'_j$ and $A'_i \cap A'_j$ is empty for all $1 \le i < j \le k$, then determine the maximum possible value of $k$.\\n\\n[For $A \subset E$, $A'$ denotes the elements of $E$ which are not included in $A$.]

Let $n \ge 2$ be an integer and $E = \{1, 2, \dots, n\}$. If $A_1, A_2, \dots, A_k$ are subsets of $E$ and exactly one of $A_i \cup A_j$, $A'_i \cup A_j$, $A_i \cup A'_j$ and $A'_i \cup A'_j$ is empty for all $1 \le i < j \le k$, then determine the maximum possible value of $k$.\\n\\n[For $A \subset E$, $A'$ denotes the elements of $E$ which are not included in $A$.]

positive_text: In triangle $ABC$, let $D$ be a point on side $BC$, not at $B$ or $C$, and let $E$ be the midpoint of segment $CD$. A line is drawn perpendicular to $BC$ at $E$, and this line meets side $AC$ at point $F$. It is given that $AF \cdot BC = AC \cdot EC$. Let $G$ be the second point (other than $A$) where the circumcircle of triangle $ADC$ intersects side $AB$. Show that the tangent to the circumcircle of triangle $AGF$ at point $F$ is also tangent to the circumcircle of triangle $BGE$.

negatives.text: Let $D$ be a point on the side $[BC]$ of the triangle $ABC$ different from the vertices and $E$ be the midpoint of $[CD]$. The line perpendicular to $BC$ at $E$ intersects the side $[AC]$ at point $F$ satisfying $AF \cdot BC = AC \cdot EC$. Let $G$ be the second point where the circumcircle of the triangle $ADC$ intersects the side $[AB]$. Prove that the tangent line of the circumcircle of the triangle $AGF$ at $F$ is also tangent to the circumcircle of the triangle $AGE$.

Let $D$ be a point on the side $[BC]$ of the triangle $ABC$ different from the vertices and $E$ be the midpoint of $[CD]$. The line perpendicular to $BC$ at $E$ intersects the side $[AC]$ at point $F$ satisfying $AF \cdot BC = AC \cdot EC$. Let $G$ be the second point where the circumcircle of the triangle $ADC$ intersects the side $[AB]$. Prove that the tangent line of the circumcircle of the triangle $ABF$ at $F$ is also tangent to the circumcircle of the triangle $BGE$.

positive_text: Consider an isosceles triangle $ABC$ with $AB = AC$. Let $D$ be the midpoint of segment $BC$, and let $E$ be the point where a perpendicular from $D$ meets $AC$. Let $F$ be the second intersection point of the line $BE$ with the circumcircle of triangle $ABD$. If $G$ is the point where lines $DE$ and $AF$ meet, prove that the lengths $DG$ and $GE$ are equal.

negatives.text: In a triangle $ABC$, $|AB| = |AC|$, $D$ is the midpoint of $[BC]$ and $E$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $D$ to the line $AB$. Let $F$ be the second point where the line $BE$ intersects the circumcircle of the triangle $ABD$. If $G$ is the intersection point of the lines $DE$ and $AF$, then show that $|DG| = |GE|$.

In a triangle $ABC$, $|AB| = |AC|$, $D$ is the midpoint of $[BC]$ and $E$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $D$ to the line $AC$. Let $F$ be the second point where the line $AE$ intersects the circumcircle of the triangle $ABD$. If $G$ is the intersection point of the lines $DE$ and $AF$, then show that $|DG| = |GE|$.

In a triangle $ABC$, $|AB| = |AC|$, $D$ is the midpoint of $[BC]$ and $E$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $D$ to the line $AC$. Let $F$ be the second point where the line $BE$ intersects the circumcircle of the triangle $ABD$. If $G$ is the intersection point of the lines $DE$ and $AF$, then show that $|DG| = |DE|$.

positive_text:
Prove that
$$
a + b + c + \sqrt{3} \geq 8abc \left( \frac{1}{a^2 + 1} + \frac{1}{b^2 + 1} + \frac{1}{c^2 + 1} \right)
$$
for all positive real numbers $a, b, c$ such that $ab + bc + ca \leq 1$.

negatives.text:
Prove that
$$
a + b + c + \sqrt{3} \geq 4abc \left( \frac{1}{a^2 + 1} + \frac{1}{b^2 + 1} + \frac{1}{c^2 + 1} \right)
$$
for all positive real numbers $a, b, c$ satisfying $ab + bc + ca \leq 1$.

positive_text: \text{Prove that } \frac{1}{x + y^{20} + z^{11}} + \frac{1}{y + z^{20} + x^{11}} + \frac{1}{z + x^{20} + y^{11}} \le 1 \text{ for all positive real numbers } x, y, z \text{ with the condition that } xyz = 1.

negatives.text: \text{Prove that } \frac{1}{x + y^{20} + z^{11}} + \frac{1}{y + z^{20} + x^{11}} + \frac{1}{z + x^{20} + y^{11}} \ge 1 \text{ for all positive real numbers } x, y, z \text{ with the condition that } xyz = 1.

\text{Prove that } \frac{1}{x + y^{20} + z^{11}} + \frac{1}{y + z^{20} + x^{11}} + \frac{1}{z + x^{20} + y^{11}} \le 1 \text{ for all positive real numbers } x, y, z \text{ with the condition that } x + y + z = 1.

positive_text:
Consider triangle $ABC$ with a point $D$ lying on side $BC$ (but not at the vertices). Let $I$ be the incenter of triangle $ABC$, $I_1$ the incenter of triangle $ABD$, and $I_2$ the incenter of triangle $ADC$. Define point $E$ as the second point where the circumcircles of triangles $AI_1I$ and $ADI_2$ intersect, and define point $F$ as the second point where the circumcircles of triangles $AII_2$ and $AI_1D$ intersect. If $AI_1 = AI_2$, prove that
$$
\frac{EI}{FI} \cdot \frac{ED}{FD} = \frac{EI_1^2}{FI_2^2}.
$$

negatives.text:
Let $D$ be a point different from the vertices on the side $BC$ of a triangle $ABC$. Let $I, I_1$ and $I_2$ be the incenters of the triangles $ABC$, $ABD$ and $ADC$, respectively. Let $E$ be the second intersection point of the circumcircles of the triangles $AI_1I$ and $ADI_2$, and $F$ be the second intersection point of the circumcircles of the triangles $AII_2$ and $AI_1D$. Prove that if $AI_1 = AI$, then
$$
\frac{EI}{FI} \cdot \frac{ED}{FD} = \frac{EI_1^2}{FI_2^2}.
$$

Let $D$ be a point different from the vertices on the side $BC$ of a triangle $ABC$. Let $I, I_1$ and $I_2$ be the incenters of the triangles $ABC$, $ABD$ and $ADC$, respectively. Let $E$ be the second intersection point of the circumcircles of the triangles $AI_1I$ and $ADI_2$, and $F$ be the second intersection point of the circumcircles of the triangles $AII_2$ and $AI_1D$. Prove that if $I_1 = I_2$, then
$$
\frac{EI}{FI} \cdot \frac{ED}{FD} = \frac{EI_1^2}{FI_2^2}.
$$

Let $D$ be a point different from the vertices on the side $BC$ of a triangle $ABC$. Let $I, I_1$ and $I_2$ be the incenters of the triangles $ABC$, $ABD$ and $ADC$, respectively. Let $E$ be the second intersection point of the circumcircles of the triangles $AI_1I$ and $ADI_2$, and $F$ be the second intersection point of the circumcircles of the triangles $AII_2$ and $AI_1D$. Prove that if $AD = DC$, then
$$
\frac{EI}{FI} \cdot \frac{ED}{FD} = \frac{EI_1^2}{FI_2^2}.
$$

positive_text: Let $S_r(n) = 1^r + 2^r + \dots + n^r$ where $r$ is a rational number and $n$ is a positive integer. Find all triples $(a, b, c)$ where $a$ and $b$ are positive rational numbers and $c$ is a positive integer such that the equation $S_a(n) = (S_b(n))^c$ has infinitely many solutions in positive integers $n$.

negatives.text: Let $S_r(n) = 1^r + 2^r + \dots + n^r$ where $r$ is a rational number and $n$ is a positive integer. Find all triples $(a, b, c)$ where $a$ and $b$ are positive rational numbers and $c$ is a positive integer for which there exist finitely many positive integers $n$ satisfying $S_a(n) = (S_b(n))^c$.

Let $S_r(n) = 1^r + 2^r + \dots + n^r$ where $r$ is a rational number and $n$ is a positive integer. Find all triples $(a, b, c)$ where $a$ and $b$ are positive rational numbers and $c$ is a positive integer for which there exist infinitely many positive integers $n$ satisfying $S_a(n) = S_b(n)^{c+1}$.

Let $S_r(n) = 1^r + 2^r + \dots + n^r$ where $r$ is a rational number and $n$ is a positive integer. Find all triples $(a, b, c)$ where $a$ and $b$ are positive rational numbers and $c$ is a positive integer for which there exist infinitely many positive integers $n$ satisfying $S_a(n) = (S_b(n))^c + 1$.

positive_text:
Find all integer values of $x$ and $y$, and all prime numbers $p$, such that the following equation holds:
$$
(x - \frac{3}{2}y)^2 + \left(p^2 - \frac{9}{4}\right)y^2 = 12p
$$

In a convex quadrilateral $ABCD$, the diagonals meet at point $E$, and $\angle AEB = 90^\circ$. A point $P$ lies on segment $AD$, not at $A$, such that $PE = EC$. The circle passing through points $B$, $C$, and $D$ intersects segment $AD$ again at a point $Q$ (not at $A$). Another circle goes through point $A$ and is tangent to the line $EP$ at point $P$. This second circle intersects segment $AC$ at a point $R$. If the points $B$, $Q$, and $R$ lie on the same straight line, prove that $\angle BCD = 90^\circ$.

negatives.text: In a convex quadrilateral $ABCD$, the diagonals intersect at the point $E$ and $\angle AEB = 90^\circ$. A point $P$ is chosen on the side $[AD]$ other than $A$ so that $PE = ED$. The circumcircle of the triangle $BCD$ intersects the side $[AD]$ at the point $Q$ other than $A$. The circle passing through $A$ and tangent to the line $EP$ at $P$ intersects the line segment $[AC]$ at the point $R$. If $B, Q, R$ are collinear, then show that $\angle BCD = 90^\circ$.

In a convex quadrilateral $ABCD$, the diagonals intersect at the point $E$ and $\angle AEB = 90^\circ$. A point $P$ is chosen on the side $[AD]$ other than $A$ so that $PE = EC$. The circumcircle of the triangle $BCD$ intersects the side $[AD]$ at the point $Q$ other than $A$. The circle passing through $A$ and tangent to the line $EP$ at $P$ intersects the line segment $[BD]$ at the point $R$. If $B, Q, R$ are collinear, then show that $\angle BCD = 90^\circ$.

In a convex quadrilateral $ABCD$, the diagonals intersect at the point $E$ and $\angle AEB = 90^\circ$. A point $P$ is chosen on the side $[AD]$ other than $A$ so that $PE = EC$. The circumcircle of the triangle $BCD$ intersects the side $[AD]$ at the point $Q$ other than $A$. The circle passing through $A$ and tangent to the line $EP$ at $P$ intersects the line segment $[AC]$ at the point $R$. If $C, Q, R$ are collinear, then show that $\angle BCD = 90^\circ$.

positive_text: Let $P$ be the set of all $2012$-tuples $(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_{2012})$, where each $x_i$ is an integer from $1$ to $20$. A set $A \subset P$ is called decreasing if, whenever it contains a tuple $(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_{2012})$, it also contains all tuples $(y_1, y_2, \dots, y_{2012})$ such that $y_i \le x_i$ for each $i$. A set $B \subset P$ is called increasing if, whenever it contains a tuple $(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_{2012})$, it also contains all tuples $(y_1, y_2, \dots, y_{2012})$ such that $y_i \ge x_i$ for each $i$. Consider the function $f(A, B) = \frac{|A \cap B|}{|A| \cdot |B|}$, where $A$ and $B$ are nonempty decreasing and increasing sets, respectively. What is the largest possible value of $f(A, B)$?

negatives.text: Let $P$ be the set of all $2012$-tuples $(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_{2012})$, where $x_i \in \{1, 2, \dots, 20\}$ for each $1 \le i \le 2012$. The set $A \subset P$ is said to be decreasing if for each $(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_{2012}) \in A$ any $(y_1, y_2, \dots, y_{2012})$ satisfying $y_i \le x_i$ ($1 \le i \le 2012$) also belongs to $A$. The set $B \subset P$ is said to be decreasing as well. Find the maximal possible value of $f(A, B) = \frac{|A \cap B|}{|A| \cdot |B|}$, where $A$ and $B$ are nonempty decreasing sets ($| \cdot |$ denotes the number of elements of the set).

Let $P$ be the set of all $2012$-tuples $(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_{2012})$, where $x_i \in \{1, 2, \dots, 20\}$ for each $1 \le i \le 2012$. The set $A \subset P$ is said to be decreasing if for each $(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_{2012}) \in A$ any $(y_1, y_2, \dots, y_{2012})$ satisfying $y_i \le x_i$ ($1 \le i \le 2012$) also belongs to $A$. The set $B \subset P$ is said to be increasing if for each $(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_{2012}) \in B$ any $(y_1, y_2, \dots, y_{2012})$ satisfying $y_i \ge x_i$ ($1 \le i \le 2012$) also belongs to $B$. Find the maximal possible value of $f(A, B) = \frac{|A \cap B|}{|A| + |B|}$, where $A$ and $B$ are nonempty decreasing and increasing sets ($| \cdot |$ denotes the number of elements of the set).

Let $P$ be the set of all $2012$-tuples $(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_{2012})$, where $x_i \in \{1, 2, \dots, 20\}$ for each $1 \le i \le 2012$. The set $A \subset P$ is said to be decreasing if for each $(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_{2012}) \in A$ any $(y_1, y_2, \dots, y_{2012})$ satisfying $y_i \le x_i$ ($1 \le i \le 2012$) also belongs to $A$. The set $B \subset P$ is said to be increasing if for each $(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_{2012}) \in B$ any $(y_1, y_2, \dots, y_{2012})$ satisfying $y_i \ge x_i$ ($1 \le i \le 2012$) also belongs to $B$. Find the maximal possible value of $f(A, B) = \frac{|A \cap B|}{|A| \cdot |B|}$, where $A$ and $B$ are nonempty decreasing and increasing sets, and each tuple in $P$ is weighted by a factor of $2$ ($| \cdot |$ denotes the number of elements of the set).

positive_text: Let $\omega_1$ be a circle with diameter $[AB]$, and let $\omega_2$ be a circle centered at point $A$. These circles intersect at two points, $C$ and $D$. Let $E$ be a point on $\omega_2$ that is outside $\omega_1$ and lies on the same side of line $AB$ as point $C$. Let the line $BE$ intersect $\omega_2$ again at a point $F$. Suppose $K$ is a point on $\omega_1$ that lies on the same side of the diameter of $\omega_1$ through $C$ as point $A$, and satisfies the condition $2 \cdot CK \cdot AC = CE \cdot AB$. Let the line $KF$ intersect $\omega_1$ again at a point $L$. Show that the reflection of point $D$ across the line $BE$ lies on the circumcircle of triangle $LFC$.

Consider triangle $ABC$ where $AC$ is longer than $AB$. A circle $\omega$ touches sides $AB$ and $AC$ at points $D$ and $E$, respectively. This circle also intersects the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ at points $K$ and $L$. Points $X$ and $Y$ are placed on $AB$ and $AC$, respectively, such that $$\frac{AX}{AB} = \frac{CE}{BD + CE} \quad \text{and} \quad \frac{AY}{AC} = \frac{BD}{BD + CE}.$$ Prove that the lines $XY$, $BC$, and $KL$ all meet at a single point.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $AC > AB$. Let a circle $\omega$ tangent to the sides $AB$ and $AC$ at $D$ and $E$ respectively, intersects the circumcircle of $ABC$ at $K$ and $L$ and $X$ and $Y$ be points on the sides $AB$ and $AC$ respectively, such that $$\frac{AX}{AB} = \frac{CE}{BD} \quad \text{and} \quad \frac{AY}{AC} = \frac{BD}{CE}.$$ Show that the lines $XY$, $BC$ and $KL$ are concurrent.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $AC > AB$. Let a circle $\omega$ tangent to the sides $AB$ and $AC$ at $D$ and $E$ respectively, intersects the circumcircle of $ABC$ at $K$ and $L$ and $X$ and $Y$ be points on the sides $AB$ and $AC$ respectively, such that $$\frac{AX}{AB} = \frac{BD}{BD + CE} \quad \text{and} \quad \frac{AY}{AC} = \frac{CE}{BD + CE}.$$ Show that the lines $XY$, $BC$ and $KL$ are concurrent.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $AC > AB$. Let a circle $\omega$ tangent to the sides $AB$ and $AC$ at $D$ and $E$ respectively, intersects the circumcircle of $ABC$ at $K$ and $L$ and $X$ and $Y$ be points on the sides $AB$ and $AC$ respectively, such that $$\frac{AX}{AB} = \frac{CE}{BD + CE} \quad \text{and} \quad \frac{AY}{AC} = \frac{BD}{BD + CE}.$$ Show that the lines $XY$, $AC$ and $KL$ are concurrent.

positive_text:
There are $n$ boxes placed around the corners of a regular $n$-gon, and a small marble. Alice and Bob are playing a game. Alice starts by putting the marble in one of the boxes. On each turn, the game has three parts:
* Alice can choose to move the marble to one of the two neighboring boxes, but only if that box was not picked by Bob on the last turn.
* Bob then picks one of the boxes.
* Alice tells Bob how far the marble is from the box he picked.
If at the end of a turn Bob can say for sure where the marble is, he wins. For every $n \ge 3$, what is the smallest number of turns Bob needs to always win?

negatives.text:
There are $n$ boxes placed on the vertices of a regular $n$-gon and a marble. Alice and Bob play a game. At the start Alice places the marble in one of the boxes. Each move consists of three stages:
* Alice, if she wishes, can secretly move the marble to any of two neighboring boxes
* Bob chooses one of the boxes
* Alice tells the distance from the chosen box to the box where the marble is located
If Bob can determine the box containing the marble at the end of some move he wins. For all values of $n \ge 3$ determine the minimal number of moves necessary for Bob to guarantee winning.

positive_text:
Suppose $a > 1$, $b > 1$, $c > 1$, $d > 1$, and let $x$ and $y$ be real numbers such that
$$
a^x + b^y = (a^2 + b^2)^x \quad \text{and} \quad c^x + d^y = 2^y (cd)^{y/2}.
$$
Show that $x$ is less than $y$.

negatives.text:
Let $a > 1$, $b > 1$, $c > 1$, $d > 1$, $x$, $y$ be real numbers satisfying
$$
a^x + b^y = (a^2 + b^2)^y \text{ and } c^x + d^y = 2^y (cd)^{y/2}.
$$
Prove that $x < y$.

Let $a > 1$, $b > 1$, $c > 1$, $d > 1$, $x$, $y$ be real numbers satisfying
$$
a^x + b^y = (a^2 + b^2)^x \text{ and } c^x + d^y = 2^x (cd)^{y/2}.
$$
Prove that $x < y$.

Let $a > 1$, $b > 1$, $c > 1$, $d > 1$, $x$, $y$ be real numbers satisfying
$$
a^x + b^y = (a^2 + b^2)^x \text{ and } c^x + d^x = 2^y (cd)^{y/2}.
$$
Prove that $x < y$.

positive_text: Suppose $n > 3$ is a whole number and we place $n$ distinct points on a flat surface. The distance between any pair of these points is a whole number. Moreover, for each point, if we list out the distances from that point to all the others and sort them from smallest to largest, the list looks the same no matter which point we start with. What are all the possible values of $n$?

negatives.text: Let $n > 3$ be a positive integer and $P_1, P_2, \dots, P_n$ be different points on the plane such that all pairwise distances between them are integers and the distances $P_iP_1, P_iP_2, \dots, P_iP_n$ rearranged in non-decreasing order differ for all $i = 1, 2, \dots, n$. Find all possible values of $n$.

Let $n > 3$ be a positive integer and $P_1, P_2, \dots, P_n$ be different points on the plane such that all pairwise distances between them are integers and the distances $P_iP_1, P_iP_2, \dots, P_iP_n$ rearranged in non-decreasing order coincide for exactly one $i = 1, 2, \dots, n$. Find all possible values of $n$.

positive_text: In a four-sided shape $ABCD$, where the diagonals meet at point $E$, we know that the segment $BE$ is $\sqrt{2}$ times as long as $ED$, and the angle $\angle BEC$ is $45^\circ$. Drop a perpendicular from point $A$ to the side $BC$, and label the foot of this perpendicular as $F$. Now, draw the circle passing through points $B$, $F$, and $D$, and let $P$ be the other point where this circle meets side $DC$. What is the measure of angle $\angle APD$?

negatives.text: In a convex quadrilateral $ABCD$, the diagonals intersect at $E$, $BE = \sqrt{2} \cdot ED$ and $\angle BEC = 45^\circ$. Let $F$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $C$ to $AB$ and $P$ be the second intersection point of the circumcircle of triangle $BFD$ and the line segment $[DC]$. Find $\angle APD$.

In a convex quadrilateral $ABCD$, the diagonals intersect at $E$, $BE = \sqrt{2} \cdot ED$ and $\angle BEC = 30^\circ$. Let $F$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $A$ to $BC$ and $P$ be the second intersection point of the circumcircle of triangle $BFD$ and the line segment $[DC]$. Find $\angle APD$.

In a convex quadrilateral $ABCD$, the diagonals intersect at $E$, $BE = \sqrt{3} \cdot ED$ and $\angle BEC = 45^\circ$. Let $F$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $A$ to $BC$ and $P$ be the second intersection point of the circumcircle of triangle $BFD$ and the line segment $[DC]$. Find $\angle APD$.

positive_text:
Suppose $x$, $y$, $z$ are nonnegative real numbers such that $x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 1$. Show that
$$
\sqrt{x+y} + \sqrt{y+z} + \sqrt{z+x} \ge 5xyz + 2.
$$

negatives.text:
Let $a$, $b$, $c$ be nonnegative real numbers satisfying $a^2 + b^2 + c^2 = 1$. Prove that
$$
\sqrt{a+b} + \sqrt{b+c} + \sqrt{c+a} \ge 5ab + 2.
$$

Let $a$, $b$, $c$ be nonnegative real numbers satisfying $a + b + c = 1$. Prove that
$$
\sqrt{a+b} + \sqrt{b+c} + \sqrt{c+a} \ge 5abc + 2.
$$

Let $a$, $b$, $c$ be nonnegative real numbers satisfying $a^2 + b^2 + c^2 = 1$. Prove that
$$
\sqrt{a+b} + \sqrt{b+c} + \sqrt{c+a} \ge 5abc + 3.
$$

positive_text:
Let line $ l $ meet the line $ AB $ at point $ F $, the sides $ AC $ and $ BC $ of triangle $ ABC $ at points $ D $ and $ E $, respectively, and the angle bisector of $ \angle BAC $ at point $ P $. Assume that $ F $ lies on the side of $ AB $ opposite to $ A $ with respect to $ BC $, that $ CD = CE $, and that $ P $ is inside triangle $ ABC $. Prove that
$$
FB \cdot FA + CP^2 = CF^2 \iff AD \cdot BE = PD^2.
$$

negatives.text:
Let a line $ l $ intersect the line $ AB $ at $ F $, the sides $ AC $ and $ BC $ of a triangle $ ABC $ at $ D $ and $ E $, respectively, and the internal bisector of the angle $ BAC $ at $ P $. Suppose that $ F $ is at the opposite side of $ A $ with respect to the line $ BC $, $ CD = CE $, and $ P $ is in the interior of the triangle $ ABC $. Prove that
$$
FB \cdot FA - CP^2 = CF^2 \iff AD \cdot BE = PD^2.
$$

Let a line $ l $ intersect the line $ AB $ at $ F $, the sides $ AC $ and $ BC $ of a triangle $ ABC $ at $ D $ and $ E $, respectively, and the internal bisector of the angle $ BAC $ at $ P $. Suppose that $ F $ is at the opposite side of $ A $ with respect to the line $ BC $, $ CD = CE $, and $ P $ is in the interior of the triangle $ ABC $. Prove that
$$
FB \cdot FA + CP^2 = CF^2 \iff AD \cdot BE = PD + 1.
$$

positive_text: Determine the smallest possible value of $\frac{1}{x} + \frac{1}{y} + \frac{1}{z}$ for positive real numbers $x, y, z$ such that $xyz = 1$, $x + y + z = 5$, and $(xy + 2x + 2y - 9)(yz + 2y + 2z - 9)(zx + 2z + 2x - 9) \geq 0$.

negatives.text: Find the minimal possible value of $\frac{1}{a} + \frac{1}{b} + \frac{1}{c}$ over all positive real numbers $a, b, c$ satisfying $abc = 1$, $a+b+c = 6$, and $(ab+2a+2b-9)(bc+2b+2c-9)(ca+2c+2a-9) \geq 0$.

Find the minimal possible value of $\frac{1}{a} + \frac{1}{b} + \frac{1}{c}$ over all positive real numbers $a, b, c$ satisfying $abc = 2$, $a+b+c = 5$, and $(ab+2a+2b-9)(bc+2b+2c-9)(ca+2c+2a-9) \geq 0$.

positive_text: Suppose triangle $ABC$ is isosceles with $AB = AC$. Let $D$ be a point on the smaller arc $AC$ of the circumcircle $\omega$ of triangle $ABC$. Let $E$ be the reflection of $B$ across line $AD$. The line $BE$ meets $\omega$ again at $F$. The tangent to $\omega$ at $F$ intersects $AC$ at point $K$, and lines $DF$ and $AB$ meet at point $L$. Prove that points $K$, $L$, and $E$ lie on a straight line.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle satisfying $|AB| = |AC|$. Let $D$ be a point on smaller arc $AC$ of circumcircle $\omega$ of $ABC$. Let $E$ be the symmetric point of $C$ with respect to the line $AD$. The line $BE$ intersects $\omega$ at $F$. The tangent line of $\omega$ at $F$ intersects the line $AC$ at $K$ and the lines $DF$ and $AB$ intersect at $L$. Show that the points $K, L, E$ are collinear.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle satisfying $|AB| = |AC|$. Let $D$ be a point on smaller arc $AC$ of circumcircle $\omega$ of $ABC$. Let $E$ be the symmetric point of $B$ with respect to the line $AD$. The line $CE$ intersects $\omega$ at $F$. The tangent line of $\omega$ at $F$ intersects the line $AC$ at $K$ and the lines $DF$ and $AB$ intersect at $L$. Show that the points $K, L, E$ are collinear.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle satisfying $|AB| = |AC|$. Let $D$ be a point on smaller arc $AC$ of circumcircle $\omega$ of $ABC$. Let $E$ be the symmetric point of $B$ with respect to the line $AD$. The line $BE$ intersects $\omega$ at $F$. The tangent line of $\omega$ at $F$ intersects the line $AB$ at $K$ and the lines $DF$ and $AC$ intersect at $L$. Show that the points $K, L, E$ are collinear.

positive_text: Let triangle $ABC$ have side lengths such that $AB > AC$. Drop a perpendicular from point $A$ to side $BC$, and call the point where it meets $BC$ as $D$. Let $K$ be the point where the angle bisector of $\angle ABC$ intersects the segment $AD$. From point $B$, drop a perpendicular to line $CK$ and call the point where it meets $CK$ as $M$. Then, let $N$ be the point where $BM$ intersects $AK$. Draw a line through $N$ that is parallel to $DM$ and let it intersect $AC$ at point $T$. Prove that $BM$ divides $\angle TBC$ into two equal parts.

negatives.text: Let triangle $ABC$ have side lengths such that $AB > AC$. Drop a perpendicular from point $A$ to side $BC$, and call the point where it meets $BC$ as $D$. Let $K$ be the point where the angle bisector of $\angle ABC$ intersects the segment $AD$. From point $B$, drop a perpendicular to line $CK$ and call the point where it meets $CK$ as $M$. Then, let $N$ be the point where $BM$ intersects $AK$. Draw a line through $N$ that is perpendicular to $DM$ and let it intersect $AC$ at point $T$. Prove that $BM$ divides $\angle TBC$ into two equal parts.

Let triangle $ABC$ have side lengths such that $AB > AC$. Drop a perpendicular from point $A$ to side $BC$, and call the point where it meets $BC$ as $D$. Let $K$ be the point where the angle bisector of $\angle ABC$ intersects the segment $AD$. From point $B$, drop a perpendicular to line $CK$ and call the point where it meets $CK$ as $M$. Then, let $N$ be the point where $BM$ intersects $AK$. Draw a line through $N$ that is parallel to $DM$ and let it intersect $AB$ at point $T$. Prove that $BM$ divides $\angle TBC$ into two equal parts.

positive_text:
In triangle $ABC$, the angle bisector from $A$ intersects the $A$-excircle at points $D$ and $E$, with $D$ lying between $A$ and $E$. Prove that
$$
\frac{\text{length of } AD}{\text{length of } AE} \le \frac{(\text{length of } BC)^2}{(\text{length of } DE)^2}.
$$

negatives.text:
In triangle $ABC$, the angle bisector from $A$ intersects the $A$-excircle at points $D$ and $E$, with $D$ lying between $A$ and $E$. Prove that
$$
\frac{|AD|}{|AE|} \le \frac{|AB|^2}{|DE|^2}.
$$

In triangle $ABC$, the angle bisector from $A$ intersects the $A$-excircle at points $D$ and $E$, with $D$ lying between $A$ and $E$. Prove that
$$
\frac{|AD|}{|AE|} \le \frac{|BC|}{|DE|}.
$$

positive_text: In a right triangle $ABC$ where $\angle C = 90^\circ$, let $D$ be the point where the perpendicular from $C$ meets $AB$. Now, reflect $D$ over side $AC$ to get point $E$, and reflect $D$ over side $BC$ to get point $F$. Let $O_1$ and $O_2$ be the centers of the circles passing through points $E, C, B$ and $F, C, A$, respectively. Show that the distance between $O_1$ and $O_2$ is exactly half the length of $AB$.

negatives.text: In a right triangle $ABC$ with $\angle ACB = 90^\circ$, let $D$ be the foot of the altitude from $C$. Let $E$ and $F$ be the reflections of $D$ with respect to $AC$ and $BC$, respectively. Let $O_1$ and $O_2$ be the circumcenters of the triangles $ECB$ and $FCA$, respectively. Prove that $$ |O_1O_2| = |AB|. $$

In a right triangle $ABC$ with $\angle ACB = 90^\circ$, let $D$ be the foot of the altitude from $C$. Let $E$ and $F$ be the reflections of $D$ with respect to $AC$ and $BC$, respectively. Let $O_1$ and $O_2$ be the circumcenters of the triangles $ECB$ and $FCA$, respectively. Prove that $$ |O_1O_2| = \frac{1}{2}|AC|. $$

positive_text:
Let $p$ be an odd prime, and $m > 1$ and $n$ be positive integers such that $\frac{m^{pn} - 1}{m^n - 1}$ is a prime. Prove that
$$
pn \mid (p-1)^n + 1.
$$

negatives.text:
Let $p$ be an odd prime, and $m > 1$ and $n$ be positive integers such that $\frac{m^{pn} + 1}{m^n + 1}$ is a prime number. Show that
$$
pn \mid (p-1)^n + 1.
$$

Let $p$ be an odd prime, and $m > 1$ and $n$ be positive integers such that $\frac{m^{pn} - 1}{m^n - 1}$ is a prime number. Show that
$$
pn \mid (p+1)^n + 1.
$$

Let $p$ be an odd prime, and $m > 1$ and $n$ be positive integers such that $\frac{m^{pn} - 1}{m^n - 1}$ is a prime number. Show that
$$
pn \mid (p-1)^{n+1} + 1.
$$

positive_text:
Consider triangle $ABC$ where $\angle B < \angle C$. Let $K$ be the center of the excircle that touches the side $AC$. If the line $AK$ meets $BC$ at point $D$, and $E$ is the center of the circle passing through points $B$, $K$, and $C$, prove that
$$
\frac{1}{|KA|} = \frac{1}{|KD|} + \frac{1}{|KE|}.
$$

negatives.text:
In triangle $ABC$ with $\angle B < \angle C$, let $K$ be the center of the incircle that is tangent to the side $[AC]$. The lines $AK$ and $BC$ intersect at $D$, and $E$ is the center of the circumcircle of $BKC$. Prove that
$$
\frac{1}{|KA|} = \frac{1}{|KD|} + \frac{1}{|KE|}.
$$

In triangle $ABC$ with $\angle B < \angle C$, let $K$ be the center of the excircle that is tangent to the side $[AC]$. The lines $AK$ and $BC$ intersect at $D$, and $E$ is the center of the circumcircle of $ABC$. Prove that
$$
\frac{1}{|KA|} = \frac{1}{|KD|} + \frac{1}{|KE|}.
$$

In triangle $ABC$ with $\angle B < \angle C$, let $K$ be the center of the excircle that is tangent to the side $[AC]$. The lines $BK$ and $AC$ intersect at $D$, and $E$ is the center of the circumcircle of $BKC$. Prove that
$$
\frac{1}{|KA|} = \frac{1}{|KD|} + \frac{1}{|KE|}.
$$

positive_text: Find all integer values of $ n $ and $ k $, and all prime numbers $ p $, such that the absolute value of $ 6n^2 - 17n - 39 $ equals $ p^k $.

negatives.text: Find all triples $ (n, k, p) $ satisfying the equation $ 6n^2 - 17n - 39 = p^k $ where $ n, k $ are integers and $ p $ is a prime.
Find all triples $ (n, k, p) $ satisfying the equation $ |6n^2 - 17n - 39| = 2p^k $ where $ n, k $ are integers and $ p $ is a prime.
Find all triples $ (n, k, p) $ satisfying the equation $ |6n^2 - 17n - 39| = p $ where $ n, k $ are integers and $ p $ is a prime.

positive_text:
Suppose you have a collection $\mathcal{S}$ of $n$ different sets, where each set has exactly $k$ elements. The collection is special in the sense that for any two distinct sets $A$ and $B$ in $\mathcal{S}$, the symmetric difference $A \Delta B$ is also a member of $\mathcal{S}$.

a) Can the number of sets in $\mathcal{S}$ be $2023$? If yes, what are the possible values for $k$?

b) Can the number of sets in $\mathcal{S}$ be $1023$? If yes, what are the possible values for $k$?

Note: The symmetric difference $A \Delta B$ is the set of elements that are in either $A$ or $B$, but not in both.

negatives.text:
Let $\mathcal{S}$ be a family of $n$ sets, each has size $k$, such that $A \cup B \in \mathcal{S}$ whenever $A, B \in \mathcal{S}, A \neq B$.

a) Is it possible that $n = 2023$? If it is, find all possible values of $k$.

b) Is it possible that $n = 1023$? If it is, find all possible values of $k$.

Notation: $A \cup B$ is the union of $A$ and $B$.

Let $\mathcal{S}$ be a family of $n$ sets, each has size $k$, such that $A \cap B \in \mathcal{S}$ whenever $A, B \in \mathcal{S}, A \neq B$.

a) Is it possible that $n = 2023$? If it is, find all possible values of $k$.

b) Is it possible that $n = 1023$? If it is, find all possible values of $k$.

Notation: $A \cap B$ is the intersection of $A$ and $B$.

Let $\mathcal{S}$ be a family of $n$ sets, each has size $k$, such that $A \Delta B \in \mathcal{S}$ whenever $A, B \in \mathcal{S}, A \neq B$.

a) Is it possible that $n = 2024$? If it is, find all possible values of $k$.

b) Is it possible that $n = 1024$? If it is, find all possible values of $k$.

Notation: $A \Delta B = (A \setminus B) \cup (B \setminus A)$.

positive_text:
Determine all real-valued functions $f$ on the real numbers such that for all real numbers $x$ and $y$, the following identity holds:
$$f(x+y)^3 = (x+2y)f(x^2) + f(f(y))(x^2+3xy+y^2).$$

negatives.text:
Find all functions $f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ such that for all real numbers $x, y$,
$$f(x+y)^3 = (x+2y)f(x^2) + f(f(y))(x^2+2xy+y^2).$$

Find all functions $f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ such that for all real numbers $x, y$,
$$f(x+y)^3 = (x+y)f(x^2) + f(f(y))(x^2+3xy+y^2).$$

Find all functions $f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ such that for all real numbers $x, y$,
$$f(x+y)^3 = (x+2y)f(x^2) + f(f(y+1))(x^2+3xy+y^2).$$

positive_text:
Let $n$ be an integer with $n \ge 3$, and suppose we are given $n$ real numbers $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$. For each $k = 1, 2, \dots, n$, define a new number $b_k$ as
$$
b_k = \frac{a_k + \max\{a_{k+1}, a_{k+2}\}}{2},
$$
with the understanding that $a_{n+1} = a_1$ and $a_{n+2} = a_2$. Also, let $b_{n+1} = b_1$. Determine the smallest value of $\lambda$ such that for every $n \ge 3$ and all real numbers $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$, the following inequality holds:
$$
\lambda \left( \sum_{i=1}^n (a_i - a_{i+1})^{2024} \right) \geq \sum_{i=1}^n (b_i - b_{i+1})^{2024}.
$$

negatives.text:
Let $n \ge 3$ be an integer and $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$ be real numbers. For each $1 \le k \le n$ the real numbers $b_1, b_2, \dots, b_{n+1}$ are defined by
$$
b_k = \frac{a_k + \max\{a_{k+1}, a_{k+2}\}}{2}
$$
and $b_{n+1} = b_1$ ($a_{n+1} = a_1$ and $a_{n+2} = a_2$). Find the smallest $\lambda$ such that the inequality
$$
\lambda \left[ \sum_{i=1}^{n} (a_i - a_{i+1})^{2023} \right] \geq \sum_{i=1}^{n} (b_i - b_{i+1})^{2024}
$$
is held for each $n \ge 3$ and all real numbers $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$.

Let $n \ge 3$ be an integer and $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$ be real numbers. For each $1 \le k \le n$ the real numbers $b_1, b_2, \dots, b_{n+1}$ are defined by
$$
b_k = \frac{a_k + \max\{a_{k+1}, a_{k+2}\}}{2}
$$
and $b_{n+1} = b_1$ ($a_{n+1} = a_1$ and $a_{n+2} = a_2$). Find the smallest $\lambda$ such that the inequality
$$
\lambda \left[ \sum_{i=1}^{n} (a_i - a_{i+1})^{2024} \right] \geq \sum_{i=1}^{n} (b_i - b_{i+1})^{2023}
$$
is held for each $n \ge 3$ and all real numbers $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$.

positive_text:
Define a function $\sigma(n)$ to be the sum of all positive divisors of a positive integer $n$. Consider an infinite sequence $(a_i)_{i=0}^{\infty}$ of positive integers, where $a_0 = 1$ and for each $n > 1$, $a_n$ is the smallest integer greater than 1 such that
$$
\sigma(a_0 a_1 \cdots a_{n-1}) \mid \sigma(a_0 a_1 \cdots a_n).
$$
How many terms of this sequence divide the number $2024^{2024}$?

negatives.text:
For an integer $n$, let $\sigma(n)$ be the sum of all positive divisors of $n$. A sequence of positive integers $(a_i)_{i=0}^{\infty}$ is defined as follows: $a_0 = 1$ and for each $n > 1$, $a_n$ is the smallest integer greater than 1 such that
$$
\sigma(a_0 a_1 \cdots a_n) \mid \sigma(a_0 a_1 \cdots a_{n-1}).
$$
Determine the number of terms of this sequence dividing the number $2024^{2024}$.

For an integer $n$, let $\sigma(n)$ be the sum of all positive divisors of $n$. A sequence of positive integers $(a_i)_{i=0}^{\infty}$ is defined as follows: $a_0 = 1$ and for each $n > 1$, $a_n$ is the smallest integer greater than 1 such that
$$
\sigma(a_0 a_1 \cdots a_{n-1}) + 1 \mid \sigma(a_0 a_1 \cdots a_n).
$$
Determine the number of terms of this sequence dividing the number $2024^{2024}$.

For an integer $n$, let $\sigma(n)$ be the sum of all positive divisors of $n$. A sequence of positive integers $(a_i)_{i=0}^{\infty}$ is defined as follows: $a_0 = 1$ and for each $n > 1$, $a_n$ is the smallest integer greater than 1 such that
$$
\sigma(a_0 a_1 \cdots a_{n-1}) \mid \sigma(a_0 a_1 \cdots a_n) + 1.
$$
Determine the number of terms of this sequence dividing the number $2024^{2024}$.

positive_text:
Suppose $a, b, c$ are numbers between 0 and $\frac{\pi}{2}$ such that
$$
\sin a + \sin b + \sin c = 1, \quad \sin a \cos 2a + \sin b \cos 2b + \sin c \cos 2c = -1.
$$
What is the value of $\sin^2 a + \sin^2 b + \sin^2 c$?

negatives.text:
Let $\alpha, \beta, \gamma \in [0; \frac{\pi}{2}]$ satisfy the conditions
$$
\sin \alpha + \sin \beta + \sin \gamma = 1, \quad \sin \alpha \cos 2\alpha + \sin \beta \cos 2\beta + \sin \gamma \cos 2\gamma = 0.
$$
Find all the possible values of the expression $\sin^2 \alpha + \sin^2 \beta + \sin^2 \gamma$.

Let $\alpha, \beta, \gamma \in [0; \frac{\pi}{2}]$ satisfy the conditions
$$
\sin \alpha + \sin \beta + \sin \gamma = 1, \quad \sin \alpha \cos 2\alpha + \sin \beta \cos 2\beta + \sin \gamma \cos 2\gamma = -1.
$$
Find all the possible values of the expression $\cos^2 \alpha + \cos^2 \beta + \cos^2 \gamma$.

Let $\alpha, \beta, \gamma \in [0; \frac{\pi}{2}]$ satisfy the conditions
$$
\sin \alpha + \sin \beta + \sin \gamma = 2, \quad \sin \alpha \cos 2\alpha + \sin \beta \cos 2\beta + \sin \gamma \cos 2\gamma = -1.
$$
Find all the possible values of the expression $\sin^2 \alpha + \sin^2 \beta + \sin^2 \gamma$.

positive_text: Suppose we have $n$ points (with $n \ge 3$) in a plane, and not all of them are on a straight line. For any point $M$, let $f(M)$ be the total distance from $M$ to each of the $n$ points. It is given that there is a point $M_1$ such that $f(M_1)$ is less than or equal to $f(M)$ for any other point $M$. If there is another point $M_2$ such that $f(M_1) = f(M_2)$, prove that $M_1$ and $M_2$ are the same point.

negatives.text: Suppose we have $n$ points (with $n \ge 3$) in a plane, and not all of them are on a straight line. For any point $M$, let $f(M)$ be the total distance from $M$ to each of the $n$ points. It is given that there is a point $M_1$ such that $f(M_1)$ is less than or equal to $f(M)$ for any other point $M$. If there is another point $M_2$ such that $f(M_1) < f(M_2)$, prove that $M_1$ and $M_2$ are the same point.

Suppose we have $n$ points (with $n \ge 3$) in a plane, and not all of them are on a straight line. For any point $M$, let $f(M)$ be the total distance from $M$ to each of the $n$ points. It is given that there is a point $M_1$ such that $f(M_1)$ is less than or equal to $f(M)$ for any other point $M$. If there is another point $M_2$ such that $f(M_1) = f(M_2)$, prove that $M_1$ and $M_2$ lie on the same line.

Suppose we have $n$ points (with $n \ge 3$) in a plane, and not all of them are on a straight line. For any point $M$, let $f(M)$ be the total distance from $M$ to each of the $n$ points. It is given that there is a point $M_1$ such that $f(M_1)$ is less than or equal to $f(M)$ for any other point $M$. If there is another point $M_2$ such that $f(M_1) = f(M_2)$, prove that the distance between $M_1$ and $M_2$ is less than 1.

positive_text:
Show that for all positive integers $n$, the following inequality is always true:
$$
\sum_{k=1}^{n} \frac{k+2}{k! + (k+1)! + (k+2)!} < \frac{1}{2}.
$$

negatives.text:
Show that for all positive integers $n$, the following inequality is always true:
$$
\sum_{k=1}^{n} \frac{k+2}{k! + (k+1)! + (k+2)!} < 1.
$$

Show that for all positive integers $n$, the following inequality is always true:
$$
\sum_{k=1}^{n} \frac{k+1}{k! + (k+1)! + (k+2)!} < \frac{1}{2}.
$$

positive_text: \text{a) Solve for all real numbers } x \text{ that satisfy}\\$$x^2 + \frac{1}{x^2 + 2x} = 1$$\\\text{b) Determine all positive real numbers } x \text{ and } y \text{ such that}\\$$x^2 + y^2 + \frac{1}{x^2 + 2x} + \frac{1}{y^2 + 2y} = 2$$

negatives.text: \text{a) Solve for all real numbers } x \text{ that satisfy}\\$$x^2 + \frac{1}{x^2 + 2x} = 2$$\\\text{b) Determine all positive real numbers } x \text{ and } y \text{ such that}\\$$x^2 + y^2 + \frac{1}{x^2 + 2x} + \frac{1}{y^2 + 2y} = 2$$

\text{a) Solve for all real numbers } x \text{ that satisfy}\\$$x^2 + \frac{1}{x^2 + 2x} = 1$$\\\text{b) Determine all positive real numbers } x \text{ and } y \text{ such that}\\$$x^2 + y^2 + \frac{1}{x^2 + 2x} + \frac{1}{y^2 + 2y} = 3$$

\text{a) Solve for all real numbers } x \text{ that satisfy}\\$$x^2 + \frac{1}{x^2 + 2x} = 1$$\\\text{b) Determine all positive real numbers } x \text{ and } y \text{ such that}\\$$x^2 + y^2 + \frac{1}{x^2 + 2y} + \frac{1}{y^2 + 2x} = 2$$

positive_text: Two players, Alex and Ben, are taking turns writing numbers to form a sequence $a_1, a_2, ..., a_{2006}$. The first number, $a_1$, is fixed as 1 and written by Alex. Then, on each turn, the next number must be at least as big as the previous one but no more than three times as large. That is, $a_n \le a_{n+1} \le 3a_n$ for each $n$ from 1 to 2005. After all 2006 numbers are written, if the sum of the first 2005 numbers and the sum of all 2006 numbers are relatively prime, then Ben wins; otherwise, Alex wins. Who can always win, no matter how the other plays?

Show that for all positive real numbers $x$, $y$, and $z$, the inequality
$$
\left( \frac{x+y}{z^2} + \frac{y+z}{x^2} + \frac{z+x}{y^2} \right) \cdot \left( \frac{x^2}{y+z} + \frac{y^2}{z+x} + \frac{z^2}{x+y} \right) \ge 3 + \frac{x+y}{z} + \frac{y+z}{x} + \frac{z+x}{y}
$$
holds true.

negatives.text:
Show that for all positive real numbers $a$, $b$, and $c$, the inequality
$$
\left( \frac{a+b}{c^2} + \frac{b+c}{a^2} + \frac{c+a}{b^2} \right) \cdot \left( \frac{a^2}{b+c} + \frac{b^2}{c+a} + \frac{c^2}{a+b} \right) \ge 3 + \frac{a}{b+c} + \frac{b}{c+a} + \frac{c}{a+b}
$$
holds true.

Show that for all positive real numbers $a$, $b$, and $c$, the inequality
$$
\left( \frac{a+b}{c^2} + \frac{b+c}{a^2} + \frac{c+a}{b^2} \right) \cdot \left( \frac{a^2}{b+c} + \frac{b^2}{c+a} + \frac{c^2}{a+b} \right) \ge 3 + \frac{a+b}{c} + \frac{b+c}{a} + \frac{c+a}{b} + \frac{1}{abc}
$$
holds true.

Show that for all positive real numbers $a$, $b$, and $c$, the inequality
$$
\left( \frac{a+b}{c^2} + \frac{b+c}{a^2} + \frac{c+a}{b^2} \right) \cdot \left( \frac{a^2}{b+c} + \frac{b^2}{c+a} + \frac{c^2}{a+b} \right) \ge 3 + \frac{a}{c} + \frac{b}{a} + \frac{c}{b}
$$
holds true.

positive_text: \text{Imagine you have two numbers, } x \text{ and } y, \text{ such that } |x+y| + |x-y| = 1. \text{ What is the smallest and largest possible value of the expression } x^2 - 6x + y^2 - 6y?

negatives.text: \text{We know that } |x+y| + |x-y| = 2. \text{ Find the least and the greatest value of expression } x^2 - 6x + y^2 - 6y.
\text{We know that } |x+y| + |x-y| = 1. \text{ Find the least and the greatest value of expression } x^2 - 6x + y^2.
\text{We know that } |x+y| + |x-y| = 1. \text{ Find the least and the greatest value of expression } x^2 + 6x + y^2 + 6y.

positive_text: In a parallelogram $ABCD$, side $BC$ is extended past point $C$ to a point $K$ such that triangle $CDK$ is isosceles with base $CK$. Similarly, side $DC$ is extended past point $C$ to a point $L$ such that triangle $CBL$ is isosceles with base $CL$. The angle bisectors of $\angle LBC$ and $\angle CDK$ meet at point $Q$. If $\angle BQD = \alpha$ and the length $KL = a$, find the radius of the circle that passes through points $A$, $L$, and $K$.

negatives.text: Side $BC$ of the parallelogram $ABCD$ is extended beyond the point $C$ and point $K$ is placed on the extension so that $\triangle CDK$ is isosceles triangle with base $CK$. Side $DC$ is extended beyond the point $C$ and point $L$ is placed on the extension so that $\triangle CBL$ is isosceles triangle with base $CL$. Bisectors of angles $\angle LBC$ and $\angle CDK$ intersect at point $Q$. Find radius of a circle circumscribed about triangle $ALK$, if $\angle QBD = \alpha$ and $KL = a$.

Side $BC$ of the parallelogram $ABCD$ is extended beyond the point $C$ and point $K$ is placed on the extension so that $\triangle CDK$ is isosceles triangle with base $CK$. Side $DC$ is extended beyond the point $C$ and point $L$ is placed on the extension so that $\triangle CBL$ is isosceles triangle with base $CL$. Bisectors of angles $\angle LBC$ and $\angle CDK$ intersect at point $Q$. Find radius of a circle circumscribed about triangle $ALK$, if $\angle BQD = \alpha$ and $KL = 2a$.

positive_text: Find the value of $\alpha$ such that the equation $|x - \frac{1}{2}| + |x - \sin \alpha| = \cos 3\alpha$ has only one solution for $x$. Then, determine what that solution is.

negatives.text: What should be the value of the parameter $\alpha$ in order that equation $|x - \frac{1}{2}| + |x - \sin \alpha| = \sin 3\alpha$ has a single solution? Find this solution.
What should be the value of the parameter $\alpha$ in order that equation $|x - \frac{1}{4}| + |x - \sin \alpha| = \cos 3\alpha$ has a single solution? Find this solution.
What should be the value of the parameter $\alpha$ in order that equation $|x - \frac{1}{2}| + |x - \sin \alpha| = 2\cos 3\alpha$ has a single solution? Find this solution.

positive_text: Consider a sequence $\{f_n\}$ where the first term is 1, the second term is 2, and each next term is the sum of the two previous terms. For example: $f_1 = 1$, $f_2 = 2$, $f_3 = 3$, $f_4 = 5$, and so on. Now imagine a list of numbers that increases by a fixed amount each time (like 2, 5, 8, 11, 14, etc.). What is the maximum number of terms from the sequence $\{f_n\}$ that can appear in a row in such a list?

negatives.text: Sequence $\{f_n\}$ is defined as follows: $f_1 = 1$, $f_2 = 2$, $f_{n+2} = f_{n+1} + f_n$ for random natural $n$. What may be the greatest number of members of the sequence $\{f_n\}$ among the consecutive members of the increasing geometric progression?

Sequence $\{f_n\}$ is defined as follows: $f_1 = 1$, $f_2 = 2$, $f_{n+2} = f_{n+1} + f_n$ for random natural $n$. What may be the greatest number of members of the sequence $\{f_n\}$ among the consecutive members of the decreasing arithmetic progression?

Sequence $\{f_n\}$ is defined as follows: $f_1 = 1$, $f_2 = 2$, $f_{n+2} = f_{n+1} + f_n$ for random natural $n$. What may be the greatest number of members of the sequence $\{f_n\}$ among the consecutive members of the decreasing geometric progression?

positive_text: Let $ \sigma(n) $ represent the sum of all positive divisors of a positive integer $ n $, and let $ \phi(n) $ represent the number of positive integers less than $ n $ that are coprime to $ n $. Show that there are infinitely many positive integers $ n $ such that $ \phi(\sigma(n)) > n $.

negatives.text: For every positive integer $ m $, let $ \sigma(m) $ be the sum of all its divisors, and $ \phi(m) $ the number of positive integers less than $ m $ and coprime with $ m $. Prove that there exists infinitely many positive integers $ n $ for which $ \phi(\sigma(n)) < n $.

positive_text: In triangle $ABC$, the angle at $A$ is at least $60^\circ$. The bisectors of angles $B$ and $C$ intersect the opposite sides at points $D$ and $E$, respectively. Show that the sum of the lengths $AD$ and $AE$ is less than or equal to the length of side $BC$.

negatives.text: Angular bisectors $BD$ and $CE$ are drawn in the triangle $ABC$ with angle $\angle BAC < 60^\circ$. Prove that $AD + AE \le BC$.
Angular bisectors $BD$ and $CE$ are drawn in the triangle $ABC$ with angle $\angle BAC \ge 60^\circ$. Prove that $AD + AE \ge BC$.
Angular bisectors $BD$ and $CE$ are drawn in the triangle $ABC$ with angle $\angle BAC \ge 60^\circ$. Prove that $AD + AE = BC$.

positive_text:
Determine all real-coefficient polynomials $P(x)$ such that for any distinct natural numbers $a, b, c, d$ where $a^2 + b^2 + c^2 = 2d^2$ and the greatest common divisor of $a, b, c, d$ is 1, the following equation holds:
$$
2P^2(d) + 2P(ab + bc + ca) = P^2(a + b + c).
$$

negatives.text:
Find all polynomials $P(x)$ with real coefficients, such that for every distinct natural $x, y, z, t$ satisfying $x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 2t^2$ and $\text{GCD}\{x, y, z, t\} = 1$, the following equality holds:
$$
2P(t)^2 + 2P(xz + yz + zx) = P^2(x + y + z).
$$

positive_text: \frac{d^2}{e} + \frac{e^2}{f} + \frac{f^2}{d} \ge \frac{d + e + f}{\sqrt{3}}\quad\text{where } d = AO, e = BO, f = CO, \text{ and point } O \text{ lies inside triangle } ABC \text{ with } \angle AOB = \angle BOC = \angle COA = 120^\circ.

negatives.text: \frac{AO^2}{BC} + \frac{BO^2}{CA} + \frac{CO^2}{AB} \ge \frac{AO + BO + CO}{\sqrt{3}}\quad\text{where } O \text{ is the point inside triangle } ABC \text{ such that } \angle AOB = \angle BOC = 90^\circ.

\frac{AO^2}{BC} + \frac{BO^2}{CA} + \frac{CO^2}{AB} \le \frac{AO + BO + CO}{\sqrt{3}}\quad\text{where } O \text{ is the point inside triangle } ABC \text{ such that } \angle AOB = \angle BOC = \angle COA = 120^\circ.

\frac{AO^2}{AB} + \frac{BO^2}{BC} + \frac{CO^2}{CA} \ge \frac{AO + BO + CO}{\sqrt{3}}\quad\text{where } O \text{ is the point inside triangle } ABC \text{ such that } \angle AOB = \angle BOC = \angle COA = 120^\circ.

positive_text: How many pairs of positive whole numbers $(n, m)$ satisfy the equation $(2^k)! = 2^n \cdot m$?

negatives.text: Find the number of pairs of positive integer numbers $(n, m)$, satisfying $(3^k)! = 2^n m$.
Find the number of pairs of positive integer numbers $(n, m)$, satisfying $(2^k)! = 3^n m$.
Find the number of pairs of positive integer numbers $(n, m)$, satisfying $(2^{k+1})! = 2^n m$.

positive_text: Determine all positive integers $ n $ such that for any polynomial $ g(x) $ with real coefficients, we can find polynomials $ p_1(x), p_2(x), \ldots, p_n(x) $ and $ q_1(x), q_2(x), \ldots, q_n(x) $ satisfying $ g(x) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (p_i^2(x) + q_i^3(x)) $.

negatives.text: Find all such positive integer $ n $ that for every polynomial $ g(x) $ with real coefficients there exist such polynomials $ p_1(x), p_2(x), \ldots, p_n(x) $ and $ q_1(x), q_2(x), \ldots, q_n(x) $ that $ g(x) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (p_i^3(x) + q_i^3(x)) $.

Find all such positive integer $ n $ that for every polynomial $ g(x) $ with real coefficients there exist such polynomials $ p_1(x), p_2(x), \ldots, p_n(x) $ and $ q_1(x), q_2(x), \ldots, q_n(x) $ that $ g(x) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (p_i^2(x) + q_i^2(x)) $.

Find all such positive integer $ n $ that for every polynomial $ g(x) $ with real coefficients there exist such polynomials $ p_1(x), p_2(x), \ldots, p_n(x) $ and $ q_1(x), q_2(x), \ldots, q_n(x) $ that $ g(x) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (p_i^2(x) + q_i(x)) $.

positive_text: Suppose $x$ and $y$ are numbers such that both $x$ and $y$ are between $-1$ and $1$. Show that $x\sqrt{1 - y^2} + y\sqrt{1 - x^2} \le 1$.

negatives.text: Let $a, b \in [-1,1]$. Prove that $a\sqrt{1-b^2} - b\sqrt{1-a^2} \le 1$.
Let $a, b \in [-1,1]$. Prove that $a\sqrt{1-b^2} + b\sqrt{1-a^2} \le 2$.

positive_text: Consider a triangle $PQR$ and a point $X$ that is not on any of the sides $PQ$, $PR$, or $QR$. For each vertex $P$, $Q$, and $R$, construct a line that goes through the vertex and is perpendicular to the segment connecting the vertex to $X$. Call these lines $l_P$, $l_Q$, and $l_R$. Let $B_P = l_Q \cap l_R$, $B_Q = l_R \cap l_P$, and $B_R = l_P \cap l_Q$. Let $H_P$, $H_Q$, and $H_R$ be the orthocenters of triangles $B_PQR$, $B_QRP$, and $B_RPQ$, respectively. Show that triangle $H_PH_QH_R$ is congruent to triangle $PQR$.

negatives.text: Let a given triangle $A_1A_2A_3$ and a point $X$ which does not lie on each of the lines $A_1A_2$, $A_1A_3$, and $A_2A_3$ be given. Denote by $l_i$ the line which passes through the point $A_i$ and is perpendicular to the line $XA_i$, for $i=1,2,3$. Let $B_1 = l_2 \cap l_3$, $B_2 = l_3 \cap l_1$, $B_3 = l_1 \cap l_2$, and let $H_1, H_2, H_3$ be the centroids of the triangles $B_1A_2A_3$, $B_2A_3A_1$, and $B_3A_1A_2$, respectively. Prove that the triangle $H_1H_2H_3$ is congruent to the triangle $A_1A_2A_3$.

Let a given triangle $A_1A_2A_3$ and a point $X$ which does not lie on each of the lines $A_1A_2$, $A_1A_3$, and $A_2A_3$ be given. Denote by $l_i$ the line which passes through the point $A_i$ and is perpendicular to the line $XA_i$, for $i=1,2,3$. Let $B_1 = l_2 \cap l_3$, $B_2 = l_3 \cap l_1$, $B_3 = l_1 \cap l_2$, and let $H_1, H_2, H_3$ be the orthocenters of the triangles $B_1A_2A_3$, $B_2A_3A_1$, and $B_3A_1A_2$, respectively. Prove that the triangle $H_1H_2H_3$ is similar to the triangle $A_1A_2A_3$.

Let a given triangle $A_1A_2A_3$ and a point $X$ which lies on one of the lines $A_1A_2$, $A_1A_3$, or $A_2A_3$ be given. Denote by $l_i$ the line which passes through the point $A_i$ and is perpendicular to the line $XA_i$, for $i=1,2,3$. Let $B_1 = l_2 \cap l_3$, $B_2 = l_3 \cap l_1$, $B_3 = l_1 \cap l_2$, and let $H_1, H_2, H_3$ be the orthocenters of the triangles $B_1A_2A_3$, $B_2A_3A_1$, and $B_3A_1A_2$, respectively. Prove that the triangle $H_1H_2H_3$ is congruent to the triangle $A_1A_2A_3$.

positive_text: Given integers $x, y, z$ such that $xy + yz + zx = 1$, show that the product $(1 + x^2)(1 + y^2)(1 + z^2)$ is the square of an integer.

negatives.text: Integers $a, b, c$ satisfy the condition $ab + bc + ca = 1$. Prove that the number $(1 + a^2)(1 + b^2)(1 + c^2)$ is a perfect cube of some natural number.
Integers $a, b, c$ satisfy the condition $ab + bc + ca = 2$. Prove that the number $(1 + a^2)(1 + b^2)(1 + c^2)$ is a perfect square of some natural number.

positive_text: Sketch the graph of the equation: $$\frac{x}{|x|} + \frac{|y|}{y} = 2y.$$

negatives.text: Sketch the graph of the equation: $$\frac{x}{|x|} + \frac{|y|}{y} = y.$$
Sketch the graph of the equation: $$\frac{x}{|x|} + \frac{|y|}{y} = 2|x|.$$
Sketch the graph of the equation: $$\frac{|x|}{x} + \frac{|y|}{y} = 2y.$$

positive_text: Consider triangle $ABC$, and two points $F$ and $L$ on side $AC$. These points are chosen such that the lengths $AF$ and $LC$ are equal, and each is less than half of the length of $AC$. If it is given that $AB^2 + BC^2 = AL^2 + LC^2$, find the measure of angle $FBL$.

negatives.text: In a triangle $ABC$, points $F$ and $L$ lie on side $AC$ such that $AF = LC < \frac{1}{2}AC$. Find an angle $FBL$, if $AB^2 + BC^2 = AF^2 + LC^2$.
In a triangle $ABC$, points $F$ and $L$ lie on side $AC$ such that $AF = LC < \frac{1}{2}AC$. Find an angle $FBL$, if $AB^2 + BC^2 = AL^2 + FC^2$.

positive_text:
Let $x$, $y$, and $z$ be nonnegative real numbers such that $x + y + z = 1$. Show that
$$
(1 - x)^2 + (1 - y)^2 + (1 - z)^2 \geq 6\sqrt{xyz}.
$$
Is it possible for both sides of the inequality to be equal?

negatives.text:
Nonnegative real numbers $a$, $b$, $c$ satisfy the equation $a + b + c = 1$. Prove the inequality
$$
(1 - a)^2 + (1 - b)^2 + (1 - c)^2 \geq 2\sqrt{abc}.
$$
Can the case of equality occur?

Nonnegative real numbers $a$, $b$, $c$ satisfy the equation $a + b + c = 2$. Prove the inequality
$$
(1 - a)^2 + (1 - b)^2 + (1 - c)^2 \geq 6\sqrt{abc}.
$$
Can the case of equality occur?

Nonnegative real numbers $a$, $b$, $c$ satisfy the equation $a + b + c = 1$. Prove the inequality
$$
(1 - a)^2 + (1 - b)^2 + (1 - c)^2 \leq 6\sqrt{abc}.
$$
Can the case of equality occur?

positive_text: Let $P$ be a point inside triangle $ABC$. Let $O_A$, $O_B$, and $O_C$ be the centers of the circles passing through the points of triangles $PBC$, $PAC$, and $PAB$ respectively. Let $O_P$ be the center of the circle passing through $O_A$, $O_B$, and $O_C$. Show that $P = O_P$ if $P$ is the point where the altitudes of triangle $ABC$ meet.

negatives.text: Let $P$ lie inside triangle $ABC$. Denote by $O_A, O_B, O_C$ the circumcenters of triangles $PBC, PAC, PAB$ respectively. Let $O_P$ be the circumcenter of triangle $O_A O_B O_C$. Prove that the point $P$ satisfies the condition $O_P = P$ if $P$ is the centroid of triangle $ABC$.

Let $P$ be a point inside triangle $ABC$. Denote by $O_A, O_B, O_C$ the circumcenters of triangles $PBC, PAC, PAB$ respectively. Let $O_P$ be the circumcenter of triangle $O_A O_B O_C$. Prove that the point $P$ satisfies the condition $O_P = P$ if $P$ is the incenter of triangle $ABC$.

Let $P$ lie inside triangle $ABC$. Denote by $O_A, O_B, O_C$ the circumcenters of triangles $PBC, PAC, PAB$ respectively. Let $O_P$ be the circumcenter of triangle $O_A O_B O_C$. Prove that the point $P$ satisfies the condition $O_P = P$ if $P$ is the circumcenter of triangle $ABC$.

positive_text: In an acute triangle $ABC$, let $P$ lie on the perpendicular bisector of side $AB$, and let $Q$ lie on the perpendicular bisector of side $BC$. Drop perpendiculars from $P$ and $Q$ to side $AC$, and call the feet of these perpendiculars $M$ and $N$, respectively. It is given that $2MN = AC$. Show that the circumcircle of triangle $PBQ$ passes through the circumcenter of triangle $ABC$.

negatives.text: In an acute triangle $ABC$, let $P$ lie on the perpendicular bisector of side $AB$, and let $Q$ lie on the perpendicular bisector of side $BC$. Drop perpendiculars from $P$ and $Q$ to side $AC$, and call the feet of these perpendiculars $M$ and $N$, respectively. It is given that $MN = AC$. Show that the circumcircle of triangle $PBQ$ passes through the circumcenter of triangle $ABC$.

In an acute triangle $ABC$, let $P$ lie on the perpendicular bisector of side $AB$, and let $Q$ lie on the perpendicular bisector of side $AC$. Drop perpendiculars from $P$ and $Q$ to side $AC$, and call the feet of these perpendiculars $M$ and $N$, respectively. It is given that $2MN = AC$. Show that the circumcircle of triangle $PBQ$ passes through the circumcenter of triangle $ABC$.

In an acute triangle $ABC$, let $P$ lie on the perpendicular bisector of side $AB$, and let $Q$ lie on the perpendicular bisector of side $BC$. Drop perpendiculars from $P$ and $Q$ to side $AC$, and call the feet of these perpendiculars $M$ and $N$, respectively. It is given that $2MN = AC$. Show that the circumcircle of triangle $PBQ$ passes through the centroid of triangle $ABC$.

positive_text: A point $P$ is inside triangle $ABC$. The points $I_A$, $I_B$, and $I_C$ are the incenters of triangles $PBC$, $PAC$, and $PAB$, respectively. Let $I_P$ be the incenter of triangle $I_A I_B I_C$. If $I_P$ is the same point as $P$, show that the following equalities are true: $$ AP - BP = AC - BC, \ BP - CP = BA - CA, \ CP - AP = CB - AB. $$

negatives.text: A point $P$ is inside triangle $ABC$. The points $I_A$, $I_B$, and $I_C$ are the incenters of triangles $PBC$, $PAC$, and $PAB$, respectively. Let $I_P$ be the circumcenter of triangle $I_A I_B I_C$. If $I_P$ is the same point as $P$, show that the following equalities are true: $$ AP - BP = AC - BC, \ BP - CP = BA - CA, \ CP - AP = CB - AB. $$

A point $P$ is inside triangle $ABC$. The points $I_A$, $I_B$, and $I_C$ are the incenters of triangles $PBC$, $PAC$, and $PAB$, respectively. Let $I_P$ be the incenter of triangle $I_A I_B I_C$. If $I_P$ is the same point as $P$, show that the following equalities are true: $$ AP + BP = AC + BC, \ BP + CP = BA + CA, \ CP + AP = CB + AB. $$

A point $P$ is inside triangle $ABC$. The points $I_A$, $I_B$, and $I_C$ are the centroids of triangles $PBC$, $PAC$, and $PAB$, respectively. Let $I_P$ be the incenter of triangle $I_A I_B I_C$. If $I_P$ is the same point as $P$, show that the following equalities are true: $$ AP - BP = AC - BC, \ BP - CP = BA - CA, \ CP - AP = CB - AB. $$

positive_text: Show that for any positive whole number $n$, the equation $a^n + 2010b^n = c^{n+1}$ has infinitely many solutions where $a$, $b$, and $c$ are natural numbers.

negatives.text: Show that for all positive integers $n$, the equation $a^n + 2010b^n = c^n$ has infinitely many natural solutions $a, b, c$.
Show that for all positive integers $n$, the equation $a^n + 2010b^n = c^{n+1}$ has exactly one natural solution $a, b, c$.
Show that for all positive integers $n$, the equation $a^n + 2011b^n = c^{n+1}$ has infinitely many natural solutions $a, b, c$.

positive_text: Let $a$, $b$, $c$ be real numbers with $0 < a \le 1$, $0 < b \le 1$, and $0 < c \le 1$. Show that the following inequality is true:$$\frac{a}{2+ab+bc} + \frac{b}{2+bc+ca} + \frac{c}{2+ca+ab} \le \frac{a+b+c}{a+b+c+abc}$$

negatives.text: Let $x$, $y$, $z$ be real numbers such that $x \in (0, 1]$, $y \in (0, 1]$, $z \in (0, 1]$. Prove the inequality:$$\frac{x}{2+xy+yz} + \frac{y}{2+yz+zx} + \frac{z}{2+zx+xy} \le \frac{x+y+z}{x+y+z+2xyz}$$

Let $x$, $y$, $z$ be real numbers such that $x \in (0, 1]$, $y \in (0, 1]$, $z \in (0, 1]$. Prove the inequality:$$\frac{x}{2+xy+yz} + \frac{y}{2+yz+zx} + \frac{z}{2+zx+xy} \le \frac{x+y+z}{x+y+z+xyz^2}$$

Let $x$, $y$, $z$ be real numbers such that $x \in (0, 1]$, $y \in (0, 1]$, $z \in (0, 1]$. Prove the inequality:$$\frac{x}{2+xy+yz} + \frac{y}{2+yz+zx} + \frac{z}{2+zx+xy} \le \frac{x+y+z}{x+y+z+\frac{1}{xyz}}$$

positive_text: In triangle $ABC$, points $K$ and $M$ lie on sides $AB$ and $BC$ respectively, such that the lengths $AK$, $KM$, and $MC$ are all equal. The lines $AM$ and $CK$ intersect at point $N$. A perpendicular is dropped from $N$ to the segment $KM$, meeting it at point $P$. Then a point $Q$ is chosen on $KM$ so that $MQ = KP$. Show that the incircle of triangle $KMB$ touches segment $KM$ at point $Q$.

negatives.text: Points $K$ and $M$ are chosen on the sides $AB$ and $BC$ of triangle $ABC$ in such a way that $AK = KM = MC$. Let $N$ be the point of intersection of $AM$ and $CK$, $P$ – the feet of perpendicular from point $N$ to the line $KM$, and $Q$ is such point inside segment $KM$, that $KQ = KP$. Prove that the incircle of $\triangle KMB$ touches $KM$ at point $Q$.

Points $K$ and $M$ are chosen on the sides $AB$ and $BC$ of triangle $ABC$ in such a way that $AK = KM = MC$. Let $N$ be the point of intersection of $AM$ and $CK$, $P$ – the feet of perpendicular from point $N$ to the line $KM$, and $Q$ is such point inside segment $KM$, that $MQ = NP$. Prove that the incircle of $\triangle KMB$ touches $KM$ at point $Q$.

Points $K$ and $M$ are chosen on the sides $AB$ and $BC$ of triangle $ABC$ in such a way that $AK = KM = MC$. Let $N$ be the point of intersection of $AM$ and $CK$, $P$ – the feet of perpendicular from point $N$ to the line $KM$, and $Q$ is such point inside segment $KM$, that $MQ = KP$. Prove that the incircle of $\triangle KMC$ touches $KM$ at point $Q$.

positive_text: In an isosceles triangle $ABC$ with base $BC$ and $\angle BAC < 90^\circ$, a point $P$ is selected inside the triangle such that $\angle BPC = 2\angle BAC$. Let $K$ be the point where the perpendicular from $A$ to the line that bisects the adjacent angle of $\angle BPC$ lands. Show that the sum of the distances from $P$ to $B$ and $P$ to $C$ is equal to twice the length from $A$ to $K$.

negatives.text: Point $P$ is chosen inside isosceles triangle $ABC$ with base $BC$ and $\angle BAC < 90^\circ$ in such a way that $\angle BPC = \angle BAC$. Let $K$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $A$ to the line which contains the bisector of the adjacent angle of $\angle BPC$. Prove that $BP + PC = 2AK$.

Point $P$ is chosen inside isosceles triangle $ABC$ with base $BC$ and $\angle BAC < 90^\circ$ in such a way that $\angle BPC = 2\angle BAC$. Let $K$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $A$ to the line which contains the bisector of the adjacent angle of $\angle BPC$. Prove that $BP + PC = AK$.

Point $P$ is chosen inside isosceles triangle $ABC$ with base $BC$ and $\angle BAC < 90^\circ$ in such a way that $\angle BPC = 2\angle BAC$. Let $K$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $P$ to the line which contains the bisector of the adjacent angle of $\angle BPC$. Prove that $BP + PC = 2AK$.

positive_text: In triangle $ ABC $, suppose $ h $ is the height from vertex $ A $ to side $ BC $, and let $ \alpha $ be the angle at $ A $. Show that the following inequality is true: $$ AB + AC \ge BC \cdot \cos \alpha + 2h \sin \alpha. $$ When is this inequality an equality?

negatives.text: In triangle $ ABC $, suppose $ h $ is the height from vertex $ A $ to side $ BC $, and let $ \alpha $ be the angle at $ A $. Show that the following inequality is true: $$ AB + AC \ge BC \cdot \sin \alpha + 2h \cos \alpha. $$ When is this inequality an equality?

positive_text: Determine all values of the constant $b$ such that for every real number $x$, at least one of the functions $f_1(x) = x^2 + 2011x + b$ or $f_2(x) = x^2 - 2011x + b$ is greater than zero.

negatives.text: Determine all values of the constant $b$ such that for every real number $x$, both functions $f_1(x) = x^2 + 2011x + b$ and $f_2(x) = x^2 - 2011x + b$ are greater than zero.
Determine all values of the constant $b$ such that for every real number $x$, at least one of the functions $f_1(x) = x^2 + 2011x + b$ or $f_2(x) = x^2 + 2011x + b$ is greater than zero.
Determine all values of the constant $b$ such that for every real number $x$, at least one of the functions $f_1(x) = x^2 + 2011x + b$ or $f_2(x) = x^2 + 2011x - b$ is greater than zero.

positive_text: Solve the equation: $$\cos(\pi x) = \left\lfloor \frac{x}{2} - \left\lfloor \frac{x}{2} \right\rfloor - \frac{1}{2} \right\rfloor.$$ Here $\lfloor a \rfloor$ means the greatest integer less than or equal to $a$.

negatives.text: Solve the equation: $$\cos \pi x = \left[ \frac{x}{2} - \left[ \frac{x}{2} \right] + \frac{1}{2} \right].$$ Here $[a]$ stands for the greatest integer number that does not exceed $a$.
Solve the equation: $$\sin \pi x = \left[ \frac{x}{2} - \left[ \frac{x}{2} \right] - \frac{1}{2} \right].$$ Here $[a]$ stands for the greatest integer number that does not exceed $a$.
Solve the equation: $$\cos \pi x = \left[ \frac{x}{2} - \left[ x \right] - \frac{1}{2} \right].$$ Here $[a]$ stands for the greatest integer number that does not exceed $a$.

positive_text:
Determine all real-valued functions $f$ defined on the real numbers that satisfy the following two conditions:

1) For all real numbers $x$ and $y$, the equation
$$
 f(2x) = f(x+y)f(y-x) + f(x-y)f(-x-y)
$$
holds.

2) The function $f$ is non-negative, i.e., $f(x) \ge 0$ for every real number $x$.

negatives.text:
Find all functions $f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, such that:

1) For all real $x, y$ the following equality holds
$$
 f(x) = f(x+y)f(y-x) + f(x-y)f(-x-y).
$$

2) $f(x) \ge 0$ for all $x$.

positive_text: A triangle $ABC$ is drawn inside a circle. Lines that just touch the circle at points $A$ and $B$ meet at a point $T$. A line goes through $T$ and runs parallel to $AC$, and it meets $BC$ at a point $D$. Show that the lengths $AD$ and $CD$ are equal.

negatives.text: Triangle $ABC$ is inscribed into the circle. Tangents at points $A$ and $C$ meet at point $T$. The line that passes through the point $T$ and is parallel to $AC$ intersects $BC$ at point $D$. Prove that $AD = CD$.

Triangle $ABC$ is inscribed into the circle. Tangents at points $A$ and $B$ meet at point $T$. The line that passes through the point $T$ and is parallel to $AB$ intersects $BC$ at point $D$. Prove that $AD = CD$.

Triangle $ABC$ is inscribed into the circle. Tangents at points $A$ and $B$ meet at point $T$. The line that passes through the point $T$ and is parallel to $AC$ intersects $AB$ at point $D$. Prove that $AD = CD$.

positive_text: In triangle $ABC$, point $M$ is the midpoint of side $BC$, and point $N$ lies on side $AB$ such that $NB = 2AN$. Given that $\angle CAB = \angle CMN$, determine the value of the ratio $\frac{AC}{BC}$.

negatives.text: In triangle $ABC$, point $M$ is the midpoint of side $BC$, and point $N$ lies on side $AB$ such that $AN = 2NB$. Given that $\angle CAB = \angle CMN$, determine the value of the ratio $\frac{AC}{BC}$.

In triangle $ABC$, point $M$ is the midpoint of side $BC$, and point $N$ lies on side $AB$ such that $NB = 2AN$. Given that $\angle CAB = \angle CMB$, determine the value of the ratio $\frac{AC}{BC}$.

In triangle $ABC$, point $M$ is the midpoint of side $BC$, and point $N$ lies on side $AB$ such that $NB = 2AN$. Given that $\angle CBA = \angle CMN$, determine the value of the ratio $\frac{AC}{BC}$.

positive_text:
A rule $f$ turns real numbers into real numbers. For any real numbers $x$ and $y$, it always satisfies the rule
$$
 f(x + 2xy) = f(x) + 2f(xy).
$$
